items.title: Households with home internet access, 2000–2020
items.prompt: The line graph below shows the percentage of households with internet access at home in four countries between 2000 and 2020. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

modelAnswer.text:
The line graph tracks the percentage of households with home internet access in Canada, Poland, Brazil and India between 2000 and 2020.

The most striking feature is the universal upward trend: all four countries recorded substantial growth, and the initially wide disparities between them had narrowed considerably by 2020. Canada had the highest rate of access at every point, while India remained at the bottom throughout.

At the start of the period, Canada was already well ahead, with 42% of households connected, compared with a mere 8% in Poland, 4% in Brazil and just 1% in India. Canadian access then rose steadily but at a diminishing rate, reaching 83% in 2012 and levelling off at 94% by 2020. Poland's trajectory was far steeper: its figure increased more than eightfold to 70% by 2012 and ultimately stood at 90%, almost matching Canada's.

Brazil and India followed a similar path, albeit from a lower base. Brazilian access climbed consistently to 58% in 2016 and 71% in 2020. India, meanwhile, made little progress in the first eight years, reaching only 6% in 2008, but its growth accelerated sharply thereafter, with the figure more than tripling between 2012 and 2020 to 52%.

items.title: Electricity generation by source, 1990–2025
items.prompt: The graph below shows the amount of electricity generated from three sources in one country between 1990 and 2025. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

modelAnswer.text:
The graph compares electricity output from coal, natural gas and renewable sources in one country across a 35-year period from 1990 to 2025.

Overall, the data reveal a fundamental shift in the country's energy supply. Coal, initially by far the largest source, declined steeply after 2000, whereas renewables, which were almost insignificant in 1990, became the leading source by 2020. Natural gas occupied a middle position, rising to a peak before tapering off.

In 1990, coal accounted for 210 TWh, dwarfing the output of natural gas (20 TWh) and renewables (8 TWh). Coal-fired generation edged up to a high of 232 TWh in 2000 but then went into sustained decline, falling to 130 TWh in 2015 and to a mere 35 TWh by 2025, around one sixth of its 1990 level.

Natural gas, meanwhile, expanded seven-fold to 140 TWh in 2010 and briefly overtook coal in 2015, before slipping back to 105 TWh. The most spectacular growth, however, was in renewables. After modest gains to 25 TWh in 2005, output surged, outstripping both gas and coal by 2020 at 140 TWh and reaching 190 TWh in 2025.

items.title: International student enrolments, 2005–2023
items.prompt: The line graph below shows the number of international students enrolled at universities in three countries from 2005 to 2023. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

modelAnswer.text:
The line graph charts the number of international students enrolled at universities in three countries (A, B and C) at three-year intervals between 2005 and 2023.

In general, all three countries ended the period with more overseas students than at the start, despite a simultaneous downturn in 2020. Country A was consistently the most popular destination, while Country C registered the most remarkable growth, eventually overtaking Country B by a wide margin.

Enrolments in Country A rose uninterrupted from 180,000 in 2005 to 340,000 in 2017. Although numbers fell back to 300,000 in 2020, they rebounded sharply to 385,000 in 2023, the highest figure on the graph.

Country B's enrolments, in contrast, were remarkably stable, fluctuating narrowly between 115,000 and 140,000 for most of the period. After slipping to a low of 110,000 in 2020, they recovered to 150,000 by 2023. Country C, meanwhile, grew from just 30,000 students in 2005 to 140,000 in 2014, at which point it surpassed Country B. Its upward trajectory was only briefly interrupted in 2020, and by 2023 it had reached 240,000, an eightfold increase over the period.

items.title: Average daily passengers by transport mode, 2010–2022
items.prompt: The graph below shows the average number of passengers using three types of public transport per day in a European city between 2010 and 2022. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

chart.title: Average daily passengers by transport mode, 2010–2022

modelAnswer.text:
The graph illustrates how many passengers, on average, used the bus, metro and tram networks each day in a European city over a twelve-year period beginning in 2010.

The metro was consistently the busiest mode of public transport, and both it and the tram became more heavily used over time, whereas bus travel gradually lost popularity. A further notable feature is the abrupt slump in all three services in 2020, from which they had mostly recovered by 2022.

At the outset, the metro carried 610,000 passengers daily, ahead of the bus with 520,000, while the tram lagged far behind at 90,000. Between 2010 and 2018, the metro gained steadily, peaking at 820,000, and tram use rose to 210,000, more than twice its initial level. Bus journeys moved in the opposite direction, easing down to 430,000.

In 2020, passenger numbers plummeted across the board, with the metro falling to 470,000, the bus to 260,000 and the tram to 130,000. The subsequent rebound was strong but uneven: by 2022 the metro had almost returned to its peak at 790,000, and the tram actually hit a new high of 225,000, yet bus usage, at 380,000, remained well below its 2010 figure.

items.title: Unemployment rate by age group, 2008–2020
items.prompt: The line graph below shows unemployment rates among three age groups in a European country between 2008 and 2020. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

modelAnswer.text:
The line graph compares unemployment rates across three age brackets, 16-24, 25-49 and 50-64, in a European country from 2008 to 2020.

What stands out most is that the youngest workers consistently faced the highest unemployment, with a rate at least double that of either older group throughout. In addition, the three lines moved broadly in tandem, climbing to a peak in 2012, easing until 2018 and then rising once more by 2020.

Among 16 to 24-year-olds, the rate nearly doubled from 12.5% in 2008 to 24.5% in 2012, the highest figure on the graph. A sustained recovery then brought it down to 11.0% by 2018, only for it to rebound to 17.5% in 2020, the sharpest late increase of any group.

The two older cohorts showed far more modest fluctuations. Unemployment among 25 to 49-year-olds rose from 5.0% to 9.0% by 2012, fell to a low of 4.0% in 2018 and edged up to 6.0% in 2020. The 50-64 group started lowest, at 3.5%, and peaked at 7.5% in 2012; however, because its rate fell more gradually, it briefly exceeded that of the middle group in 2016 and 2018.

items.title: World fish production by method, 1980–2020
items.prompt: The graph below shows world fish production from wild capture and from aquaculture (fish farming) between 1980 and 2020. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

modelAnswer.text:
The graph depicts the quantity of fish produced worldwide through wild capture and aquaculture, measured in million tonnes, from 1980 to 2020.

Overall, while wild capture accounted for the greater share of production throughout, it plateaued from around 2000 onwards. Aquaculture, by contrast, expanded relentlessly and by 2020 had almost drawn level with the traditional method.

In 1980, the wild catch totalled 68 million tonnes, dwarfing the mere 5 million tonnes supplied by fish farming. Over the next twenty years, wild capture grew steadily, peaking at 94 million tonnes in 2000. Thereafter, it stagnated, hovering within a narrow band of 89 to 92 million tonnes and finishing the period at 90 million tonnes.

Aquaculture followed a markedly different path. Its output rose modestly at first, to 13 million tonnes in 1990, before gathering pace and reaching 32 million tonnes in 2000. Growth accelerated further in the following two decades, with production jumping from 44 to 76 million tonnes between 2005 and 2015. By 2020, fish farms were generating 88 million tonnes, over seventeen times their 1980 level and only marginally below the volume of wild-caught fish.

items.title: Population aged 65+ (% of total), 1960–2040
items.prompt: The graph below shows the proportion of the population aged 65 and over in four countries between 1960 and 2020, with projections to 2040. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

modelAnswer.text:
The graph presents the percentage of the population aged 65 and over in Japan, Italy, the USA and Mexico from 1960 to 2020, as well as projected figures up to 2040.

Overall, all four populations have been ageing and are projected to continue doing so. The most notable development is Japan's rapid transformation from a relatively young society into the oldest of the four, whereas Mexico has consistently had the smallest proportion of older people.

In 1960, Italy and the USA had similar shares of over-65s, at 9.3% and 9.2% respectively, while the figures for Japan and Mexico were considerably lower, at 5.7% and 3.4%. Italy's proportion increased steadily, reaching 20.3% in 2010. Japan's, however, accelerated sharply from the 1980s onwards, surpassing Italy's by 2010 at 23.0%. items.title: Electricity demand over 24 hours: winter vs summer
items.prompt: The graph below shows electricity demand in a city on a typical day in winter and a typical day in summer. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

chart.title: Electricity demand over 24 hours: winter vs summer

modelAnswer.text:
The graph illustrates fluctuations in a city's electricity demand, measured in gigawatts, across a typical winter day and a typical summer day.

In general, winter demand was higher than summer demand for almost the entire day. While both followed a broadly similar daily cycle, with a trough in the early hours, the timing of their peaks differed: winter consumption was greatest in the early evening, whereas summer consumption peaked in the afternoon.

In winter, demand began at 32 gigawatts at midnight and fell to a low of 28 gigawatts at 03:00. It then climbed steeply during the morning to 42 gigawatts at 09:00 and held relatively steady at around 40 gigawatts until mid-afternoon. A sharp evening surge followed, taking demand to a daily high of 47 gigawatts at 18:00, before it eased back to 33 gigawatts by the end of the day.

Summer demand was consistently lower overnight, bottoming out at 19 gigawatts at 03:00, some nine gigawatts below the winter figure. From 06:00, however, it rose continuously to reach 43 gigawatts at 15:00, briefly overtaking winter demand. It then declined steadily through the evening, returning to 23 gigawatts at midnight.

items.title: House price index (2000 = 100), 2000–2020
items.prompt: The line graph below shows changes in average house prices in three cities between 2000 and 2020, using 2000 as the base year (index = 100). Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

modelAnswer.text:
The line graph traces movements in average house prices in Cities X, Y and Z over the two decades from 2000, using an index in which the 2000 price level is set at 100.

Overall, prices ended the period higher in all three cities, but the extent of growth varied greatly, with City X far outperforming the others. It is also evident that all three markets suffered a downturn between 2008 and 2012.

City X experienced the most dramatic appreciation. Its index surged to 185 by 2008, and although it slipped to 160 in 2012, the recovery that followed was vigorous, pushing the index to 255 in 2020. In other words, house prices there rose by 155% over the twenty years.

City Y displayed the same general shape on a smaller scale, climbing to 140 in 2008, falling to 115 in 2012 and then recovering to 150. City Z, by contrast, stagnated for much of the period. After edging up to 105 in 2004, its prices dropped below their original level, bottoming out at 80 in 2012, and they did not exceed the base figure again until the final year, when the index stood at 118.

items.title: Monthly visitors to a seaside town, 2010 and 2020
items.prompt: The graph below shows the number of visitors to a seaside town each month in 2010 and 2020. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

chart.title: Monthly visitors to a seaside town, 2010 and 2020

modelAnswer.text:
The graph compares monthly visitor numbers to a seaside town in 2010 and 2020.

In both years, tourism was heavily concentrated in the summer, with August the peak month. The key difference, however, is that the seasonal pattern became much less pronounced over the decade: summer numbers fell substantially, while the quieter months attracted more visitors.

In 2010, the town received between 11,000 and 15,000 visitors a month during the first quarter. Numbers then rose steeply from April, reaching 90,000 in July and a peak of 96,000 in August, roughly nine times the February low. This was followed by an equally steep decline to 24,000 in October and just 13,000 in November.

By 2020, the summer surge had become far more modest. August remained the busiest month, but with only 65,000 visitors, while July saw 60,000, some 30,000 fewer than a decade earlier. Conversely, arrivals outside the peak season were consistently higher. January and February brought in 18,000 and 17,000 visitors respectively, and the figures for October and December, at 35,000 and 28,000, far exceeded their 2010 equivalents. Only in September were the two years broadly similar, at 50,000 and 48,000.

items.title: Cars per 1,000 people, 1970–2020
items.prompt: The graph below shows car ownership per 1,000 people in four countries from 1970 to 2020. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

modelAnswer.text:
The graph charts levels of car ownership, expressed as cars per 1,000 people, in Germany, South Korea, Turkey and the Netherlands between 1970 and 2020.

Overall, car ownership rose substantially in every country. Germany and the Netherlands started from a much higher base and remained ahead throughout, but South Korea closed much of the gap in the later decades, while Turkey's growth, though steady, left it with the lowest rate by some distance.

The two European countries initially had similar levels, with 195 and 180 cars per 1,000 people respectively in 1970, and both rose sharply over the following decade. Thereafter their paths diverged somewhat: ownership in Germany jumped to 515 by 2000 and, after a slight dip in 2010, reached 580 in 2020, whereas the Netherlands experienced slower growth, finishing on 490.

In 1970, by contrast, cars were a rarity in South Korea and Turkey, with just 2 and 3 per 1,000 people. Turkey held a slight lead until 1980, but South Korea subsequently surged ahead, with ownership rising more than sevenfold between 1990 and 2020 to 375. Turkey's figure climbed far more gradually, reaching 165 by the end of the period.

items.title: Library loans by format, 2012–2024
items.prompt: The graph below shows the number of items borrowed from public libraries in a town in three different formats between 2012 and 2024. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

modelAnswer.text:
The graph compares the number of items borrowed from a town's public libraries in print, e-book and audiobook formats over the period 2012 to 2024.

Overall, printed books, though still the most popular format at the end of the period, saw a marked decline in borrowing, while digital and audio formats grew strongly. The most abrupt change occurred in 2020, when print loans slumped and e-book loans surged.

Printed book loans fell steadily from 480,000 in 2012 to 380,000 in 2018, before plunging to 250,000 in 2020. Although they partially recovered to 300,000 in 2022, they had eased back to 290,000 by 2024, around 40% below their initial level.

E-books, which accounted for a mere 15,000 loans in 2012, overtook audiobooks within two years and increased steadily to 110,000 by 2018. Their number then almost doubled to 205,000 in 2020, bringing them within reach of printed books, and despite a minor dip, reached 215,000 in 2024. Audiobooks followed a slower but more consistent upward path. After remaining at around 30,000 for the first two years, their loans rose uninterruptedly to 160,000 by the final year, over five times the 2012 figure.

items.title: Adult smoking rates by sex, 1975–2020
items.prompt: The graph below shows the percentage of adult men and women who smoked cigarettes in one country between 1975 and 2020. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

modelAnswer.text:
The graph tracks the percentage of adult men and women who smoked cigarettes in one country at five-year intervals between 1975 and 2020.

Overall, smoking became much less common among both men and women over the period. Although men smoked at a higher rate throughout, the gender gap narrowed dramatically, largely because the male rate fell continuously while the female rate initially rose.

In 1975, more than half of adult men smoked (52%), almost double the proportion of women (28%). Male smoking then declined without interruption, at a fairly steady pace, so that by 2000 it had fallen to 30%, and by 2020 it stood at just 15%, less than a third of its original level.

The trend among women was less straightforward. Their smoking rate climbed during the first decade, peaking at 33% in 1985, when it was just 8 points below the male figure. It then entered a gradual decline, falling only modestly to 27% by 2000, before dropping more rapidly to 12% in 2020. As a result, the difference between the sexes shrank from 24 percentage points at the start of the period to a mere 3 points at the end.

items.title: Global water use by sector, 1900–2000
items.prompt: The graph below shows global water use by three sectors between 1900 and 2000. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

modelAnswer.text:
The graph illustrates global water consumption, in cubic kilometres per year, by agriculture, industry and households between 1900 and 2000.

Overall, water use rose across all three sectors, with growth becoming markedly steeper from the middle of the century. Agriculture was consistently the dominant consumer, using more water than the other two sectors combined at every point, whereas domestic use remained the smallest.

At the start of the century, agriculture already accounted for 500 km³, compared with 40 km³ for industry and a mere 20 km³ for domestic use. Agricultural consumption grew gradually to 900 km³ by 1940, after which it soared, reaching 1,450 km³ in 1960 and 2,800 km³ in 2000.

Industrial use showed a similar acceleration after 1940, increasing sixfold from 120 km³ to 720 km³ between 1940 and 1980. Unlike the other sectors, however, it then levelled off, edging up to only 790 km³ by the end of the century. Domestic consumption, meanwhile, increased more steadily, although it too gathered pace in the second half of the period, more than doubling between 1960 and 1980 and rising to 400 km³ in 2000, twenty times its 1900 level.

items.title: New car sales by fuel type, 2014–2024
items.prompt: The graph below shows annual sales of new cars by fuel type in one country between 2014 and 2024. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

chart.title: New car sales by fuel type, 2014–2024

modelAnswer.text:
The graph illustrates how sales of new cars in one country were divided between petrol, diesel, electric and hybrid models over the decade from 2014 to 2024.

Overall, the market underwent a significant transformation. Diesel sales collapsed and petrol sales, after an initial rise, also contracted, although petrol remained the best-selling fuel type. Meanwhile, electric and hybrid cars rose from near-insignificance to become major players.

In 2014, petrol and diesel cars were almost equally popular, selling 1,150,000 and 1,100,000 units respectively. Their paths soon diverged, however. Petrol sales climbed to a high of 1,300,000 in 2018 before falling to 700,000 by 2024, whereas diesel sales plummeted from 2016 onwards, reaching just 90,000 in 2024, less than a tenth of their original level.

Electric and hybrid vehicles, by contrast, sold only 5,000 and 30,000 units respectively in 2014, and growth remained modest until 2018. From then on, both expanded rapidly. Hybrids reached 320,000 in 2022, overtaking diesel, and continued rising to 410,000. Electric car sales were even more spectacular, surging to 480,000 in 2024 and thereby overtaking hybrids to become the second most popular category.

items.title: Birth rate (births per 1,000 people), 1950–2020
items.prompt: The graph below shows birth rates in three countries between 1950 and 2020. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

modelAnswer.text:
The graph compares birth rates, expressed as births per 1,000 people, in Countries P, Q and R between 1950 and 2020.

The overall trend was one of decline in all three countries, although the pace and timing varied. Country P consistently had the highest birth rate, whereas Country R, having started well above Country Q, underwent such a steep fall that it ended the period with the lowest rate.

Countries P and R initially followed a similar pattern, with their birth rates rising slightly between 1950 and 1960, to 45 and 38 respectively. Thereafter, both declined, but at very different speeds. Country R's rate plunged to 20 by 1980, and it continued to edge downwards, eventually reaching 9 in 2020, a quarter of its 1950 figure. Country P, meanwhile, experienced a more gradual but uninterrupted decrease from 1960, falling to 28 in 1990 and 15 in 2020, one third of its peak.

Country Q, by contrast, had a comparatively low birth rate from the outset, at 22 in 1950. It declined moderately to 14 by 1980 and then remained almost flat, fluctuating between 12 and 13 for three decades before dipping to 11, just above Country R's figure.

items.title: International visitor arrivals, 2015–2023
items.prompt: The line graph below shows the number of overseas visitors to three countries between 2015 and 2023. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

modelAnswer.text:
The graph presents annual international visitor arrivals in Spain, Thailand and Mexico between 2015 and 2023.

The three countries followed a broadly similar trajectory, with steady growth to 2019, a sudden collapse in 2020 and a subsequent recovery. However, the scale of both the downturn and the rebound differed markedly: Spain regained and slightly exceeded its former level, whereas Thailand was still well short of it in 2023.

Spain was consistently the leading destination apart from the disrupted years. Its arrivals climbed from 68 million in 2015 to 84 million in 2019, while Mexico and Thailand, both starting at around 30 million, reached 45 million and 40 million respectively.

The drop in 2020 was severe for Spain and Thailand, whose figures plummeted to 19 million and 7 million. Mexico proved far more resilient, falling only to 24 million and, in 2021, briefly overtaking Spain with 32 million arrivals against 31 million. Thailand, meanwhile, sank further to a negligible 0.4 million that year. The recovery thereafter was rapid for Spain, which reached a peak of 85 million by 2023, and fairly solid for Mexico, at 42 million, but Thailand's 28 million remained around 70% of its 2019 total.

items.title: Recycling rates by material, 2000–2020
items.prompt: The graph below shows the recycling rates of four types of material in a city between 2000 and 2020. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

modelAnswer.text:
The graph compares the percentage of paper, glass, aluminium cans and plastic recycled in a city at five-year intervals between 2000 and 2020.

Overall, recycling rates improved for all four materials over the two decades. Paper was recycled most extensively throughout, while plastic lagged well behind the others, although it recorded the largest relative increase.

Paper began the period with a recycling rate of 45%, which rose quickly to 66% in 2010 and then more slowly to 72% in 2020. Glass showed a comparable but steeper trajectory, more than doubling from 30% to 68%, so that by the end of the period it had almost caught up with paper.

Aluminium cans registered the sharpest gains in the first decade, with their recycling rate soaring from 20% to 52%. Growth then slowed, and after peaking at 60% in 2015 the rate dipped marginally to 58%, the only decline shown on the graph. Plastic, by contrast, started from a strikingly low base of just 3%. Its rate rose gradually but consistently, reaching 30% in 2020; while this represented a tenfold increase, it was still only around half the rate for aluminium cans, the next lowest material.

items.title: Average one-way commute time, 2004–2024
items.prompt: The graph below shows the average one-way commuting time in four cities between 2004 and 2024. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

modelAnswer.text:
The graph compares the average length of a one-way commute in Cities A, B, C and D over the twenty years from 2004 to 2024.

Overall, the cities followed different long-term trends: commuting times lengthened considerably in City A and City C, contracted in City D and changed little in City B. All four, however, saw a temporary reduction in 2020, and City A ended the period with the longest commute.

In 2004, commuters in City D faced the longest journeys, at 45 minutes, whereas those in City C had the shortest, at just 22 minutes. Over the following twelve years, City A's average rose steadily from 38 to a peak of 52 minutes, and City C's climbed even more steeply to 40 minutes. City D moved in the opposite direction, falling to 37 minutes, so that by 2016 it had been overtaken by both. City B, meanwhile, remained remarkably consistent at around half an hour.

In 2020, times dropped across the board, most noticeably in City A, where they fell by 11 minutes to 41. The subsequent rebound left City A on 49 minutes and City C on 44, twice its initial figure, while City B returned to 31 minutes and City D edged up to 33.

items.title: Telephone subscriptions per 100 people, 1995–2025
items.prompt: The graph below shows the number of mobile phone and landline telephone subscriptions per 100 people in one country from 1995 to 2025. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

modelAnswer.text:
The graph tracks mobile phone and landline subscriptions per 100 people in one country between 1995 and 2025.

The two forms of telephone service moved in opposite directions. Mobile subscriptions expanded rapidly, overtaking landlines in the early 2000s and eventually exceeding the size of the population, whereas landline subscriptions, after peaking in 2000, fell steadily for the remainder of the period.

At the beginning of the period, landlines were far more widespread, with 48 subscriptions per 100 people against a mere 6 for mobiles. Landline numbers rose marginally to 52 in 2000 but declined thereafter, gradually at first and then more sharply, dropping to 33 in 2015 and to just 17 by 2025, less than a third of their peak.

Mobile subscriptions, by contrast, soared in the first decade, climbing to 38 in 2000 and then to 82 in 2005, by which point they had clearly surpassed landlines. Growth continued strongly until 2010, when the figure reached 110, meaning subscriptions outnumbered people. From then on, growth slowed markedly, with the rate increasing only modestly to 124 in 2015 and 131 in 2025.

items.title: Students by subject area and sex, 2023
items.prompt: The bar chart below shows the percentage of male and female students enrolled in five subject areas at a university in 2023. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

chart.title: Students by subject area and sex, 2023

modelAnswer.text:
The bar chart illustrates how male and female students were distributed across five fields of study at a particular university in 2023.

It is immediately apparent that the gender balance varied considerably by subject. Men formed the majority in only two areas, Engineering and Business, while women predominated in the other three. The disparity was most pronounced in Engineering and least marked in Medicine.

Engineering stood out as an overwhelmingly male field: 78% of its students were men, more than three and a half times the proportion of women (22%). Business also had a male majority, but a modest one, at 55% against 45%.

Female students, by contrast, clearly dominated Education, where they accounted for almost three-quarters of enrolments (74%), leaving men with just 26%. Arts followed a similar though less extreme pattern, with women comprising 62% of the cohort and men 38%. Medicine came closest to parity; female students held only a slight edge there, making up 56% of the total compared with 44% for their male counterparts. Engineering and Education therefore represented opposite extremes in terms of gender composition.

items.title: Average weekly household spending, 1990–2020
items.prompt: The chart below shows average weekly household spending on five categories in one country in 1990, 2005 and 2020. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

modelAnswer.text:
The chart compares the average weekly sums spent by households in one country on housing, food, transport, leisure and clothing at three points between 1990 and 2020.

The most notable feature is the sharp and sustained rise in housing costs, which were consistently the largest outlay and grew far faster than any other item. Expenditure on food, transport and leisure also increased steadily, whereas clothing was the sole category to decline.

In 1990, households spent $95 a week on housing, only marginally more than the $80 devoted to food. Over the following three decades, however, the two diverged markedly: housing costs rose to $150 in 2005 and $240 in 2020, an increase of $145, while spending on food edged up to just $110. By the end of the period, therefore, households were spending more than twice as much on housing as on food.

Transport and leisure registered comparable growth. Transport spending almost doubled from $55 to $105, bringing it close to the level of food, and leisure spending more than doubled, climbing from $40 to $90. Clothing, by contrast, barely changed, increasing slightly to $38 in 2005 before slipping to $30 in 2020, the lowest figure recorded for any category.

items.title: Adult participation in sports and exercise, 2008 and 2023
items.prompt: The bar chart below shows the percentage of adults in one country who took part in six sports and exercise activities in 2008 and 2023. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

chart.title: Adult participation in sports and exercise, 2008 and 2023

modelAnswer.text:
The bar chart shows what percentage of adults in one country engaged in six forms of sport and exercise at least monthly, comparing 2008 with 2023.

The period saw a clear shift in preferences: gym-based exercise replaced swimming at the top of the ranking, and running and yoga also gained substantially in popularity. Swimming and football, on the other hand, lost ground, while cycling held steady.

Swimming was the most widely practised activity in 2008, with 21% of adults taking part, but by 2023 this had fallen to 13%. Over the same period, gym participation rose from 14% to 24%, making it comfortably the most common activity by the end of the period.

Among the remaining activities, the growth in running was particularly striking, with the proportion of participants nearly doubling from 9% to 17%. Yoga saw the sharpest relative increase of all, more than tripling from a mere 3% to 11%. By contrast, football declined modestly from 10% to 7%, and cycling was virtually unchanged, edging up by a single percentage point to 12%.

items.title: Main method of travel to work in four cities
items.prompt: The chart below shows the main methods of travelling to work used by residents of four cities. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

chart.title: Main method of travel to work in four cities

modelAnswer.text:
The chart illustrates how commuters in four cities, Northport, Kelby, Arden and Southam, chose to travel to work, broken down into four modes of transport.

What stands out is that each city had a distinctive commuting profile. Cars were the principal means of travel in Northport and Arden, but public transport led in Kelby and cycling in Southam. Walking, meanwhile, played a relatively small role in all four cities.

Northport was by far the most car-dependent city, with 62% of its workers driving, roughly three times the proportion using public transport (20%). Cycling was almost negligible there, at just 6%. Arden also favoured the car, though less heavily, at 45%, and it had a more even spread across the other modes, with 25% using public transport and 20% cycling.

Kelby and Southam presented a sharp contrast. In Kelby, public transport was the choice of 48% of commuters, well ahead of the car at 30%, while in Southam cycling accounted for 45%, making driving (18%) a relatively minor option. Walking figures were broadly similar throughout, ranging from 10% in Kelby and Arden to 15% in Southam.

items.title: Renewable electricity generation, 2022
items.prompt: The bar chart below shows the amount of electricity generated from renewable sources in six countries in 2022. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

modelAnswer.text:
The bar chart provides a breakdown of renewable electricity generation in six countries in 2022, distinguishing between hydro, wind and solar power.

The most striking feature is the dominance of Country A, whose hydroelectric output alone exceeded the total renewable generation of any other country. Beyond this, the countries fall into three pairs according to their principal source: hydro in A and E, wind in B and D, and solar in C and F.

Country A generated 380 TWh from hydro, supplemented by a relatively modest 70 TWh from wind and 40 TWh from solar. Country E shared this reliance on hydro, producing 140 TWh, but its wind and solar output was minimal, at 15 TWh and a mere 5 TWh.

Wind was the leading source in Countries B and D, which generated 120 TWh and 110 TWh respectively. However, Country B had a far more balanced mix, with substantial hydro output (95 TWh), whereas Country D relied on hydro for only 20 TWh. Solar power, meanwhile, was most significant in Country C, reaching 90 TWh, the highest solar figure among the six countries, and in Country F, where it produced 60 TWh. Country F also recorded the lowest hydro figure overall, just 8 TWh.

items.title: Employment by sector, 2022
items.prompt: The chart below shows the proportion of workers employed in agriculture, industry and services in four countries in 2022. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

modelAnswer.text:
The chart compares the distribution of employment across agriculture, industry and services in Vietnam, Mexico, Poland and Canada in 2022.

In every country, services provided the largest share of jobs, but the extent of this varied markedly. Vietnam stood apart as the only country with a substantial agricultural workforce and a roughly even three-way split, whereas Canada's economy was overwhelmingly service-based.

Vietnam's workers were distributed almost equally between the three sectors: 37% were in services, 33% in agriculture and 30% in industry. Its agricultural share was nearly three times that of Mexico and more than sixteen times that of Canada.

Mexico and Poland occupied the middle ground, with services employing around three-fifths of workers in each (62% and 60% respectively). The two differed mainly in the balance between the other sectors: Poland had the largest industrial workforce of the four countries, at 32%, and only 8% in agriculture, while Mexico's figures were 26% and 12%.

At the other extreme, Canada had 79% of its workforce in services, the highest proportion shown, leaving just 19% in industry and a negligible 2% in agriculture.

items.title: Average graduate salaries by field
items.prompt: The bar chart below shows the average annual salaries of university graduates in six fields one year and five years after graduation. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

modelAnswer.text:
The chart shows the average annual salaries earned by graduates in six disciplines at two points in their careers: one year and five years after graduating.

All six groups saw their earnings rise over the four-year interval, but the scale of the increase varied widely. Computing graduates were the best paid at both stages, while those who had studied fine art consistently earned the least. Law stood out for the speed of its salary growth.

One year after graduation, computing ($48,000) and engineering ($45,000) led the way, with nursing, law and teaching clustered in the thirties ($38,000, $36,000 and $33,000 respectively). Fine art trailed well behind at $22,000.

By the five-year point, the gap between the higher- and lower-paid fields had widened considerably. Computing salaries had climbed to $78,000, and law graduates, whose pay nearly doubled to $70,000, had overtaken engineers, who were earning $66,000. In contrast, the gains for nursing and teaching were comparatively modest, at $9,000 each, bringing their averages to $47,000 and $42,000. Fine art graduates remained at the bottom of the scale, earning $30,000, less than 40% of the figure for computing.

items.title: Visitors to city attractions, 2010 and 2020
items.prompt: The chart below shows the number of visitors to five tourist attractions in a city in 2010 and 2020. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

modelAnswer.text:
The chart illustrates visitor numbers at five of a city's tourist attractions in 2010 and 2020.

Over the ten-year period, the popularity of the attractions shifted noticeably. The science museum overtook the castle to become the most visited site and the aquarium suffered a steep decline, whereas the botanic gardens and the art gallery both gained visitors.

The castle attracted 640,000 visitors in 2010, the highest figure for either year, but this dropped by 120,000 to 520,000 in 2020. Over the same period, the science museum enjoyed the largest increase of any attraction, with visitor numbers climbing by 180,000, from 410,000 to 590,000, which made it the clear leader by the end of the decade.

The aquarium's decline was even more pronounced than the castle's. Its visitor numbers fell from 350,000 to just 150,000, less than half the original figure, leaving it with the smallest audience of all five attractions by 2020. By contrast, the art gallery grew from 190,000 to 260,000, while the botanic gardens remained relatively stable, rising marginally from 280,000 to 300,000, and consequently moved above the aquarium in the rankings.

items.title: CO₂ emissions per person, 1990 and 2020
items.prompt: The bar chart below shows carbon dioxide emissions per person in eight countries in 1990 and 2020. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

modelAnswer.text:
The bar chart compares per capita carbon dioxide emissions in eight countries in 1990 and 2020.

The chart reveals a clear divergence between two groups of countries. The four highest emitters of 1990, the USA, Australia, Germany and the UK, all cut their emissions per person over the thirty years, whereas China, Brazil and India recorded increases. China's growth was by far the most dramatic.

In 1990, emissions were highest in the USA, at 19.4 tonnes per person, and Australia, at 16.2 tonnes. Although both figures had fallen by 2020, the reduction was far greater in the USA (to 14.2 tonnes) than in Australia (to 15.0 tonnes), so Australia ended the period with the highest per capita output. Germany and the UK achieved the steepest cuts: Germany's figure fell from 12.8 to 7.7 tonnes, and the UK's roughly halved, from 10.0 to 4.9 tonnes.

China, by contrast, saw its emissions per person almost quadruple, rising from 2.0 to 7.6 tonnes and very nearly drawing level with Germany. Increases in Brazil (1.5 to 2.1 tonnes) and India (0.7 to 1.7 tonnes) were much smaller in absolute terms, and Nigeria's figure actually fell slightly, from 0.9 to 0.6 tonnes, the lowest on the chart in 2020.

items.title: Weekly online shoppers by age group, 2015 and 2025
items.prompt: The bar chart below shows the percentage of people in five age groups in one country who shopped online at least once a week in 2015 and 2025. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

chart.title: Weekly online shoppers by age group, 2015 and 2025

modelAnswer.text:
The chart shows the percentage of people in five age brackets in one country who shopped online at least once a week in 2015, compared with 2025.

The habit of weekly online shopping spread across every age group over the ten years. The 25–34 group remained the most active throughout, but the gap between younger and older shoppers narrowed considerably, as the steepest proportional rises were among the over-50s.

In 2015, weekly online shopping was concentrated among those aged under 50, with rates ranging from 29% in the 35–49 group to 38% among 25–34-year-olds. The figures for older people were far lower: 16% for the 50–64 group and a mere 5% for those aged 65 and above.

A decade later, the 25–34 group still led, with more than two-thirds (68%) shopping online weekly. The 35–49 age group had more than doubled its rate to 61%, overtaking 16–24-year-olds, whose participation grew by a comparatively modest 21 points to 52%. Meanwhile, the proportion of 50–64-year-olds nearly tripled to 47%, and the over-65s recorded the most remarkable change of all, rising more than sixfold from 5% to 32%.

items.title: Reasons for taking evening courses, by age
items.prompt: The chart below shows the main reasons given by adults of different ages for taking part-time evening courses at a college. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

chart.title: Reasons for taking evening courses, by age

modelAnswer.text:
The chart illustrates the reasons adults in three age brackets gave for attending part-time evening courses at a college.

A clear generational divide is evident. For learners under 50, the main motivations were professional, with career progression and career change dominating, whereas the over-50s were driven predominantly by personal interest and, to a lesser extent, the opportunity to socialise.

Among those under 30, career progression was by far the leading reason, given by 42%, followed by a change of career (26%). The 30–50 age group showed a similar but more evenly balanced profile: career progression (30%) and career change (28%) were almost equally important, and this group was also the most likely to be studying at an employer's request (18%). Personal interest was a secondary motive for both groups, at 15% and 20%, and very few learners in either group mentioned meeting people.

For the over-50s, the picture was reversed. Personal interest accounted for 55% of responses, more than the three work-related reasons combined, and 20% saw the courses as a way to meet people. Career-related reasons, meanwhile, were marginal: only 8% cited career progression, 12% a change of career and 5% an employer requirement.

Among those under 30, career progression was by far the leading reason, given by 42%, followed by a change of career (26%). items.title: Daily domestic water use per person
items.prompt: The bar chart below compares average daily household water use per person for six activities in two countries. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

chart.title: Daily domestic water use per person

modelAnswer.text:
The bar chart compares daily domestic water consumption per person in two countries, broken down into six categories of use.

Residents of Country A used more water than those of Country B in every category, and in most cases around twice as much. Showers and baths were the largest single use in both countries, but the most dramatic disparity concerned gardening, which was a major use of water in Country A yet almost negligible in Country B.

Showering and bathing accounted for 68 litres per person per day in Country A, compared with 30 litres in Country B. A similar ratio applied to toilet use (45 and 22 litres), laundry (32 and 15 litres) and other purposes (12 and 6 litres), all of which were roughly twice as high in Country A.

Garden watering was the notable exception to this pattern. In Country A, it consumed 40 litres per person each day, placing it third among the six activities, whereas the equivalent figure in Country B was a mere 3 litres, the smallest amount on the chart. At the other end of the spectrum, kitchen use and drinking showed the least variation, at 18 litres in Country A and 14 litres in Country B.

items.title: New homes completed by type and region, 2023
items.prompt: The chart below shows the number of new homes completed in four regions of a country in 2023, by type of property. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

chart.title: New homes completed by type and region, 2023

modelAnswer.text:
The chart provides a regional breakdown of new home completions in 2023, distinguishing between four types of property.

The South stood out as by far the most active region, completing almost as many homes as the North and East combined. Apartments were the dominant property type in the South and West, whereas detached houses were most numerous in the North and East. Terraced housing, by contrast, formed the smallest category everywhere.

A total of 55,000 homes were completed in the South, of which 26,000 were apartments, as many as in the other three regions put together. The South also led in detached houses (14,000), semi-detached houses (9,000) and terraced houses (6,000). The West, although it had the lowest overall total at 26,000, followed a broadly similar pattern, with apartments accounting for 12,000 of its new homes.

The North and East each completed 29,000 homes, but their mix was quite different. Detached houses were the largest group in both, at 9,000 and 11,000 respectively, with semi-detached homes close behind (7,000 and 8,000). Apartments were less significant, particularly in the East, where just 6,000 were built, and terraced houses numbered only 5,000 and 4,000.

items.title: National park visitors by season, 2021–2023
items.prompt: The chart below shows the number of visitors to a national park in each season from 2021 to 2023. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

modelAnswer.text:
The chart illustrates seasonal visitor numbers at a national park over three consecutive years, from 2021 to 2023.

Summer was the park's peak season throughout, and winter the quietest. Overall, however, the park became busier over the period, with the most sustained growth occurring in spring and winter, the two seasons that increased year on year.

Summer attracted the largest numbers by a wide margin, rising from 210,000 visitors in 2021 to 260,000 the following year, before easing slightly to 245,000 in 2023; this was the only season to record a fall in the final year. Autumn followed an almost opposite pattern: after a marginal dip from 120,000 to 115,000, it rose sharply to 150,000, its highest level in the period.

Spring, meanwhile, grew steadily from 85,000 to 110,000 and then 140,000, an overall increase of 55,000 that brought it within striking distance of the autumn figure. Although winter remained by far the least popular season, it showed the strongest relative growth, with visitor numbers more than doubling from 30,000 to 70,000 over the two years, via 45,000 in 2022.

items.title: Daily unpaid household work by sex
items.prompt: The bar chart below shows the average time men and women in five countries spent on unpaid household work each day. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

chart.title: Daily unpaid household work by sex

modelAnswer.text:
The bar chart compares the average daily time spent on unpaid domestic work by men and women in five countries.

Women consistently undertook more unpaid household work than men, but the extent of the imbalance differed markedly between countries. It was greatest in Country X and smallest in Country Y, while men's contribution was highest in Countries Z and W.

In Country X, women devoted 290 minutes a day to domestic tasks, almost five hours and the highest figure shown, whereas men spent just 45 minutes, meaning that women did more than six times as much. Country V displayed a similar, if less pronounced, imbalance: women's 240 minutes were exactly three times the 80 minutes recorded for men.

The division of labour was considerably more even elsewhere. Men in Country Z spent 170 minutes on household work, the most for any male group, and those in Country W 150 minutes; women in these countries spent 245 and 225 minutes respectively, a gap of 75 minutes in each case. Country Y had the narrowest difference, just 60 minutes, as women there spent the least time of any female group (170 minutes) and men 110 minutes.

items.title: Life expectancy at birth, 2022
items.prompt: The chart below shows life expectancy at birth for men and women in six countries in 2022. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

modelAnswer.text:
The chart shows the life expectancy at birth of men and women in six countries in 2022.

In all six countries, women could expect to outlive men, typically by five years or so. Life expectancy was highest in Japan and lowest in Kenya for both sexes, while Russia was unusual in having a gender gap roughly twice as large as those elsewhere.

Japan and Spain had the highest figures, with Japanese women expected to live to 87.1 and men to 81.1, and the equivalent Spanish figures only slightly lower, at 85.9 and 80.4. Chile followed, at 82.1 years for women and 77.2 for men. At the other end of the scale, Kenyan men had a life expectancy of just 60.2 years, more than 20 years below that of Japanese men, and Kenyan women 65.4.

The most striking feature, however, was the disparity in Russia. There, women could expect to reach 77.8 years, but men only 67.0, a difference of 10.8 years. In fact, Russian men had a lower life expectancy than men in Egypt (69.5), even though Russian women lived considerably longer than Egyptian women, whose figure was 74.1. Egypt, in turn, had the smallest gender gap on the chart, at 4.6 years.

items.title: Recorded music revenue by format
items.prompt: The chart below shows global revenue from recorded music by format in 2010, 2015, 2020 and 2025. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

modelAnswer.text:
The chart tracks global revenue from four recorded music formats, CD, vinyl, downloads and streaming, at five-yearly intervals from 2010 to 2025.

The period was marked by the spectacular rise of streaming, which went from a negligible source of income to overwhelmingly the largest. Revenue from CDs and downloads contracted sharply, while vinyl, despite remaining a relatively small format, enjoyed sustained growth.

In 2010, CDs were the principal source of revenue, earning $8.4 billion, double the figure for downloads ($4.2 billion). Both formats subsequently declined, though at different rates: CD income fell steadily to $1.1 billion by 2025, whereas downloads held up reasonably well until 2015, at $3.9 billion, before collapsing to $1.2 billion in 2020 and a mere $0.5 billion in 2025.

Streaming revenue, meanwhile, rose from just $0.4 billion in 2010 to $2.9 billion in 2015, and then surged to $13.4 billion in 2020, exceeding all the other formats combined. By 2025 it had reached $20.8 billion, more than fifty times its initial level. Vinyl followed a more modest but equally consistent upward trend, increasing more than tenfold from $0.2 billion to $2.1 billion and eventually outperforming CDs.

chart.title: Teenage ownership of digital devices, 2012 and 2024

modelAnswer.text:
The chart compares the percentage of teenagers aged 13 to 17 in one country who owned each of five digital devices in 2012 and 2024.

The most significant development was the rapid spread of smartphones, which went from being owned by fewer than half of teenagers to near-universal ownership, displacing games consoles as the most common device. Ownership of every other device also grew, with the sole exception of games consoles.

In 2012, games consoles led the way, owned by 70% of teenagers, ahead of laptops at 52% and smartphones at 45%. Twelve years later, smartphone ownership had surged by 51 percentage points to 96%, while laptops saw a more moderate rise to 71%. Games consoles, by contrast, became slightly less widespread, with ownership slipping to 62%, though they remained the third most common device.

Tablets and smartwatches were owned by comparatively few teenagers but recorded notable gains. The proportion with a tablet more than doubled, from under a fifth (18%) to 44%, while smartwatches, which none of the teenagers owned in 2012, had been taken up by 29% by 2024.

items.title: Airport passenger numbers, 2019 and 2023
items.prompt: The chart below shows the number of passengers who used six international airports in 2019 and 2023. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

modelAnswer.text:
The chart compares the number of passengers passing through six international airports in 2019 and 2023.

The six airports were split evenly between those that gained and those that lost passengers over the period. Although Airport A retained its position as the busiest and Airport F remained the quietest, the gaps between several airports narrowed noticeably.

Airport A handled 86 million passengers in 2019, 15 million more than Airport B. By 2023, however, its total had slipped to 79 million, whereas Airport B had grown to 76 million, leaving the two almost level. Airport C suffered the steepest decline of all, from 64 million to 51 million, and was consequently overtaken, albeit narrowly, by Airport D, which rose from 48 million to 52 million.

A similar contrast can be seen between the two smallest airports. Passenger numbers at Airport E fell by more than a quarter, from 35 million to 25 million, whereas Airport F grew by almost a third, from 22 million to 29 million, the largest increase recorded. As a result, Airport F ended the period only 4 million passengers behind Airport E.

items.title: Food spending by income group, 2024
items.prompt: The chart below shows how households in three income groups in one country divided their food spending in 2024. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

modelAnswer.text:
The chart illustrates how food expenditure was distributed across four categories by low-, middle- and high-income households in one country in 2024.

Groceries were the largest component of food spending for every group, but their share fell markedly as income increased. Conversely, the more households earned, the greater the proportion they devoted to restaurant meals and, to a lesser extent, work or school meals, while takeaway spending varied little.

For low-income households, groceries absorbed 72% of the food budget, leaving relatively little for other categories: 14% went on takeaways, 8% on restaurants and 6% on work or school meals. Middle-income households spent a smaller share on groceries (58%) and more than twice as much, proportionally, on restaurants (18%), with takeaways and work or school meals at 16% and 8%.

The contrast was sharpest in the high-income group. Here, groceries accounted for only 41% of food spending, while restaurants made up 32%, four times the share recorded for low-income households. Work or school meals also reached their highest level, at 12%, double the proportion for the lowest income group. Takeaways, by contrast, remained remarkably consistent, representing between 14% and 16% of spending in all three groups.

items.title: Household energy use, 1990
items.prompt: The pie charts below show how energy was used in an average household in one country in 1990 and 2020. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

modelAnswer.text:
The pie charts show how energy consumption in a typical home in one country was divided between five uses in 1990 and 2020.

It is clear that heating living space consumed the largest share of household energy in both years, although its dominance weakened over the period. Meanwhile, appliances rose from a minor category to the second largest, at the expense of every other use.

In 1990, space heating alone absorbed 58% of the energy used in the home, and together with water heating (22%) it accounted for four-fifths of the total. The remaining three uses were comparatively insignificant: appliances took 8%, cooking 7% and lighting a mere 5%.

By 2020, this pattern had shifted considerably. The share devoted to space heating had contracted to 44%, and water heating had slipped to 18%, so the two combined now made up just 62%. Cooking and lighting also edged down, to 6% and 3% respectively. In sharp contrast, the proportion consumed by appliances more than tripled to 29%, overtaking water heating and becoming the only category to expand over the thirty-year period.

items.title: University income, 2005
items.prompt: The charts below show the main sources of income for a university in 2005 and 2025. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

modelAnswer.text:
The two charts compare the proportions of a university's income that came from five different sources in 2005 and 2025.

The most notable development over the twenty years was a reversal in the roles of government funding and student fees: the university shifted from relying chiefly on the state to depending on tuition payments. The three smaller sources, meanwhile, remained broadly stable.

In 2005, government grants were the institution's main source of revenue, supplying 48% of the total, whereas tuition fees contributed 27%. Research contracts made up a further 15%, leaving donations (4%) and miscellaneous income (6%) with only a marginal role.

By 2025, the balance had tipped decisively towards fees. Their share had climbed to 49%, while government grants had shrunk to 21%, a fall of 27 percentage points and considerably less than half their earlier level. In other words, the positions of the two main sources had almost exactly swapped. Research contracts grew modestly to 18%, and donations and other income each edged up by a single point, to 5% and 7% respectively, so these three categories together still generated less than a third of the university's income.

items.title: Men
items.prompt: The pie charts below show the main reasons why male and female employees left their jobs at a large company in 2024. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

modelAnswer.text:
The charts break down the reasons why male and female staff resigned from a large company in 2024.

The most striking contrast is that men left overwhelmingly for pay and promotion, while women's departures were distributed far more evenly across several motives, among which work-life balance and family commitments featured prominently.

For male employees, a better salary elsewhere was by far the leading factor, at 38%, and career progression accounted for a further 24%, meaning that these two reasons together explained 62% of resignations. Work-life balance lagged well behind at 12%, and relocation and retirement were each responsible for 10%, while family reasons were the least cited, at just 6%.

Among female employees, the pattern was much flatter. Work-life balance ranked first with 23%, but it was only marginally ahead of better pay (22%) and family reasons (21%), and career progression was not far behind at 19%. The gender gap was widest for family reasons, which were more than three times as common among women as among men, and for salary, where the male figure was 16 points higher. By contrast, relocation was almost identical for the two groups, at 10% and 9%, and retirement was less common among women (6%).

items.title: Travel to campus, 2000
items.prompt: The charts below show how students at a college travelled to campus in 2000 and 2020. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

modelAnswer.text:
The two charts compare the ways in which students at a college travelled to campus in 2000 and 2020.

The overriding trend is a marked shift away from the car towards more sustainable modes of transport, particularly cycling. As a result, students' choices were considerably more balanced in 2020 than they had been two decades earlier.

In 2000, the car was clearly the preferred option, accounting for 46% of journeys, and when combined with the bus (30%) it covered more than three-quarters of all trips to campus. Walking and cycling were relatively uncommon, at 12% and 8% respectively, and only 4% of students commuted by train.

By 2020, reliance on the car had diminished substantially, with its share falling to 21%, so that the bus, despite a slight dip to 28%, became the leading mode. The most remarkable growth occurred in cycling, which more than tripled to 25% and thus overtook both walking and the car. Rail travel also gained ground, almost trebling from 4% to 11%, while walking increased modestly to 15%. Consequently, no single mode of transport accounted for even a third of journeys by the end of the period.

modelAnswer.text:
The two charts compare the ways in which students at a college travelled to campus in 2000 and 2020.

The overriding trend is a marked shift away from the car towards more sustainable modes of transport, particularly cycling. As a result, students' choices were considerably more balanced in 2020 than they had been two decades earlier.

In 2000, the car was clearly the preferred option, accounting for 46% of journeys, and when combined with the bus (30%) it covered more than three-quarters of all trips to campus. Walking and cycling were relatively uncommon, at 12% and 8% respectively, and only 4% of students commuted by train.

Rail travel also gained ground, almost trebling from 4% to 11%, while walking increased modestly to 15%. Consequently, no single mode of transport accounted for even a third of journeys by the end of the period.

items.title: Country A, 2020
items.prompt: The pie charts below show the age structure of the populations of two countries in 2020. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

modelAnswer.text:
The charts illustrate how the populations of two countries were distributed across five age groups in 2020.

The two countries display almost opposite demographic profiles: Country A's population was heavily weighted towards the young, whereas Country B's was concentrated in the older age brackets.

In Country A, the proportion of the population fell consistently with each successive age group. Children under 15 constituted the largest segment, at 41%, and when the 15–29 group (28%) is added, it becomes clear that over two-thirds of the population were under 30. The share then tapered to 16% for those aged 30–44 and 11% for the 45–64 age group, and people aged 65 and over made up a mere 4%.

Country B, by contrast, had a markedly older population. The largest group was aged 45–64, at 28%, and the over-65s accounted for almost a quarter (24%), a proportion six times higher than in Country A. Those aged 30–44 represented 19%, while the younger groups were comparatively small: 16% were aged 15–29 and only 13% were children, less than a third of the equivalent figure for Country A. In other words, more than half of Country B's population was 45 or older.

items.title: Household spending, 1980
items.prompt: The charts below show the proportion of household spending on different items in one country in 1980 and 2020. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

modelAnswer.text:
The charts illustrate the proportion of household expenditure that went on six categories of goods and services in one country in 1980 and 2020.

The most significant development was a reversal in the relative importance of food and housing: food was the largest expense in 1980, whereas housing had become dominant by 2020. Leisure also gained ground considerably, while clothing became a relatively minor item.

In 1980, food consumed 31% of household budgets, well ahead of housing, which accounted for 19%. Miscellaneous items made up 17%, and the remaining spending was split fairly evenly between transport (13%), clothing (11%) and leisure (9%).

Four decades later, housing costs absorbed a third of all spending (33%), an increase of 14 percentage points, while the share devoted to food had fallen to 14%, less than half its earlier level. Leisure spending doubled to 18%, overtaking both transport and other items, whereas clothing shrank from 11% to just 5%. Transport and other items, by contrast, remained broadly stable, at 15% each, which suggests that the major shifts were concentrated in essentials such as food and shelter, as well as in discretionary leisure spending.

items.prompt: The pie charts below show the sources of electricity generation in one country in 2000, 2012 and 2024. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

modelAnswer.text:
The charts compare the contribution of five energy sources to electricity generation in one country at three points between 2000 and 2024.

Over the period, the country's electricity mix was transformed: coal, initially the dominant source, was largely displaced by wind and solar power, with gas also expanding its share. Nuclear and hydroelectric generation, by contrast, remained fairly constant.

In 2000, coal supplied just over half of all electricity (52%), with gas (20%) and nuclear (18%) making up most of the remainder. Hydro accounted for 8%, and wind and solar generated a negligible 2%.

The following twelve years saw the beginning of a shift. Coal's share contracted to 38%, while gas climbed to 28% and wind and solar more than quadrupled to 9%. This trend accelerated markedly after 2012, so that by 2024 wind and solar had become the largest source, providing 34% of electricity, whereas coal had plummeted to only 12%, a fall of 40 percentage points since 2000. Gas edged up further to 30%, making it the second most important source. Throughout the period, nuclear power declined only slightly, from 18% to 15%, and hydro remained almost unchanged at 8–9%.

items.title: Waste collected, 2005
items.prompt: The charts below show the types of waste collected by a city council in 2005 and 2025. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

modelAnswer.text:
The charts show how the waste collected by a city council was made up in 2005 and 2025, broken down into six categories.

While food and garden waste remained the single largest category throughout, the composition of the waste stream changed notably over the twenty years, most obviously through a doubling of plastics and a marked decline in paper and card.

In 2005, organic material from kitchens and gardens accounted for 34% of the total, followed by paper and card at 24%. Together, these two categories represented well over half of all waste collected. Plastics made up 11%, glass 9% and metals 6%, while unclassified waste constituted the remaining 16%.

By 2025, the share of food and garden waste had eased to 29%, and paper and card had declined more steeply, by 9 percentage points to 15%. Plastics, on the other hand, doubled from 11% to 22%, thereby overtaking paper to share second place with other waste, which had also grown to 22%. Glass and metals, already minor categories, each dipped slightly, to 7% and 5% respectively. Consequently, the gap between the largest and the smaller categories had narrowed considerably by the end of the period.

items.title: Purpose of visit, 2014
items.prompt: The pie charts below show the main reasons international visitors gave for travelling to one country in 2014 and 2024. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

modelAnswer.text:
The charts compare the reasons international visitors gave for coming to a particular country in 2014 and 2024.

Leisure travel dominated in both years and became even more prevalent over the decade, whereas business travel declined dramatically. Educational visits, though still a small category, also grew substantially.

In 2014, holidays were the purpose of 44% of visits, with business trips a clear second at 28%. A further 18% of visitors came to see friends or relatives, while study and other reasons were marginal, at 5% each.

Ten years later, the proportion of holidaymakers had risen to 51%, meaning that just over half of all visitors were tourists. The most striking change, however, was in business travel, whose share was exactly halved to 14%, causing it to slip behind visits to friends and relatives, which rose modestly to 21%. Study, meanwhile, doubled its share to 10%, becoming a considerably more significant motive than before, and the residual category of other reasons remained negligible at 4%. Taken together, these changes indicate that the country's visitor profile became increasingly centred on personal rather than professional travel.

items.title: University X graduates
items.prompt: The charts below show what graduates from two universities were doing six months after completing their degrees. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

modelAnswer.text:
The charts show the destinations of graduates from University X and University Y six months after graduation.

Although full-time employment was the most frequent outcome for both groups, graduates of University X were markedly more likely to have secured a full-time post, whereas those from University Y were more often engaged in further study or part-time work.

Full-time work accounted for 58% of University X graduates but only 41% of their counterparts at University Y, a gap of 17 percentage points. Conversely, further study was considerably more common among University Y graduates (26%, against 17% for University X), and the same was true of part-time employment, at 19% compared with 12%.

The remaining categories were relatively small for both institutions. Unemployment stood at 6% for University X and slightly higher, at 9%, for University Y, while the proportion engaged in other activities was similar, at 7% and 5% respectively. Taking full-time and part-time work together, 70% of University X graduates were employed in some capacity six months after finishing their degrees, compared with three-fifths of those from University Y, indicating a noticeably stronger employment outcome for the former.

items.title: Sources of river pollution, 2023
items.prompt: The pie chart below shows the main sources of water pollution in a river basin in 2023. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

modelAnswer.text:
The chart breaks down the sources of water pollution in a river basin in 2023 into six categories.

The most notable feature is the dominance of agricultural run-off, which was the largest single contributor. More broadly, pollution was concentrated in three main sources, with agriculture, urban sewage and industry together accounting for roughly four-fifths of the total.

Agricultural run-off was responsible for 37% of the pollution, more than double the share attributable to industrial discharge (18%). Urban sewage ranked second at 26%, so agricultural and domestic sources combined generated almost two-thirds of all contamination entering the river system. Industrial discharge completed the three principal sources, bringing their joint share to 81%.

The three remaining sources were considerably less significant. Run-off from roads accounted for 9%, precisely half the industrial figure, while mining contributed 6% and miscellaneous sources a mere 4%. Collectively, these minor sources made up less than a fifth of the pollution, which is less than the contribution of urban sewage on its own. This distribution suggests that pollution in the basin stemmed overwhelmingly from a small number of large-scale sources rather than being evenly spread.

items.title: Home language, 2005
items.prompt: The pie charts below show the main languages spoken at home by children in a city school district in 2005 and 2025. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

modelAnswer.text:
The charts compare the languages that children in a city school district spoke at home in 2005 and 2025.

Although English-only households remained in the majority throughout, their share contracted markedly over the two decades, while every other language group expanded, pointing to a considerably more multilingual school population by 2025.

In 2005, English was the sole home language for 78% of children. Spanish was by far the most widely spoken alternative, at 9%, whereas Polish and Mandarin were each spoken by just 3% of pupils and Arabic by only 2%. Other languages accounted for the remaining 5%.

Twenty years later, the English-only group had fallen by 17 percentage points to 61%, meaning that the proportion of children speaking another language at home had risen from 22% to 39%. Spanish remained the leading minority language, edging up to 12%. The fastest growth, though, was in Arabic, which tripled to 6%, and Polish, which more than doubled to 7%, overtaking Mandarin in the process. Mandarin itself grew to 5%, and the combined share of other languages almost doubled, reaching 9%.

items.title: Streaming market share, 2019
items.prompt: The charts below show the market share of five video streaming services in one country in 2019 and 2024. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

modelAnswer.text:
The charts show how the market for video streaming in one country was shared among five services in 2019 and 2024.

The market became noticeably more competitive over the five years: Service A retained the largest share but lost much of its dominance, while the smaller providers, especially Services D and E, made substantial gains.

In 2019, Service A was unrivalled, with 52% of the market, more than double the share of its nearest competitor, Service B (21%). Service C held 14%, and Services D and E were marginal players, with 8% and 5% respectively.

By 2024, Service A's share had shrunk to 34%, and although it was still the leader, it no longer accounted for even half of the market. Service B slipped slightly to 19%, whereas Service C edged up to 16%. The most striking gains were made by the two smallest services: Service D more than doubled its share to 17%, overtaking Service C, and Service E nearly trebled its share to 14%. Consequently, the four challengers together held around two-thirds of the market by 2024, compared with less than half five years earlier.

items.title: Council budget, 2010
items.prompt: The pie charts below show how a city council allocated its budget in 2010 and 2025. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

modelAnswer.text:
The charts compare the allocation of a city council's budget across six service areas in 2010 and 2025.

The standout development over the fifteen-year period was the rapid growth of social care, which overtook education to become the largest item of expenditure. This expansion was accompanied by a shrinking share for most other services, nearly all of which received a smaller proportion of the budget by 2025.

In 2010, education absorbed 34% of council spending, comfortably ahead of social care at 22%. Transport accounted for 15%, while housing and administration each took 10%, and parks and culture received the smallest share, at 9%.

By 2025, the share devoted to social care had climbed to 35%, an increase of 13 percentage points, whereas education had slipped to 30%. Transport and administration were both cut back, to 12% and 7% respectively, but the sharpest proportional reduction was in parks and culture, whose share almost halved to just 5%. Housing was the only other area to gain funding, and even then only marginally, rising by a single point to 11%. Taken together, education and social care accounted for almost two-thirds of the budget in 2025, compared with 56% in 2010.
