items.title: Tourist accommodation, 2008
items.prompt: The pie charts below show the types of accommodation used by international tourists in one country in 2008 and 2023. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

modelAnswer.text:
The charts compare the types of accommodation chosen by international tourists in one country in 2008 and 2023.

While hotels remained the most common choice throughout, their lead was greatly reduced by the rapid growth of rented apartments, which had become a serious rival by 2023. All the other forms of accommodation lost a small amount of ground.

In 2008, hotels were used by 55% of international visitors, over three times as many as those staying with friends or relatives (17%). Hostels and campsites were each chosen by a tenth of tourists, and rented apartments were the least popular option, accounting for just 8%.

Fifteen years later, the proportion staying in hotels had declined by 16 percentage points to 39%. Meanwhile, the remaining categories each dipped slightly: staying with friends or relatives fell to 15%, hostels to 8% and campsites to 7%, so campsites went from joint third place to become the least popular type of accommodation.

items.title: Emissions by sector, 1990
items.prompt: The charts below show greenhouse gas emissions by sector in one country in 1990 and 2020. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

modelAnswer.text:
The charts break down one country's greenhouse gas emissions by sector in 1990 and 2020.

The most notable change over the thirty years was that transport replaced energy supply as the principal source of emissions. More generally, the shares attributable to energy supply and industry contracted, while every other sector accounted for a larger proportion by 2020.

In 1990, energy supply was responsible for 36% of emissions, well ahead of industry (22%) and transport (16%). Buildings contributed 14%, and agriculture and waste were comparatively minor sources, at 9% and 3% respectively.

By 2020, the picture had been transformed. The share generated by energy supply had dropped by 15 percentage points to 21%, and industry's contribution had also shrunk, to 17%. Transport, by contrast, rose from 16% to 27%, making it the largest single source of emissions. Buildings and agriculture both gained ground as well, reaching 18% and 13% respectively, so that buildings overtook industry. Waste remained the smallest category, edging up by just one point to 4%. As a result, emissions were spread more evenly across the main sectors at the end of the period than at the beginning.

items.prompt: The pie charts below show the main sources of news used by adults in one country in 2005, 2015 and 2025. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

modelAnswer.text:
The charts compare the main sources from which adults in one country obtained their news at three points between 2005 and 2025.

Over the two decades, there was a pronounced shift from traditional to digital media. Television, newspapers and radio all lost popularity, while social media grew from a negligible share to become the leading source of news.

In 2005, television was clearly dominant, used by 48% of adults, and newspapers were a strong second at 27%. Radio (13%) and news websites (10%) played a smaller role, and social media was used by a mere 2%.

By 2015, the balance was beginning to change. Television's share had eroded to 40%, and newspapers had lost roughly half of their audience share, falling to 14%. At the same time, news websites more than doubled to 22%, and social media drew level with newspapers at 14%. The following decade saw this shift accelerate: social media surged to 36%, eighteen times its 2005 figure, overtaking television, which slipped to 29%. News websites held steady at 21%, whereas newspapers dwindled to just 6%, less than a quarter of their original share, and radio fell to 8%.

items.title: Women's occupations, 1970
items.prompt: The pie charts below show the occupations of working women in one country in 1970 and 2020. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

modelAnswer.text:
The charts illustrate how the occupations of working women in one country changed between 1970 and 2020.

The overall pattern is a marked movement away from clerical and manufacturing work towards higher-level professional and managerial positions, with professional work becoming the most common occupation by 2020. Domestic and care work, by contrast, remained remarkably stable.

In 1970, clerical jobs employed the largest share of working women, at 32%, and manufacturing accounted for a further 21%, so together these two sectors employed more than half of the female workforce. Retail and sales and domestic and care work each represented 17%, whereas professional occupations made up only 10% and managerial roles a mere 3%.

Fifty years later, professional work had risen to 31%, more than three times its earlier level, and the share of women in managerial positions had increased fivefold to 15%. Meanwhile, clerical work had almost halved to 17%, and manufacturing had undergone the steepest decline, shrinking to just 5% of female employment. Retail and sales fell only slightly, to 14%, and domestic and care work edged up by a single point to 18%, making it the second largest category.

items.title: Underground railway systems in six cities
items.prompt: The table below gives information about the underground railway systems in six cities. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

chart.title: Underground railway systems in six cities

modelAnswer.text:
The table provides details of the underground railway networks in six cities, specifically their opening dates, route lengths and annual passenger numbers.

In general, there is a broad correlation between age and scale: the earliest networks are the most extensive and carry the greatest numbers of passengers, whereas those opened more recently are considerably smaller. The one notable exception to this pattern is Port Maren.

The two oldest systems clearly dominate. Riverton's network, opened in 1890, is the longest by a wide margin at 402 km, almost twice the length of Castelle's 225 km. Nevertheless, Castelle, which dates from 1902, is the busiest, handling 1,450 million passengers a year against Riverton's 1,210 million. Norwick (1935) and Ashbury (1967) operate far more modest systems of 118 km and 96 km respectively, with annual ridership of 520 million and 310 million.

Port Maren breaks the trend. Although it did not open until 2001, its network of 184 km is the third longest, and it carries 870 million passengers annually, well ahead of both Norwick and Ashbury. Delmont, by contrast, has the youngest and smallest system: opened in 2014, it covers just 62 km and serves 145 million passengers, exactly a tenth of Castelle's total.

modelAnswer.text:
The table compares the percentage of adults aged 25–34 with a university degree in five countries in 2000, 2010 and 2020.

At the lower end of the table, progress was more uneven. Germany saw only a marginal increase in the first decade, from 22% to 26%, before a more substantial rise to 36%. Italy, meanwhile, remained at the bottom throughout, yet its rate nearly tripled, from 10% to 29%, which represents the largest relative increase of any country.

items.title: Working hours and paid holiday, full-time workers, 2023
items.prompt: The table below shows average weekly working hours and the number of days of paid annual holiday for full-time workers in six countries. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

chart.title: Working hours and paid holiday, full-time workers, 2023

modelAnswer.text:
The table sets out the average weekly working hours of full-time employees in six countries in 2023, alongside the number of days of paid annual leave and public holidays they received.

Longer working weeks generally go hand in hand with less paid leave, whereas the number of public holidays varies within a narrow range and does not follow the same pattern.

Country A offers the most favourable conditions, combining the shortest average week of 36.5 hours with the largest leave entitlement of 30 days. Countries E and C are broadly comparable, with employees working 37.9 and 39.2 hours respectively and receiving 28 and 25 days of paid holiday. When public holidays are included, workers in these three countries enjoy between 36 and 39 days off a year.

The picture is markedly different in Countries D, F and B, where average hours exceed 41. Country D has the longest working week, at 44.6 hours, and just 14 days of annual leave, although its 16 public holidays are the highest figure in the table. Country B stands out for the least generous leave allowance of only 10 days, a third of that in Country A, despite a working week of 41.8 hours, while Country F sits between these extremes at 42.3 hours and 20 days.

items.title: Consumer spending by category, 2022 (% of total)
items.prompt: The table below shows the proportion of total consumer spending on six categories in five countries in 2022. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

chart.title: Consumer spending by category, 2022 (% of total)

modelAnswer.text:
The table breaks down consumer expenditure in five countries in 2022 into six categories, showing each as a proportion of total spending.

It is clear that spending priorities differed considerably between the countries. Leisure and housing generally absorbed the largest shares, while health and education consistently attracted the least, although Country D departed from the general pattern by spending most heavily on food and drink.

Leisure was the single largest category in Countries A, B and E, accounting for 36%, 29% and 28% of expenditure respectively. In Country A, this was three times the share allocated to food and drink, which, at 12%, was the lowest food figure in the table. Country C, by contrast, spent most on housing (31%), with leisure making up a quarter of its total.

Country D presents a notably different profile. Food and drink made up 35% of its spending, well ahead of housing at 22% and leisure at 20%, and it also devoted the highest proportion to education, at 11%. However, it allocated only 3% to health, the smallest share for this category, whereas Country E spent 12%, four times as much. Education was a minor expense elsewhere, falling as low as 2% in Country C.

items.title: Average weekly consumption per person (grams)
items.prompt: The table below shows the average amount of six types of food eaten per person per week in one country in 1980, 2000 and 2020. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

modelAnswer.text:
The table details how much of six different foods the average person in one country consumed each week in 1980, 2000 and 2020, measured in grams.

The data reveal a marked change in diet over the four decades. Consumption of bread, red meat and fish fell consistently, while that of poultry and fresh fruit grew. As a result, by 2020 fresh fruit had overtaken bread as the most widely eaten item, and poultry had edged ahead of red meat.

Bread was by far the most heavily consumed food in 1980, at 950 grams a week, but this figure dropped by more than a third to 610 grams by 2020. Red meat followed a similar downward path, falling from 650 to 410 grams. Fish intake was the most stable of the declining items, easing only slightly from 160 to 135 grams.

Poultry saw the most dramatic growth, more than doubling from 190 to 430 grams. Fresh fruit also became increasingly popular, rising from 540 grams in 1980 to 700 grams in 2000 and 760 grams at the end of the period. Confectionery was the only item to fluctuate, climbing from 120 to 175 grams in 2000 before dipping slightly to 160 grams.

items.title: Top destinations for students studying abroad
items.prompt: The table below shows the five most popular destinations for students from one country who studied abroad in 2012 and 2024. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

chart.title: Top destinations for students studying abroad

modelAnswer.text:
The table presents data on the five leading study-abroad destinations for students from one country, giving both the number of students and each destination's share of the total in 2012 and 2024.

The most notable development is that, while overall numbers rose substantially, the United States lost much of its dominance, with Canada emerging as the fastest-growing destination. As a result, students in 2024 were spread far more evenly across the main countries.

Between the two years, the total number of students studying overseas increased by 16,800, from 56,000 to 72,800. The United States was the only major destination to attract fewer students, as its intake slipped from 21,400 to 18,900, causing its share to shrink from 38% to 26%. The United Kingdom, in second place in both years, gained 3,000 students, reaching 15,300, yet its share remained virtually stable at 21–22%.

Canada's rise was particularly striking: its student numbers grew more than two and a half times, from 5,600 to 14,600, doubling its share to 20% and lifting it above Australia (13,100). Germany, though still the smallest named destination, also more than doubled its intake to 5,800, whereas the figure for other countries edged down from 5,500 to 5,100.

items.title: Access to safe water and sanitation (% of population)
items.prompt: The table below shows the percentage of the population with access to safe drinking water and basic sanitation in five world regions in 2000 and 2020. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

chart.title: Access to safe water and sanitation (% of population)

modelAnswer.text:
The table shows the percentage of the population in five world regions with access to safe drinking water and basic sanitation in 2000 and 2020.

It is evident that provision of both services expanded everywhere over the two decades, but access to sanitation remained lower than access to safe water in every region. Europe enjoyed near-universal coverage throughout, while Sub-Saharan Africa trailed well behind on both measures.

Safe water was already widely available in most regions in 2000, ranging from 80% in South Asia to 98% in Europe. By 2020, these four regions had all reached 92% or more, with Europe at 99%. Sub-Saharan Africa was the clear outlier: less than half its population (46%) had safe water at the start of the period, and although this rose by 19 percentage points, about a third of people still lacked access in 2020.

The gaps in sanitation were far wider. South Asia made the most striking progress, its coverage soaring from 22% to 60%, while East Asia also recorded a substantial rise of 28 points, reaching 83%. Latin America improved from 70% to 87%, and Europe from an already high 92% to 95%. In Sub-Saharan Africa, however, the figure increased only modestly, from 23% to 33%, leaving it the lowest in the table.

items.title: Energy use per person and renewable share, 2023
items.prompt: The table below shows energy consumption per person and the share of energy from renewable sources in six countries in 2023. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

chart.title: Energy use per person and renewable share, 2023

modelAnswer.text:
The table compares six countries in terms of per capita energy consumption in 2023, the share of that energy derived from renewable sources, and the change in this share since 2013.

Two points stand out. First, levels of energy use bear little relation to reliance on renewables: some heavy consumers depend almost entirely on other sources, whereas relatively modest consumers make extensive use of renewable energy. Second, the renewable share rose in every country over the decade, although to very different degrees.

Canada and Saudi Arabia were the heaviest users, consuming 350 GJ and 310 GJ per person respectively, yet their renewable profiles diverged sharply. Canada obtained 29% of its energy from renewable sources, compared with a mere 1% in Saudi Arabia, where the share had grown by only a single point. items.title: Percentage of guests satisfied, by hotel
items.prompt: The table below shows the results of a survey in which guests at three hotels were asked whether they were satisfied with five aspects of their stay. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

chart.title: Percentage of guests satisfied, by hotel

modelAnswer.text:
The table summarises the results of a survey in which guests at Hotel Aurora, Harbour Inn and Parkside Lodge indicated whether they were satisfied with five aspects of their stay.

Overall, satisfaction levels were generally high, but each hotel displayed a distinctive profile of strengths and weaknesses. Hotel Aurora excelled in cleanliness and location, Harbour Inn in value for money and staff, and Parkside Lodge in food, while the single poorest rating was for Parkside's location.

Hotel Aurora achieved the highest figures in the table for room cleanliness (94%) and location (90%), and its staff were also well regarded, with 86% of guests satisfied. Its clear weak point, however, was value for money: only 61% were satisfied, the lowest result in this category and 27 points below Harbour Inn.

Harbour Inn's guests were the most positive about staff friendliness (90%) and value (88%), yet food quality received the lowest rating of the three hotels, at 65%. Parkside Lodge, by contrast, led the way for food, with 84% satisfied, and also scored well for cleanliness (88%). Its staff, though, drew a comparatively modest 72%, and its location was the least popular aspect across all three hotels, satisfying barely more than half of guests (55%).

items.title: Quarterly unit sales, 2024 (thousands)
items.prompt: The table below shows the quarterly sales of four products sold by a company in 2024. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

modelAnswer.text:
The table sets out quarterly sales figures, in thousands of units, for four products sold by a company in 2024, together with their totals for the year.

Overall, the company's combined sales rose in every quarter, surging in the last three months of the year. Product D was the top seller over the year, but the most striking trend was the rapid expansion of Product C, in contrast to the gradual decline of Product B.

Combined sales edged up from 445 thousand in Q1 to 480 thousand in Q3, before leaping by a third to 640 thousand in Q4. Product D accounted for the largest share of annual sales, at 770 thousand units, although its performance was uneven: sales slipped from 200 to 160 thousand between Q1 and Q3 before rebounding to 220 thousand. Product A, meanwhile, grew in each quarter, from 120 to 210 thousand, for a total of 615 thousand.

Product C began the year as the weakest performer, at just 45 thousand, yet its sales rose more than threefold to 140 thousand by Q4, lifting its annual total to 340 thousand. Product B, by contrast, recorded a steady fall from 80 to 70 thousand, leaving it with the lowest total of 303 thousand.

items.title: Population, area and density of six cities
items.prompt: The table below gives information about the population, land area and population density of six major cities. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

chart.title: Population, area and density of six cities

modelAnswer.text:
The table provides data on the population, land area and population density of six large cities.

The most striking feature is the variation in density, which depends as much on land area as on population size. Mumbai is by far the most crowded city despite occupying the smallest area, while Cairo, the largest city by area, is the least densely populated.

Lagos has the largest population, at 15.4 million, and because its area is a relatively compact 1,171 km², it has the second-highest density, at 13,151 people per km². Mumbai, with 12.5 million inhabitants living in just 603 km², is even more densely populated, with 20,730 people per km², more than six times the figure for Cairo.

Tokyo presents a contrasting case. Although its population of 14.0 million is the second largest, it is spread over 2,194 km², giving a moderate density of 6,381. Cairo and Lima, each with around ten million residents, cover the largest areas, at 3,085 km² and 2,672 km², so their densities are the lowest, at 3,306 and 3,743 respectively. Toronto is the smallest city by population, at only 2.8 million, but its limited area of 630 km² results in a density of 4,444, slightly higher than those of Cairo and Lima.

items.title: Households owning selected appliances (%)
items.prompt: The table below shows the percentage of households in one country that owned five household appliances in 1970, 1990, 2010 and 2020. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

modelAnswer.text:
The table charts the percentage of households in one country owning five household appliances in 1970, 1990, 2010 and 2020.

Ownership of every appliance was considerably higher in 2020 than in 1970, with the sharpest growth occurring between 1970 and 2010. By the end of the period, refrigerators, washing machines and microwave ovens were found in almost every home, whereas dishwashers and tumble dryers remained far less widespread.

Refrigerators and washing machines were already fairly common in 1970, owned by 58% and 64% of households respectively. Refrigerator ownership rose to 96% within twenty years and plateaued at 99% from 2010, while washing machines followed a more gradual path to 97%.

The microwave oven underwent the most dramatic transformation, from being absent from homes entirely in 1970 to featuring in almost half (47%) by 1990 and 93% by 2020. Tumble dryers were similarly rare at first, at 1%, and climbed to 57% in 2010, but they were the only appliance to decline thereafter, dipping to 55%. Dishwasher ownership, meanwhile, rose steadily from a mere 3% but still stood at just under half (49%) in the final year.

items.title: Doctors and nurses per 10,000 people
items.prompt: The table below shows the number of doctors and nurses per 10,000 people in six countries in 2010 and 2022. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

modelAnswer.text:
The table presents the number of doctors and nurses per 10,000 people in six countries, comparing figures for 2010 and 2022.

Two features are immediately apparent: nurses outnumbered doctors in every country in both years, and staffing levels improved almost everywhere over the period. There was, however, a striking gap between the best-provided countries, A and E, and the least well-provided, D and F.

Country A had the highest density of both professions, with doctors increasing from 38 to 45 and nurses from 110 to 118. Country E, although slightly behind, recorded the largest absolute gain in nurses, a rise of 25 to reach 104. Country B, by contrast, saw almost no change in its doctor ratio (26 to 28), and it was the only country in which nurse numbers fell, from 85 to 81.

At the lower end, Country C made notable progress, with its doctor ratio climbing from 11 to 19 and its nurse ratio from 25 to 40. Country D more than doubled its nurses from 14 to 30, although it still had only 9 doctors per 10,000 people in 2022. Country F remained far behind the rest, with just 3 doctors and 11 nurses per 10,000 people by the end of the period.

modelAnswer.text:
The table compares the average daily time spent on five forms of media by four age groups in one country in 2024.

The dominant pattern is a sharp contrast between generations: streaming and social media account for most of young people's media time, whereas broadcast TV, radio and print become steadily more important with age. The oldest group spends more time on broadcast TV than any group spends on any other single medium.

The 16–24 age group devotes 185 minutes a day to video streaming and 160 minutes to social media, but only 25 minutes to broadcast TV and a negligible 2 minutes to newspapers. For those aged 25–44, streaming still leads at 120 minutes, but use is more evenly spread across social media (95), radio or podcasts (75) and TV (70).

Among older people, the picture is reversed. Broadcast TV accounts for 155 minutes a day among 45- to 64-year-olds and a remarkable 270 minutes among the over-65s, more than ten times the figure for the youngest group. Radio and podcasts follow the same upward trend, peaking at 110 minutes, as do printed newspapers, which occupy 42 minutes of the oldest group's day. In contrast, streaming and social media fall to just 20 and 15 minutes respectively for this group.

items.title: New titles published by genre
items.prompt: The table below shows the number of new books published in one country in six genres in 2004, 2014 and 2024. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

modelAnswer.text:
The table shows the number of new books published in six genres in one country at ten-year intervals between 2004 and 2024.

The most notable trend is the divergence between genres: fiction, children's books and self-help all expanded markedly, whereas output of science and technology and travel titles contracted. Fiction remained the dominant genre throughout, while self-help recorded by far the fastest growth.

New fiction titles increased by 6,700 over the two decades, from 11,200 to 17,900, consolidating their leading position. Children's books, the second largest category, also rose substantially, from 6,500 to 10,100. Most striking of all, however, was the surge in self-help publishing: from a modest 1,300 titles in 2004, the smallest figure in the table, output climbed to 3,400 in 2014 and 5,800 in 2024, overtaking first biography and then science and technology.

The remaining genres moved in the opposite direction. Science and technology titles fell steadily from 4,800 to 3,900, while travel publishing more than halved, sinking from 2,100 to just 900. Biography was the only genre to fluctuate, edging up from 2,900 to 3,100 before slipping to 2,600, slightly below its starting level.

items.title: Climate data for Port Sella (monthly averages)
items.prompt: The table below shows the average monthly temperature, rainfall and hours of sunshine in one city. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

chart.title: Climate data for Port Sella (monthly averages)

modelAnswer.text:
The table provides monthly averages for temperature, rainfall and daily sunshine in the city of Port Sella.

The data show a pronounced seasonal pattern, with hot, sunny and almost completely dry summers contrasting with mild, wet winters that receive considerably less sunshine. Temperature and sunshine rise and fall together, whereas rainfall follows the reverse pattern.

Temperatures climb gradually from a low of 11°C in January to a peak of 27°C in both July and August, a difference of 16 degrees, before falling back to 12°C in December. Hours of sunshine mirror this trend closely: the city receives only 4.5 hours a day in January and 4.2 in December, but almost three times as much in midsummer, when the figure reaches 11.8 hours in July.

Rainfall, in contrast, is concentrated in the cooler months. December is the wettest month, with 110 mm, and November and January are almost as wet, at 92 mm and 98 mm respectively. Precipitation then declines sharply through spring, to 22 mm in May, and virtually disappears in summer, with July recording just 1 mm. The rains return from September, when 18 mm falls, rising steeply to 58 mm in October.

items.title: Prices of everyday items, 2024 (US$)
items.prompt: The table below shows the prices of six everyday items in five cities in 2024 (in US dollars). Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

modelAnswer.text:
The table shows how much six everyday goods and services cost in five cities in 2024, with all prices given in US dollars.

It is clear that City A was the most expensive of the five cities for nearly every item, whereas City D was consistently the cheapest. Petrol was the only item that did not follow this pattern, being dearest in City E.

The gap between the most and least expensive cities was widest for the monthly transport pass, which cost $132.00 in City A but just $19.00 in City D, roughly a seventh of the price. City C and City E occupied an intermediate position, at $85.00 and $60.00 respectively, while City B's pass was relatively affordable at $28.00. Leisure costs followed a similar pattern: a restaurant meal ranged from $28.00 in City A to $6.50 in City D, and a cinema ticket from $16.00 to $4.00, a fourfold difference.

For everyday purchases, the differences were smaller in absolute terms but still considerable. Coffee cost $5.20 in City A, almost four times the $1.40 charged in City D, and bread $3.90 compared with $0.90. Petrol, however, was priced highest in City E at $2.10 and City C at $1.85, with City A's figure of $1.60 only third highest.

items.title: Attendance at cultural events at least once in 2023 (%)
items.prompt: The table below shows the percentage of people in different age groups who attended four types of cultural event at least once in 2023. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

chart.title: Attendance at cultural events at least once in 2023 (%)

modelAnswer.text:
The table shows the percentage of people in five age brackets who attended a theatre, a cinema, a live music concert or a museum or gallery at least once in 2023.

Age clearly shaped cultural preferences. Cinema-going and concert attendance declined consistently as people got older, whereas the theatre and museums gained in popularity up to the 55–74 group before falling back among the over-75s, who were the least active group overall.

The cinema was the most widely attended event for all groups under 55, drawing 82% of 16- to 24-year-olds, but its appeal diminished steadily with age, to 44% of those aged 55–74 and only 20% of those aged 75 and above. Live music followed an even steeper downward path: while more than half of the youngest group (57%) went to a concert, only 8% of the oldest did so, a seventh of the figure.

Museums and galleries, by contrast, became progressively more popular with age, rising from 34% of the youngest group to 52% of 55- to 74-year-olds, at which point they overtook the cinema as the most popular activity. Theatre attendance doubled over the same age range, from 18% to 36%. Among the over-75s, however, both declined, to 28% and 24% respectively.

items.title: Exports by category (US$ billion)
items.prompt: The table below shows the value of five categories of goods exported by one country in 2010 and 2024. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

modelAnswer.text:
The table compares the value, in billions of US dollars, of five categories of goods exported by one country in 2010 and 2024, alongside the percentage change in each.

Although the country's export earnings rose substantially overall, the categories performed very differently. Machinery replaced vehicles as the leading export, pharmaceuticals grew at a remarkable rate, and textiles and vehicles were the only categories to shrink.

Total exports increased by 27%, from $68.3 billion to $86.6 billion. Machinery expanded by $9.5 billion, or 52%, to reach $27.9 billion. Vehicles, by contrast, had been the most valuable category in 2010, at $22.1 billion, but their value fell by 11% to $19.6 billion, pushing them into second place.

Pharmaceuticals recorded the most spectacular growth, with exports rising by 167%, from $6.3 billion to $16.8 billion. This gain of $10.5 billion, the largest of any category in absolute terms as well, lifted the sector from the smallest category to the third largest. Food products also grew steadily, by 44%, to $14.1 billion. Textiles, however, suffered the sharpest decline, losing almost a third of their value as exports dropped from $11.7 billion to $8.2 billion, leaving them the smallest category by 2024.

items.title: Employment in technology occupations by sex, 2024 (thousands)

chart.title: Employment in technology occupations by sex, 2024 (thousands)

modelAnswer.text:
The table provides a breakdown by sex of employment in five technology occupations in one country in 2024, with figures in thousands, and also indicates the proportion of each workforce made up of women.

Men were in the majority in all five occupations, but the degree of imbalance varied considerably. Women were most poorly represented in software development, IT support and cyber-security, while data analysis and web and UX design came much closer to parity.

Software development was the largest field by a wide margin, employing 412 thousand men, over four times the number of women (98 thousand). Women therefore accounted for just 19% of software developers, the same proportion as among IT support technicians, where 44 thousand women worked alongside 188 thousand men. Cyber-security, the smallest of the five occupations, had the lowest female share of all, at 18%, with only 16 thousand women compared with 73 thousand men.

The two remaining occupations presented a markedly different picture. Web and UX design was the most balanced, with 49 thousand women and 57 thousand men, meaning that women made up 46% of the workforce. Data analysis was only slightly less even, with 71 thousand women and 96 thousand men, giving a female share of 43%.

modelAnswer.text:
The table provides a breakdown by sex of employment in five technology occupations in one country in 2024, with figures in thousands, and also indicates the proportion of each workforce made up of women.

Men were in the majority in all five occupations, but the degree of imbalance varied considerably. Women were most poorly represented in software development, IT support and cyber-security, while data analysis and web and UX design came much closer to parity.

Software development was the largest field by a wide margin, employing 412 thousand men, over four times the number of women (98 thousand). Women therefore accounted for just 19% of software developers, the same proportion as among IT support technicians, where 44 thousand women worked alongside 188 thousand men. Cyber-security, the smallest of the five occupations, had the lowest female share of all, at 18%, with only 16 thousand women compared with 73 thousand men.

The two remaining occupations presented a markedly different picture. Web and UX design was the most balanced, with 49 thousand women and 57 thousand men, meaning that women made up 46% of the workforce. Data analysis was only slightly less even, with 71 thousand women and 96 thousand men, giving a female share of 43%.

items.title: Ashfield, 1995
items.prompt: The maps below show the village of Ashfield in 1995 and at the present time. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

modelAnswer.text:
The maps compare the village of Ashfield in 1995 with its current layout. The most striking development is that the countryside surrounding the village core has been almost entirely built over, turning a rural settlement into a larger residential community with modern amenities, although its basic framework of river, road and church is unchanged.

In 1995, Ashfield consisted of little more than a church and two blocks of houses on the northern side of Main Road, which crossed the village from west to east, with the River Ash flowing along its northern edge. Farmland occupied the north-east and a far larger area to the south-west, a village shop sat just south of the road, and a footpath led southwards, with extensive woodland to its east.

Today, the south-western fields have given way to three housing estates, divided by a newly built road, Ash Lane. In the north-east, a primary school and a playing field now occupy the former farmland. South of Main Road, the shop has been replaced by a considerably larger supermarket with a car park beside it, while the trees have been reduced to a small cluster in the south-eastern corner. Finally, the footpath has been converted into a cycle path, though the section alongside the supermarket no longer exists.

items.title: Brenton town centre, 2000
items.prompt: The maps below show the centre of a small town called Brenton in 2000 and today. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

modelAnswer.text:
The maps illustrate how the centre of Brenton was reorganised between 2000 and the present day. The overriding change is that the central High Street has been closed to traffic, with a new road built in the north, while several facilities have been replaced or relocated.

Several features remain as they were: the town hall on the northern side of the High Street, the two rows of shops flanking it and the block of shops in the south-west. The High Street, however, has been converted into a pedestrian zone, and New Road now crosses the northern part of the town from west to east. Meanwhile, the park in the north-west has shrunk, and part of its former area has become a children's play area.

To the south, the cinema and the open-air market have been swept away to accommodate a sizeable shopping centre, and Mill Road, which formerly ran south from the High Street, has disappeared. The large car park in the south-east has made way for a bus station reached by a short road from the east. Parking is now provided in a multi-storey car park in the north-east, and the market occupies a smaller site immediately behind the town hall.

items.title: University campus, 2010
items.prompt: The maps below show changes to a university campus between 2010 and 2025. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

modelAnswer.text:
The two plans show how a university campus was redeveloped between 2010 and 2025. What stands out is the considerable expansion of buildings, particularly in the south and north of the site, which came at the cost of most of the car parking and all of the woodland, while the central teaching building and the lake were left untouched.

In the north, the cluster of trees that once separated the original student halls from the lake has been cleared, and a second block of student halls has been constructed in its place. The library on the western side, meanwhile, has been enlarged in both directions.

The southern half of the campus has been transformed most radically. modelAnswer.text:
The maps depict an island before and after it was developed for tourism. In essence, a largely untouched, tree-covered island has been converted into a small resort, with accommodation, dining and water-based facilities added, while its southern beach has been preserved.

Originally, the island was entirely undeveloped: a beach stretched along its southern coast, and the remainder of the land was covered in trees.

After the development, much of this woodland was cleared, and trees now survive only in the northern part of the island. At the heart of the island stands a reception building, flanked to the east by a restaurant. Tourist accommodation takes the form of five huts, three of which are situated towards the west and two towards the east. A curving footpath connects the two groups of huts, passing in front of the reception and the restaurant, while a straight path leads directly south from the reception to the beach.

The shoreline has also been altered. A pier now projects into the sea from the eastern part of the beach, and a designated swimming area has been created in the water off the western end of the beach. The sea surrounding the island is otherwise unchanged.

items.title: Leenford: proposed supermarket sites
items.prompt: The map below shows two possible sites, A and B, for a new supermarket in the town of Leenford. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

modelAnswer.text:
The map presents two possible sites, A and B, for a new supermarket in the town of Leenford. The key difference is that site A would be located within the built-up area, close to housing and the town centre, whereas site B lies on the periphery, separated from the town by the motorway, the river and the railway.

The town is centred on a commercial area crossed by Queen's Road, with the station immediately to the east and a park to the west. Residential areas occupy the north-west and north, and Station Road runs eastwards from the western edge, north of the centre, as far as the motorway, which bisects the eastern part of the map from north to south. The River Leen and the railway both cross the southern half of the town.

Site A sits in the north-east, adjoining the northern housing area and bordered by the motorway to the east. It lies just north of the eastern end of Station Road, the main route leading westwards across the town.

Site B, in contrast, occupies the far south-eastern corner, on the eastern side of the motorway and south of both the river and the railway. Its only neighbours are farmland to the north and, across the motorway, an industrial estate.

items.title: City hospital grounds, 2005
items.prompt: The maps below show the grounds of a city hospital in 2005 and at the present time. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

modelAnswer.text:
The maps compare the grounds of a city hospital in 2005 and today. In short, the site has become far more intensively used, as open space has been built on to provide additional medical services and parking, although the central hospital building and its access road from Hill Road are unchanged.

The northern part of the site has undergone the most extensive change. What was once vacant land in the north-east is now occupied by a multi-storey car park and, further east, a helipad. Next to them, the nurses' housing has been replaced by a somewhat larger cancer treatment centre, while the clinic in the north-west has given way to a health centre.

Further south, parking arrangements have been reorganised: the single staff and visitor car park in the south-west has been split, with visitors now using the southern section and staff the northern one. On the eastern side of the grounds, the garden, which once stretched from near Hill Road as far as the level of the hospital's northern wall, has been reduced to a strip in the north, as a children's hospital now stands on its southern half. A short road connecting the main building with the garden completes the changes.

items.title: Grange Park, 1980
items.prompt: The plans below show a public park when it first opened in 1980 and as it is today. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

modelAnswer.text:
The two plans show Grange Park at its opening in 1980 and as it appears today. The most notable development is that much of the park's natural and ornamental landscape has been replaced by facilities for active recreation, while its core layout, the central lake with paths approaching from the west and east, has survived intact.

In 1980, the park was dominated by greenery: woodland occupied both the north-west and the south-east, and a large area of flower gardens lay to the north of the lake. The only facilities were tennis courts in the south-west and a café and toilets in the north-east.

Since then, the tennis courts have been turned into a skate park, and the south-eastern woodland has given way to an outdoor gym. The trees in the north-west have been cut back to make space for a children's playground, and the flower gardens have been replaced by a somewhat smaller wildflower meadow. The café has been enlarged to incorporate a visitor centre, with the toilets relocated from the far corner to a spot just east of it. Access has also been improved, with a cycle path now leading from the southern boundary to the lake and a car park alongside it.

In 1980, the park was dominated by greenery: woodland occupied both the north-west and the south-east, and a large area of flower gardens lay to the north of the lake. The only facilities were tennis courts in the south-west and a café and toilets in the north-east.

Since then, the tennis courts have been turned into a skate park, and the south-eastern woodland has given way to an outdoor gym. The trees in the north-west have been cut back to make space for a children's playground, and the flower gardens have been replaced by a somewhat smaller wildflower meadow. The café has been enlarged to incorporate a visitor centre, with the toilets relocated from the far corner to a spot just east of it. Access has also been improved, with a cycle path now leading from the southern boundary to the lake and a car park alongside it.

modelAnswer.text:
The maps illustrate the redevelopment of a city harbour area between 1985 and 2025. Broadly speaking, a working industrial waterfront has been reinvented as a residential and leisure district, with almost every industrial feature either replaced or adapted for a new purpose.

At the water's edge, a promenade now runs the full length of the harbour, and the two cranes have disappeared, with two marina jetties extending into the water slightly further east. Dock Road and the harbour itself are the only features left entirely unaltered.

items.title: Regional airport, 2000
items.prompt: The maps below show a regional airport in 2000 and after its expansion in 2024. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

modelAnswer.text:
The two maps compare a regional airport in 2000 with the same site following its expansion in 2024. The most significant changes are the doubling of the number of runways and terminals and the addition of a rail connection, with the surrounding farmland disappearing entirely.

In 2000, the airport comprised a single terminal at its centre, reached by a short road from the motorway to the north, together with one runway stretching across the southern part of the site. A car park adjoined the terminal to the east, and farmland covered the land to the west and south-east.

By 2024, a second runway had been laid parallel to the first, slightly further north, while a new terminal, Terminal 2, had been built on the western farmland, served by a separate access road from the motorway. Rail passengers can now reach the airport via a line from the west, which terminates at a small station just north of the terminals. On the eastern side, the original car park has been replaced by a multi-storey facility on the same site, and a hotel now stands immediately to its east. Terminal 1, its access road and the original runway are unchanged.

items.title: Seaview, 1950
items.prompt: The maps below show the coastal town of Seaview in 1950 and 2020. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

modelAnswer.text:
The maps depict Seaview, a coastal town, in 1950 and 2020. Over this seventy-year period, the town evolved from a modest fishing community set among farmland and trees into a tourism-focused resort, with most of its open land developed, while its seafront and principal landmarks were largely retained.

The southern part of the town has kept its essential character. The beach, Coast Road, the hotel and the church are all still in place, but the fishermen's cottages in the west now house cafés and shops, and the pier no longer extends as far out to sea. In addition, a walkway has been laid along the full length of the seafront.

North of the coast road, the transformation has been far more dramatic. The railway that once crossed the town from west to east has been removed altogether, and the extensive farmland beyond it has been built over, with housing in the north-west and a large block of holiday apartments to its east. The woodland in the north-east has been cleared for a car park, and a new route, Hill Road, now runs northwards from Coast Road, separating the apartments from the car park.

items.title: School grounds, 2000
items.prompt: The maps below show changes to the grounds of a secondary school between 2000 and 2024. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

modelAnswer.text:
The plans compare the grounds of a secondary school in 2000 and 2024. The overall trend has been one of expansion, with new teaching, sports and catering facilities added largely on former open ground, whereas the core of the school, including its access road, car park and playground, was preserved.

The main building remains at the centre of the site, reached from School Lane to the south by the original road, with the playground directly in front of it and the car park in the south-western corner. To its east, however, the modest gym has been replaced by a sports hall of greater size, beyond which a canteen has been added.

The most substantial changes have taken place in the northern half of the grounds. The playing field, which formerly extended across much of the north-west, has been cut back to a narrower strip to make room for a science block, and the small staff room nearby has been removed. Meanwhile, the garden in the north-east has been divided between tennis courts and a vegetable garden, the latter occupying the far eastern edge.

items.title: Library ground floor – current
items.prompt: The plans below show the ground floor of a public library at present and a proposed redesign. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

modelAnswer.text:
The floor plans show the existing ground floor of a public library alongside a proposed redesign. The proposal represents a clear shift away from traditional reading space towards technology and flexible study areas, with the entrance, reception, office and toilets left as they are.

Visitors entering from the south would still find the reception and returns desk immediately ahead of them. Beyond it, however, the newspapers and magazines section would give way to self-service machines. On either side, the fiction and non-fiction collections, which currently fill the south-western and south-eastern corners, would each lose a substantial part of their present depth; the space released would accommodate a café on the western side and a computer room on the eastern side.

The northern half of the floor would also be reorganised. The spacious reference and reading room in the north-west would be subdivided into a quiet study area and a set of meeting rooms, whereas the children's books section would be reinvented as a children's area with a story corner, occupying the same floor space. The office and toilets in the north-eastern corner would remain unaltered.

items.title: Museum ground floor, 1990
items.prompt: The plans below show the ground floor of a museum in 1990 and today. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

modelAnswer.text:
The plans compare the ground floor of a museum in 1990 with its current layout. Broadly speaking, back-of-house areas and one of the permanent galleries have made way for visitor facilities and more varied exhibition spaces, while the entrance area and the local history gallery have been retained.

On entering from the south, visitors still pass through the same entrance hall, beyond which the former ticket office now serves as an information desk. The local history gallery to the west is unchanged, but the natural history gallery that once occupied the south-eastern part of the floor has disappeared, its space now shared between a gift shop at the front and a café behind it. In addition, a lift has been installed in the south-eastern corner.

The northern side of the building has been reconfigured more extensively. The painting gallery, which previously stretched across nearly half the width of the floor, has been reduced in size, allowing an interactive science zone to be inserted beside it. The storage area and offices further east are no longer present, having been replaced by an education room and a space for temporary exhibitions.

The plans compare the ground floor of a museum in 1990 with its current layout. Broadly speaking, back-of-house areas and one of the permanent galleries have made way for visitor facilities and more varied exhibition spaces, while the entrance area and the local history gallery have been retained.

On entering from the south, visitors still pass through the same entrance hall, beyond which the former ticket office now serves as an information desk. The local history gallery to the west is unchanged, but the natural history gallery that once occupied the south-eastern part of the floor has disappeared, its space now shared between a gift shop at the front and a café behind it. In addition, a lift has been installed in the south-eastern corner.

The northern side of the building has been reconfigured more extensively. The painting gallery, which previously stretched across nearly half the width of the floor, has been reduced in size, allowing an interactive science zone to be inserted beside it. The storage area and offices further east are no longer present, having been replaced by an education room and a space for temporary exhibitions.

items.title: Station area, 1995
items.prompt: The maps below show the area around a railway station in 1995 and after redevelopment in 2025. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

modelAnswer.text:
The maps depict the area around a railway station before and after its redevelopment, in 1995 and 2025 respectively. In essence, a district of industrial and disused land has been regenerated into a mixed-use area centred on public transport, with the railway line, the station and Station Road the only features left intact.

To the north of the railway, the changes have largely involved converting existing sites. The access road that ran from the station up to Station Road has been replaced by a pedestrianised square, and the car park immediately east of the station has been divided between a bus interchange and a taxi rank. Similarly, the goods depot on the western side has given way to an office block, and across Station Road the post office has been replaced by a hotel.

South of the tracks, a formerly disused stretch of land has been developed for the first time. Its western portion is now occupied by apartments, the centre by a park and the eastern end by a car park. These new facilities are linked to the station by a footbridge spanning the railway line from the park.

items.title: Hollin Farm, 2005
items.prompt: The maps below show a farm in 2005 and the same site after it was converted into an eco-park in 2024. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

modelAnswer.text:
The maps show Hollin Farm in 2005 and the same site in 2024, following its conversion into an eco-park. The essential shift has been from agriculture to recreation and conservation, with fields and farm buildings repurposed, although the framework of the site, namely the roads, farmhouse, stream and woodland, remains exactly as before.

The farmhouse still sits in the north, reached by a short road from Country Road, and the cluster of trees to its west has been kept. The two former farm buildings to the east have both been given new functions: the barn now serves as a visitor centre, while the cattle shed has been converted into toilets and showers. A small car park has also been laid out just south of Country Road, alongside the trees.

The greatest changes are to the farmland itself. The western wheat field has been partly transformed into a wildflower meadow, with the remainder of the field given over to a pond overlooked by a bird hide. To the east, the grazing land has become a camping area. These areas are now framed by a nature trail, which descends the western side of the site, follows the stream and climbs back up the eastern side.

modelAnswer.text:
The floor plans show how the ground floor of a shopping centre changed between 2010 and 2024. Although the physical structure of the building, including the central walkway, the three entrances and the size of every unit, is identical in both years, the mix of tenants has shifted markedly from conventional shops towards leisure, dining and everyday services.

North of the walkway, two of the four units, the clothes shop and the supermarket at the eastern end, have retained their original use. By contrast, the department store in the north-west has been converted into a food court, and the adjacent bookshop has been replaced by a phone shop.

The transformation is more thorough on the southern side, where only the shoe shop survives. Its western neighbour, formerly an electronics store, now houses a gym, while the bank to its east has been turned into a parcel locker and click-and-collect facility. Continuing eastwards, the travel agent has been succeeded by a pharmacy, and the café occupying the south-eastern corner has given way to a cinema. In total, of the nine units shown, only three are used in the same way as in 2010.

items.title: Sports complex – before
items.prompt: The maps below show a community sports complex before and after its redevelopment. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

modelAnswer.text:
The maps compare a community sports complex before and after it was redeveloped. In general, the complex now offers a far wider range of facilities, with the formerly unused grass area put to use and two existing facilities modernised, although its overall layout around the central leisure centre is unchanged.

The leisure centre itself, the car park beside Park Avenue in the south-west and the athletics track in the north-east all remain in their original form. The football pitch in the north-west, however, has been replaced by a 3G artificial pitch of the same size, and the outdoor pool to the north of the leisure centre has been superseded by a slightly larger indoor pool.

The southern half of the complex has undergone the most radical transformation. The open grass area that previously stretched from the car park to the eastern boundary has been entirely built over, with tennis courts nearest the car park, a climbing wall to their east and a small café in the south-eastern corner. These new facilities are separated from the leisure centre by a newly laid running path, which leads eastwards from the corner of the car park to the edge of the site.

items.title: Housing estate, 1970
items.prompt: The maps below show a housing estate in 1970 and after regeneration in 2020. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

modelAnswer.text:
The maps depict a housing estate in 1970 and after its regeneration in 2020. The overarching change is a move away from high-rise blocks and neglected land towards lower-density housing, community services and landscaped green space, all within an unchanged street pattern.

The estate is still divided into quarters by Ring Road, running east to west, and Oak Avenue, running north to south. In the north-west, the tower blocks have been cleared and replaced by low-rise flats on the western side and houses to their east. Across Oak Avenue, the terraced houses remain, but the open grassland behind them has been landscaped into a park with a play area at its eastern end.

South of Ring Road, the garages and car park that once filled the south-western quarter have been scaled down to a single car park, and the land released now accommodates a community centre and, to their north, a strip of allotments. The shops beside Oak Avenue have been retained, while the former waste ground in the south-east has been put to use, with a medical centre in its southern part and a cluster of trees to the north.

items.title: Hadley: proposed bypass routes
items.prompt: The map below shows the town of Hadley and two proposed routes for a new bypass road. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

modelAnswer.text:
The map shows the town of Hadley together with two alternative routes proposed for a bypass. Both routes would divert traffic from the A12 around the town, branching off to the west and rejoining it to the east; the key difference is that the northern option would affect the school and the woodland, while the southern option would cross farmland.

Currently, the A12 runs directly through Hadley town centre from west to east. The centre is flanked by housing to the north and south, and the River Hale flows southwards to the west of the town. The surrounding area contains a school in the north-west, woodland in the north-east and farmland in the south-east.

Route 1 would swing north from the A12, skirting the school closely on its western side, then cross the river and run parallel to the northern boundary of the map, well beyond the housing. It would subsequently cut through the northern fringe of the woodland before descending to meet the A12 east of the town.

Route 2 would follow a mirror-image course to the south. After crossing the river, it would pass some distance south of the housing and then bisect the farmland in the south-east before looping north to rejoin the A12.

items.title: Riverside district, 1990
items.prompt: The maps below show a riverside district of a city in 1990 and 2025. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

modelAnswer.text:
The maps illustrate the transformation of a city's riverside district between 1990 and 2025. The overall picture is one of post-industrial regeneration: heavy industry and derelict land have given way to homes, workplaces and cultural and leisure facilities, while the district's road network and its residential streets in the south-west have survived unchanged.

On the northern bank of the River Tane, the factory has been converted into apartments, and the neighbouring warehouses have been replaced by an office development. Further east, beyond Old Bridge, the wasteland has been landscaped as a riverside park. These buildings are now fronted by a riverside walkway that follows the northern bank along the whole width of the district.

South of the river, the terraced housing remains in place, but the power station beside it has been repurposed as an arts centre, and the previously undeveloped land to the east of Old Bridge has been turned into a car park. Finally, pedestrian access across the river has been improved by a new footbridge, which links the eastern end of the terraced housing with the northern bank, between the apartments and the offices.

chart.title: Recycling glass bottles
steps: Collection: Bottles left in street bottle banks
Transport: Lorry takes bottles to recycling plant
Sorting by colour: Clear, green and brown separated
Cleaning: Labels and caps removed; washed with high-pressure water
Crushing: Glass broken into small pieces called cullet
Melting: Cullet mixed with sand, heated to 1,500°C
Moulding: Molten glass shaped into new bottles

items.title: Production of olive oil
items.prompt: The diagram below shows the stages in the production of olive oil. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

chart.title: Production of olive oil
steps: Harvesting: Olives shaken from trees onto nets (Oct–Dec)
Washing: Leaves and dirt removed
Crushing: Olives and stones ground into a paste
Malaxation: Paste slowly stirred for 30–40 minutes
Centrifuge: Oil separated from water and solids
Settling: Oil left to rest in steel tanks for 4–6 weeks
Filtering: Remaining particles removed
Bottling: Oil sealed in dark glass bottles
By-product use: Leftover pulp dried and burned as fuel

modelAnswer.text:
The diagram illustrates the sequence of steps involved in manufacturing olive oil, from gathering the fruit to disposing of the residue.

In total, the process comprises nine linear stages. It starts with the seasonal harvest and culminates in bottling, with a final step in which the waste pulp is recovered as a source of energy.

Harvesting takes place from October to December, when the olives are shaken from the trees and caught in nets. After being washed to clear away leaves and dirt, the fruit is crushed, stones included, into a paste. This paste is then subjected to malaxation, a slow stirring phase lasting 30–40 minutes, before being fed into a centrifuge, which separates the oil from water and solid matter.

The extracted oil is subsequently left to settle in steel tanks for four to six weeks, a considerably longer period than the stirring phase, and is then filtered to eliminate any remaining particles. Once clarified, it is sealed in dark glass bottles. Meanwhile, the pulp left over from production is dried and burned as fuel, ensuring that the by-product is put to good use.

items.title: Life cycle of the honeybee
items.prompt: The diagram below shows the life cycle of the honeybee. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

chart.title: Life cycle of the honeybee
steps: Egg: Laid by the queen in a wax cell; hatches after 3 days
Larva: Fed royal jelly then pollen and honey; 6 days
Cell capped: Worker bees seal the cell with wax
Pupa: Develops legs, wings and eyes; about 12 days
Adult emerges: Chews through the wax cap at day 21
Worker bee: Cleans, feeds larvae, then collects nectar; lives 5–6 weeks

modelAnswer.text:
The diagram charts the development of the honeybee through the six stages of its life cycle, which begins with an egg and ends with a mature worker bee.

It is evident that the entire transformation from egg to adult is completed within 21 days, much of it inside a sealed wax cell, whereas the adult worker survives for just five to six weeks before the cycle begins anew with fresh eggs.

Initially, the queen deposits an egg in a wax cell, and three days later this hatches into a larva. For the following six days, the larva is fed first on royal jelly and subsequently on pollen and honey, after which worker bees cap the cell with wax.

Sealed within, the insect enters the pupal stage, lasting about 12 days, during which it develops legs, wings and eyes. On day 21, the fully formed adult chews its way out through the wax cap. It then takes on the role of a worker bee, initially cleaning and feeding larvae before progressing to collecting nectar. As new eggs are laid by the queen, the cycle is repeated continuously.

items.title: Producing drinking water from seawater
items.prompt: The diagram below shows how drinking water is produced from seawater at a desalination plant. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

chart.title: Producing drinking water from seawater
steps: Intake: Seawater drawn in through screened pipe
Pre-treatment: Sand filters remove particles and algae
High-pressure pump: Water pressurised to about 60 bar
Reverse osmosis: Membranes separate fresh water from salt
Brine discharge: Salty waste diluted and returned to the sea
Remineralisation: Calcium and magnesium added
Disinfection: Small amount of chlorine added
Storage & supply: Water stored in reservoir, then piped to homes

modelAnswer.text:
The diagram explains how seawater is converted into potable water at a desalination facility.

In essence, the treatment follows eight consecutive stages, from the intake of raw seawater to the delivery of drinking water to homes. At the heart of the process lies reverse osmosis, which splits the flow into fresh water for further treatment and salty waste that is discharged.

To begin with, seawater is drawn into the plant through a screened pipe, after which it is pre-treated using sand filters that trap particles and algae. A high-pressure pump then raises the pressure of the water to approximately 60 bar, enabling it to pass through reverse osmosis membranes, where the fresh water is separated from the salt.

The resulting salty waste is diluted and returned to the sea. The desalinated water, by contrast, is remineralised through the addition of calcium and magnesium, before being disinfected with a small quantity of chlorine. Finally, the treated water is held in a storage reservoir, from which it is piped to residential properties, completing its transformation from seawater into a safe supply for household consumption.

items.title: Manufacturing paper from wood
items.prompt: The diagram below shows how paper is made from wood. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

chart.title: Manufacturing paper from wood
steps: Tree felling: Softwood trees cut in managed forests
Debarking & chipping: Bark removed; logs cut into chips
Pulping: Chips cooked with chemicals to separate fibres
Bleaching: Pulp whitened
Mixing: Pulp mixed with water and recycled fibre
Forming: Mixture sprayed onto moving mesh; water drains away
Pressing & drying: Sheet pressed between rollers and dried over heated cylinders
Reeling & cutting: Paper wound onto large reels, then cut to size

modelAnswer.text:
The diagram sets out the eight stages involved in converting timber into paper.

Broadly speaking, the process falls into three phases: the preparation of the raw wood, the chemical treatment of that wood to create pulp, and the mechanical formation of the paper itself. It begins in managed forests and ends with the paper being reeled and trimmed to size. Notably, recycled fibre is introduced part-way through, so the finished product is not made from newly felled wood alone.

Initially, softwood trees are felled, after which their bark is stripped away and the logs are reduced to chips. These chips are then cooked with chemicals, a step known as pulping, which separates the wood fibres. The resulting pulp is bleached to whiten it and subsequently combined with water and recycled fibre.

At the forming stage, this mixture is sprayed onto a moving mesh, through which the water drains, leaving a damp sheet behind. The sheet is then pressed between rollers and dried over a series of heated cylinders. In the last step, the finished paper is wound onto large reels and later cut into sheets of the required dimensions.

modelAnswer.text:
The diagram sets out the eight stages involved in converting timber into paper.

Broadly speaking, the process falls into three phases: the preparation of the raw wood, the chemical treatment of that wood to create pulp, and the mechanical formation of the paper itself. It begins in managed forests and ends with the paper being reeled and trimmed to size. Notably, recycled fibre is introduced part-way through, so the finished product is not made from newly felled wood alone.

Initially, softwood trees are felled, after which their bark is stripped away and the logs are reduced to chips. These chips are then cooked with chemicals, a step known as pulping, which separates the wood fibres. The resulting pulp is bleached to whiten it and subsequently combined with water and recycled fibre.

At the forming stage, this mixture is sprayed onto a moving mesh, through which the water drains, leaving a damp sheet behind. The sheet is then pressed between rollers and dried over a series of heated cylinders. In the last step, the finished paper is wound onto large reels and later cut into sheets of the required dimensions.

items.title: Pumped-storage hydroelectricity
items.prompt: The diagram below shows how a pumped-storage hydroelectric power station works. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

chart.title: Pumped-storage hydroelectricity
steps: Night: low demand: Cheap surplus electricity taken from the grid
Pumping: Water pumped from lower reservoir up a tunnel
Upper reservoir: Water stored on the mountain top
Day: high demand: Valves opened
Water released: Water flows down through the tunnel
Turbines: Falling water spins turbines connected to generators
Electricity supplied: Power sent to the national grid
Lower reservoir: Water collected, ready to be pumped again

modelAnswer.text:
The diagram explains how a pumped-storage hydroelectric plant functions over a cycle of night and day, using the same body of water repeatedly.

In essence, the system consists of eight repeating stages and operates in two distinct modes: during periods of low demand at night it consumes electricity to move water uphill, whereas during periods of high demand in the daytime it releases that water to generate power.

At night, inexpensive surplus electricity is drawn from the grid and used to pump water from the lower reservoir up through a tunnel. The water is then held in an upper reservoir on the mountain top, where it waits until it is needed. Crucially, this pumping phase relies on electricity at a time when it is both cheap and plentiful.

Once demand rises during the day, valves are opened and the water is allowed to flow back down the tunnel. As it falls, it drives turbines linked to generators, and the electricity this produces is fed into the national grid. The water then collects in the lower reservoir, where it remains until it can be pumped up once more, at which point the entire cycle resumes.

items.title: Rainwater harvesting in a house
items.prompt: The diagram below shows how rainwater is collected and used in a house. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

chart.title: Rainwater harvesting in a house
steps: Rainfall on roof: Rain runs off the roof surface
Gutters & downpipe: Water channelled from roof edge
Leaf filter: Leaves and debris removed
Underground tank: Filtered water stored below the garden
Pump: Water pumped into the house when needed
Household use: Toilets, washing machine and garden watering
Overflow: Excess water drains to soakaway when tank is full

modelAnswer.text:
The diagram depicts a domestic rainwater harvesting system, showing how rain falling on a house is captured, filtered, stored and eventually put to use.

The process consists of seven stages, starting with rainfall on the roof and culminating in the use of the water within the household, while a separate overflow route handles any surplus once the storage tank has reached capacity.

Rain initially runs off the roof surface and is channelled from its edge into gutters and a downpipe. From there, it passes through a leaf filter designed to trap leaves and debris, and the filtered water is then stored in an underground tank buried beneath the garden.

Whenever water is required, it is pumped from this tank into the house, where it serves three purposes: flushing toilets, supplying the washing machine and watering the garden. Should the tank become full, however, the excess water is not retained; instead, it drains away to a soakaway. In this way, the system both makes use of rainwater and prevents surplus water from building up once storage is exhausted.

items.title: Making hard cheese
items.prompt: The diagram below shows the process of making hard cheese. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

chart.title: Making hard cheese
steps: Milk collection: Fresh milk delivered from dairy farms
Pasteurisation: Heated to 72°C for 15 seconds, then cooled
Adding culture & rennet: Milk begins to set
Curd forms: Milk separates into solid curd and liquid whey
Cutting & heating: Curd cut into cubes; whey drained off
Salting & moulding: Curd salted and pressed into moulds
Ripening: Stored at 10°C for 3–24 months
Packaging: Cut, wrapped and labelled for sale

modelAnswer.text:
The diagram outlines the sequence of steps by which fresh milk is transformed into packaged hard cheese.

There are eight stages in total, beginning with the delivery of milk and ending with packaging, and it combines heating, cutting and pressing with a long period of controlled storage. Of the stages for which a duration is given, ripening is by far the most time-consuming, lasting anywhere from three months to two years, whereas pasteurisation takes a matter of seconds.

Initially, milk is transported from dairy farms, after which it is pasteurised by being heated to 72°C for just 15 seconds and then cooled. Culture and rennet are subsequently introduced, prompting the milk to set, and it separates into solid curd and liquid whey.

The curd is next cut into cubes and heated, and the whey is drained off, so that only the solid part is carried forward. It is then salted and pressed into moulds. Following this, the cheese is ripened at a cool 10°C for between 3 and 24 months. Finally, it is cut, wrapped and labelled for sale, at which point the product is ready to leave the production line.
