items.title: Publishing a new book
items.prompt: The diagram below shows the stages involved in publishing a new book. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

chart.title: Publishing a new book
steps: Manuscript submitted: Author or agent sends text to publisher
Assessment: Editor decides; rejected manuscripts returned to author
Contract signed: Fees and deadlines agreed
Editing: Structure and language revised with author
Design & typesetting: Cover designed; pages laid out
Proofreading: Final errors corrected
Printing: Books printed and bound
Marketing & distribution: Books sent to shops and online retailers

modelAnswer.text:
The diagram illustrates the eight stages through which a new book passes on its way from the author's desk to the retailer.

The process is essentially linear, beginning with the submission of a manuscript and concluding with the marketing and distribution of the printed books. Its one decision point comes early on, when an editor at the publisher either accepts the manuscript or returns it to the author.

To begin with, the text is submitted to a publisher either by the author or by an agent. It is then assessed by an editor, and any manuscript that is rejected is sent back, meaning the process ends there. For successful manuscripts, a contract is signed setting out fees and deadlines, after which the editing phase begins, with the structure and language being revised in collaboration with the author.

The book next moves into design and typesetting, where the cover is created and the pages are laid out. Proofreading follows, allowing any remaining errors to be corrected. Finally, the books are printed and bound before being marketed and dispatched to bookshops and online retailers.

items.title: Life cycle of the Atlantic salmon
items.prompt: The diagram below shows the life cycle of the Atlantic salmon. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

chart.title: Life cycle of the Atlantic salmon
steps: Eggs: Laid in gravel of upper river; hatch in spring
Alevin: Stay in gravel, feeding on yolk sac
Fry: Emerge to feed in the river
Parr: Live in river for 1–3 years
Smolt: Turn silver; migrate downstream to the sea
Adult at sea: Feed and grow in the ocean for 1–4 years
Return migration: Swim back up the same river to spawn

modelAnswer.text:
The diagram traces the life cycle of the Atlantic salmon across seven stages, from eggs laid in a river to mature adults returning to breed.

What stands out is that the fish spends its early life in fresh water and its adult life at sea, before a return migration to the river where it began brings the cycle full circle.

The cycle begins in the gravel of the upper river, where eggs are laid and hatch in spring. items.title: Producing cement and concrete
items.prompt: The diagram below shows how cement is produced and then used to make concrete. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

chart.title: Producing cement and concrete
steps: Quarrying: Limestone and clay extracted
Crushing: Raw materials crushed and mixed
Grinding: Mixture ground into fine powder
Rotating kiln: Heated to 1,450°C to form clinker
Cooling & grinding: Clinker ground with gypsum to make cement
Bagging: Cement packed into bags
Mixing concrete: 15% cement, 10% water, 25% sand, 50% gravel
Pouring & setting: Concrete poured into moulds and left to harden

modelAnswer.text:
The diagram depicts the production of cement from raw materials and its subsequent use as an ingredient in concrete.

In total, there are eight stages, the first six of which relate to cement manufacture and the final two to the making of concrete. A striking feature is that cement, despite being the focus of most of the process, forms only a modest share of the finished concrete, which consists mainly of gravel and sand.

The raw materials, limestone and clay, are first quarried and then crushed and blended together. This mixture is ground into a fine powder and fed into a rotating kiln, where it is heated to 1,450°C to form clinker. Once cooled, the clinker is ground again, this time with gypsum, to produce cement, which is packed into bags.

In the concrete-making stage, the cement is combined with sand, gravel and water in fixed proportions. Gravel constitutes half of the mix and sand a quarter, while cement and water account for just 15% and 10% respectively. The concrete is then poured into moulds and left to set hard.

items.title: Producing ethanol fuel from sugar cane
items.prompt: The diagram below shows how ethanol fuel is produced from sugar cane. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

chart.title: Producing ethanol fuel from sugar cane
steps: Growing: Sugar cane grows for 12–18 months
Harvesting: Cane cut by machine
Crushing: Juice extracted by rollers
Bagasse: Fibrous waste burned to power the factory
Fermentation: Yeast added; sugar turns into alcohol
Distillation: Ethanol separated from water
Blending: Ethanol mixed with petrol
Distribution: Fuel delivered to filling stations

modelAnswer.text:
The diagram sets out the eight stages involved in converting sugar cane into ethanol fuel.

Broadly, the process moves from agriculture to industrial processing and finally to distribution. One noteworthy aspect is that a by-product is put to use: the fibrous waste generated when the cane is crushed is burned to provide the energy that powers the factory. Only the growing stage is given a duration, and at up to a year and a half it clearly dominates the overall timescale.

The cane is cultivated for a lengthy period of 12–18 months before being harvested mechanically. It is then passed through rollers, which extract the juice, leaving behind the fibrous residue known as bagasse; rather than being discarded, this is burned as fuel for the plant.

The extracted juice subsequently undergoes fermentation, with yeast being added so that the sugar is converted into alcohol. Distillation then separates the ethanol from the water it contains, after which the ethanol is blended with petrol. In the final stage, the finished fuel is transported to filling stations, completing the journey from field to forecourt.

items.title: Processing university applications
items.prompt: The flow chart below shows how applications to an undergraduate university course are processed. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

chart.title: Processing university applications
steps: Online application: Student submits form, grades and personal statement
Eligibility check: Incomplete applications returned for correction
Academic review: Tutors score application
Interview: Shortlisted applicants invited (online or on campus)
Decision: Offer, waiting list or rejection
Offer accepted: Student confirms place and pays deposit
Results confirmed: Final exam grades checked against offer
Enrolment: Student registers and receives ID card

modelAnswer.text:
The flow chart outlines how applications for undergraduate university courses are handled, from initial submission to final enrolment.

The procedure comprises eight stages and, although it is broadly linear, it contains several filtering points at which applicants may be returned, held back or turned down. Only those who satisfy each requirement ultimately enrol and receive a student ID card.

The process is initiated when a student submits an online application comprising their grades and a personal statement. This undergoes an eligibility check, with incomplete submissions being returned for correction. Eligible applications are then scored by tutors in an academic review, the first point at which the content of the application itself is judged, and shortlisted candidates are invited to an interview, which may take place online or on campus.

Following the interview, a decision is reached, with the applicant being made an offer, placed on a waiting list or rejected. Those who accept an offer confirm their place and pay a deposit, after which their final examination grades are checked against the terms of the offer. Once these are confirmed, the student enrols formally and is issued with an ID card.

items.title: Composting household food waste
items.prompt: The diagram below shows how household food waste is turned into compost. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

chart.title: Composting household food waste
steps: Kitchen caddy: Vegetable peelings and food scraps collected
Compost bin: Waste added in garden bin with leaves and cardboard
Decomposition: Worms and bacteria break waste down
Turning: Mixed every 2–3 weeks to add air
Maturing: Left for 6–12 months until dark and crumbly
Garden use: Compost spread on soil
Plant growth: Vegetables grown and eaten; scraps return to caddy

modelAnswer.text:
The diagram depicts the seven-stage cycle through which household food waste is converted into compost and ultimately helps to produce new food.

The most notable feature of the process is its circular nature: it starts with scraps collected in the kitchen and ends with vegetables whose leftovers return to that same point. Of the individual stages, maturing is by far the most protracted, lasting between six months and a year, far longer than the two- to three-week interval between turnings.

To begin with, peelings and food scraps are gathered in a kitchen caddy before being transferred to a garden compost bin, where they are combined with leaves and cardboard. Worms and bacteria then set about decomposing this material, and the contents of the bin are turned every two to three weeks to aerate them.

Next, the compost is left to mature for 6–12 months, by which time it has become dark and crumbly. It is then spread on the soil and used to grow vegetables, which are eventually eaten. The scraps from these return to the caddy, allowing the cycle to repeat indefinitely.

modelAnswer.text:
The diagram depicts the seven-stage cycle through which household food waste is converted into compost and ultimately helps to produce new food.

The most notable feature of the process is its circular nature: it starts with scraps collected in the kitchen and ends with vegetables whose leftovers return to that same point. Of the individual stages, maturing is by far the most protracted, lasting between six months and a year, far longer than the two- to three-week interval between turnings.

To begin with, peelings and food scraps are gathered in a kitchen caddy before being transferred to a garden compost bin, where they are combined with leaves and cardboard. Worms and bacteria then set about decomposing this material, and the contents of the bin are turned every two to three weeks to aerate them.

Next, the compost is left to mature for 6–12 months, by which time it has become dark and crumbly. It is then spread on the soil and used to grow vegetables, which are eventually eaten. The scraps from these return to the caddy, allowing the cycle to repeat indefinitely.

items.title: Producing black tea
items.prompt: The diagram below shows the stages in the production of black tea. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

chart.title: Producing black tea
steps: Plucking: Top two leaves and a bud picked by hand
Withering: Leaves spread on racks for 12–18 hours
Rolling: Leaves rolled to break cell walls
Oxidation: Leaves turn copper-brown over 1–3 hours
Drying: Hot air at 120°C stops oxidation
Sorting & grading: Leaves sieved by size
Tasting: Samples checked by professional tasters
Packing & export: Packed in foil-lined sacks

modelAnswer.text:
The diagram charts the eight stages involved in the production of black tea, from harvesting the leaves to preparing them for export.

In broad terms, the first half of the process transforms the fresh leaves, whereas the second half is concerned with quality control and packaging. The process begins with leaves being picked by hand and ends with the finished tea being packed for shipment overseas. Withering, at 12–18 hours, is considerably lengthier than oxidation, which takes only one to three hours.

Production begins with plucking, a delicate task in which the top two leaves and a bud are picked by hand. These are then laid out on racks to wither before being rolled, a step which breaks down their cell walls. The rolled leaves are left to oxidise, gradually turning copper-brown, until this reaction is halted by a stream of hot air at 120°C.

Once dried, the leaves are sieved so that they can be sorted and graded by size. Samples are subsequently evaluated by professional tasters, and in the final stage the tea is packed into foil-lined sacks ready for export.

items.title: Recycling plastic bottles into clothing fibre
items.prompt: The diagram below shows how plastic bottles are recycled into polyester fibre for clothing. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

chart.title: Recycling plastic bottles into clothing fibre
steps: Collection: Bottles collected from homes
Sorting: PET bottles separated from other plastics
Washing: Labels and caps removed
Shredding: Bottles cut into flakes
Melting: Flakes melted at 260°C
Extrusion: Liquid pushed through tiny holes to form threads
Spinning: Threads stretched and spun into yarn
Weaving & sewing: Fabric made into jackets and T-shirts

modelAnswer.text:
The diagram explains how discarded plastic bottles, collected from ordinary households, are reprocessed into polyester fibre and ultimately into clothing.

The process involves eight sequential stages and can be seen as a transformation from solid waste to wearable fabric: the bottles are first prepared and broken down, then melted and reformed into threads, and finally woven and sewn into garments. Notably, the only temperature specified is that of the melting stage, the point at which the bottles lose their original form.

Initially, bottles are collected from households and taken to be sorted, with PET bottles being separated from other plastics, a step that ensures only PET continues through the process. After being washed and stripped of their labels and caps, they are shredded into flakes. These flakes are melted at a temperature of 260°C, and the resulting liquid is extruded, meaning that it is forced through tiny holes to create fine threads.

In the penultimate stage, the threads are stretched and spun into yarn. This yarn is then woven into fabric, which is sewn to produce clothing such as jackets and T-shirts, bringing the process to a close.

items.title: Formation of coal
items.prompt: The diagram below shows the stages in the formation of coal. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

chart.title: Formation of coal
steps: Swamp forest: Plants grow in warm wetlands
Plant debris: Dead plants fall into water and do not fully decay
Peat: Layers build up and compress
Burial: Covered by sand and mud over millions of years
Lignite: Heat and pressure remove water
Bituminous coal: Further compression; higher carbon content
Anthracite: Hardest coal, about 90% carbon
Mining: Extracted from underground seams

modelAnswer.text:
The diagram outlines the natural process by which coal is formed and the point at which it is finally extracted by humans for use.

It is clear that coal formation is an extremely slow, eight-stage process spanning millions of years, during which buried plant matter is progressively compressed into increasingly carbon-rich forms of coal, culminating in anthracite. Only the last stage involves human activity.

The sequence starts in warm, swampy wetlands, where plants flourish. When these plants die, they fall into the water and, crucially, fail to decompose fully, so that successive layers of debris accumulate and are compressed into peat. Over millions of years, this peat is buried beneath deposits of sand and mud.

Heat and pressure then drive out the water, converting the compressed peat into lignite, the first of the three types of coal shown. With further compression, lignite becomes bituminous coal, which has a higher carbon content, and ultimately anthracite, the hardest variety, containing approximately 90% carbon. At the final stage, this coal is extracted by mining underground seams, marking the shift from a natural process to a human one.

items.title: Solar water heating system
items.prompt: The diagram below shows how a solar water heating system provides hot water for a house. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

chart.title: Solar water heating system
steps: Solar panel on roof: Sunlight heats fluid in dark pipes
Hot fluid rises: Fluid carried to the storage cylinder
Heat exchanger: Coil transfers heat to household water
Hot water storage: Water kept in insulated cylinder
Backup boiler: Heats water on cloudy days
Cooled fluid: Returned to the panel by pump

modelAnswer.text:
The diagram explains how a solar water heating system provides a house with hot water, using sunlight as its primary source of energy.

The system operates as a continuous six-stage loop in which a fluid circulates between a roof-mounted solar panel and a storage cylinder, collecting heat at one end and releasing it at the other, before being pumped back to begin again. A backup boiler supplements the system when the weather is cloudy.

The cycle begins on the roof, where sunlight heats a fluid flowing through the dark pipes of the solar panel. Once heated, the fluid rises and is carried to the storage cylinder, where a coil acting as a heat exchanger transfers its heat to the household water. This water is then retained in an insulated cylinder so that it stays hot until required.

On overcast days, a backup boiler is used to heat the water. Having given up its heat, the cooled fluid is pumped back up to the panel on the roof, where it is warmed once again by the sun, allowing the process to repeat without interruption.

items.title: Processing wool into yarn
items.prompt: The diagram below shows how raw sheep's wool is processed into yarn. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

chart.title: Processing wool into yarn
steps: Shearing: Fleece removed from sheep in spring
Skirting & grading: Dirty edges removed; wool graded by quality
Scouring: Washed in warm soapy water to remove grease
Drying: Warm air dries the wool
Carding: Fibres combed straight into a soft web
Spinning: Fibres twisted into yarn
Dyeing: Yarn coloured in large vats
Winding: Yarn wound into balls or cones

modelAnswer.text:
The diagram depicts the process by which fleece shorn from sheep is transformed into finished yarn.

In total, there are eight stages, which can be broadly divided into two phases: the first four prepare and clean the raw wool, whereas the final four convert the clean fibres into yarn that is coloured and wound for use.

The process starts in spring, when sheep are sheared and their fleece is removed. This is followed by skirting and grading, in which the soiled edges are trimmed off and the wool is sorted according to its quality. The wool is then scoured in warm, soapy water to strip away grease, and subsequently dried with warm air. These preparatory steps ensure that the wool is clean before any processing of the fibres begins.

Once dry, the wool is carded, a step in which the fibres are combed straight into a soft web. These fibres are then spun, meaning they are twisted together to form yarn. The yarn is dyed in large vats and, in the final stage, wound into balls or cones, at which point it is ready for use.

modelAnswer.text:
The diagram depicts the process by which fleece shorn from sheep is transformed into finished yarn.

In total, there are eight stages, which can be broadly divided into two phases: the first four prepare and clean the raw wool, whereas the final four convert the clean fibres into yarn that is coloured and wound for use.

The process starts in spring, when sheep are sheared and their fleece is removed. This is followed by skirting and grading, in which the soiled edges are trimmed off and the wool is sorted according to its quality. The wool is then scoured in warm, soapy water to strip away grease, and subsequently dried with warm air. These preparatory steps ensure that the wool is clean before any processing of the fibres begins.

Once dry, the wool is carded, a step in which the fibres are combed straight into a soft web. These fibres are then spun, meaning they are twisted together to form yarn. The yarn is dyed in large vats and, in the final stage, wound into balls or cones, at which point it is ready for use.

items.title: Recycling old smartphones
items.prompt: The diagram below shows how old smartphones are recycled. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

chart.title: Recycling old smartphones
steps: Drop-off: Phones returned to shops or by post
Data wiping: Personal data erased
Testing: Working phones repaired and resold
Dismantling: Battery and screen removed from faulty phones
Battery recycling: Lithium and cobalt recovered
Shredding: Remaining parts shredded
Metal recovery: Gold, silver and copper extracted
Reuse: Materials sold to manufacturers

modelAnswer.text:
The diagram outlines how old smartphones are processed for recycling, from the moment they are handed in to the point at which their materials re-enter manufacturing.

Of the eight stages, testing is pivotal, since it determines which of two routes a phone will take: working devices are repaired and resold, while faulty ones are dismantled and broken down so that their constituent materials can be recovered and sold on.

Phones are first returned, either to shops or by post, after which all personal data stored on them is wiped. They are then tested, and those found to be in working order are repaired and put back on the market. Defective handsets, by contrast, are dismantled, with the battery and screen being removed. Notably, both routes begin only after the data-wiping stage, so no phone is tested while it still holds personal information.

The batteries are recycled to recover lithium and cobalt, whereas the remaining components are shredded. Gold, silver and copper are then extracted from this shredded material. Finally, all of the recovered materials are sold to manufacturers for reuse, which brings the process to an end.

items.title: International tourist arrivals, 2014–2024
items.prompt: The bar chart below shows the number of international tourists visiting one country between 2014 and 2024, and the pie chart shows the main purposes of their visits in 2024. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

modelAnswer.text:
The two charts provide information about international tourism in one country: the bar chart tracks annual arrivals between 2014 and 2024, and the pie chart shows why visitors came in the final year.

Arrivals followed a broadly upward trajectory over the decade, interrupted only by a sharp slump in 2020 from which the sector had more than recovered by 2024. Leisure was by far the dominant motive for travel, accounting for over half of all visits.

In 2014 the country received 8.2 million foreign visitors, a figure that rose steadily to 11.1 million by 2018. This growth was abruptly reversed in 2020, when arrivals collapsed to 3.4 million, roughly 30% of the 2018 level. A strong recovery followed, with numbers more than doubling to 7.8 million in 2022 and then climbing to a ten-year high of 12.6 million in 2024, some 1.5 million above the pre-2020 peak.

Regarding the purpose of visits, holidaymakers made up 54% of tourists in 2024, almost three times the proportion who came to see family or friends (19%). Business travel accounted for a similar share, at 15%, while study and medical treatment were comparatively minor reasons, representing just 8% and 4% respectively.

items.title: Population of Marlow City, 1950–2020
items.prompt: The line graph below shows the population of a city between 1950 and 2020, and the table shows the types of housing in the city in 1950 and 2020. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

parts.title: Housing stock by type (% of homes)

modelAnswer.text:
The line graph charts the population of Marlow City from 1950 to 2020, and the accompanying table shows how the composition of its housing stock changed between the start and end of that period.

The most striking features are the city's sustained population growth, with the number of residents multiplying six times over, and a fundamental shift in housing from terraced houses to apartments.

Marlow City's population stood at 0.4 million in 1950 and grew at a fairly steady pace to 1.2 million by 1980, tripling in thirty years. The following decade saw only marginal growth, to 1.3 million, but expansion resumed thereafter and gathered pace after 2000, so that the city was home to 2.4 million people by 2020.

This growth coincided with a transformation in the type of homes available. In 1950, terraced houses accounted for 61% of the housing stock, around five times the proportion of apartments (12%). By 2020, however, the positions had been reversed: apartments comprised 58% of homes, while the share of terraced houses had shrunk to 24%. Detached houses also became less prevalent, falling from 18% to 11%, and other types of accommodation changed little, edging down from 9% to 7%.

items.title: Average monthly temperature
items.prompt: The graph below shows average monthly temperatures in one city, and the bar chart shows the average monthly rainfall there. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

modelAnswer.text:
The line graph compares the average monthly maximum and minimum temperatures in one city, and the bar chart presents its average monthly rainfall.

The city experiences consistently high temperatures, with the maximum fluctuating within a narrow band of just four degrees. Rainfall, by contrast, varies enormously, with a pronounced wet season from May to September and very dry conditions around the turn of the year.

Maximum temperatures are highest in March and April, at 33°C, and lowest in July and August, at 29°C, remaining between 30°C and 32°C in every other month. Minimum temperatures fluctuate more widely, from a low of 18°C in December and January to 26°C in May, and they hold steady at 25°C from June to September. As a result, the gap between the maximum and minimum is widest in December and January, at 13 degrees, and narrowest in July and August, at just four.

Rainfall is low from November to March, ranging from 8mm in January to 45mm in March. It then increases sharply, surging from 110mm in April to 260mm in May and peaking at 370mm in July. Although it falls back gradually to 290mm in September, a steep decline follows, to 180mm in October and just 35mm in November.

items.title: Car ownership
items.prompt: The table below shows car ownership in one country in three years, and the pie charts show how people travelled to work in 1995 and 2025. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

modelAnswer.text:
The table sets out figures on car ownership in one country in 1995, 2010 and 2025, while the pie charts illustrate how people travelled to work in 1995 and 2025.

Although car ownership increased throughout the period, the car's dominance as a means of commuting weakened somewhat, with rail, cycling and home working all gaining ground.

The number of cars on the country's roads rose by almost 8 million over the thirty years, from 14.2 million to 22.1 million, with the sharpest growth occurring between 1995 and 2010. Car density followed the same pattern, increasing from 280 to 360 vehicles per 1,000 people in the first fifteen years but only to 385 by 2025. Correspondingly, the proportion of households without a car fell from 33% to 25% by 2010, before levelling off at 23%.

Turning to commuting, the car remained the principal mode of transport, although its share slipped from 64% to 57%. Bus travel and walking both declined, to 8% each, from 14% and 12% respectively. Train use, on the other hand, increased from 6% to 10%, and cycling from 4% to 7%. Perhaps most notably, working from home, which did not feature in 1995, accounted for 10% of workers by 2025.

modelAnswer.text:
The table sets out figures on car ownership in one country in 1995, 2010 and 2025, while the pie charts illustrate how people travelled to work in 1995 and 2025.

Although car ownership increased throughout the period, the car's dominance as a means of commuting weakened somewhat, with rail, cycling and home working all gaining ground.

The number of cars on the country's roads rose by almost 8 million over the thirty years, from 14.2 million to 22.1 million, with the sharpest growth occurring between 1995 and 2010. Car density followed the same pattern, increasing from 280 to 360 vehicles per 1,000 people in the first fifteen years but only to 385 by 2025. Correspondingly, the proportion of households without a car fell from 33% to 25% by 2010, before levelling off at 23%.

Turning to commuting, the car remained the principal mode of transport, although its share slipped from 64% to 57%. Bus travel and walking both declined, to 8% each, from 14% and 12% respectively. Train use, on the other hand, increased from 6% to 10%, and cycling from 4% to 7%. Perhaps most notably, working from home, which did not feature in 1995, accounted for 10% of workers by 2025.

items.title: Average world coffee price, 2014–2024
items.prompt: The line graph shows the average world price of coffee between 2014 and 2024, and the bar chart shows coffee exports from four countries in 2014 and 2024. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

modelAnswer.text:
The line graph traces the average world price of coffee from 2014 to 2024, while the bar chart compares the coffee exports of four producing countries in the first and final years of that period.

Coffee prices followed a pronounced V-shaped pattern, bottoming out in 2020 before surging to a decade high. Over the same timeframe, Brazil consolidated its position as the largest exporter, and export volumes either rose or held steady in all four nations.

Starting at US$4.4 per kilogram in 2014, the world price fell continuously to US$2.6 in 2020, a drop of around 40%. The subsequent recovery was far steeper: within two years the price had doubled to US$5.2, and by 2024 it had reached US$6.1, well above its initial level.

Brazil's exports rose from 2.1 to 2.6 million tonnes, widening its lead over Vietnam, the second largest exporter, whose volumes barely changed (1.5 and 1.6 million tonnes). Colombia's exports remained static at 0.7 million tonnes. Ethiopia, by contrast, was by far the smallest exporter, yet it recorded the most rapid proportional growth, with its exports doubling from 0.2 to 0.4 million tonnes.

items.title: Total student numbers, 2019–2025
items.prompt: The bar chart below shows the number of students at a university from 2019 to 2025, and the pie charts show the students' places of origin in 2019 and 2025. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

modelAnswer.text:
The bar chart presents undergraduate and postgraduate enrolment at a university between 2019 and 2025, and the pie charts break down the student body by place of origin in the first and last of those years.

The university expanded over the six years, largely because of a surge in postgraduate numbers, and its intake became markedly more international, even though students from the home region remained the single largest group.

Undergraduates vastly outnumbered postgraduates throughout, but their numbers grew only modestly, from 14.5 thousand to 16.1 thousand. Postgraduate enrolment, by contrast, rose at an accelerating pace, from 3.2 thousand in 2019 to 5.1 thousand in 2023 and 6.4 thousand in 2025, precisely double its starting level. As a result, the total number of students increased from 17.7 thousand to 22.5 thousand.

The make-up of the student body also changed considerably. In 2019, over half of all students (55%) came from the university's home region, while 30% were from other regions and only 15% from overseas. By 2025, the home-region share had contracted to 44%, and that of other regions had edged down to 28%. International students, meanwhile, had almost doubled their share to 28%, drawing level with those from other regions.

items.title: Electricity generation by source, 2024
items.prompt: The pie chart below shows how a country's electricity was generated in 2024, and the line graph shows electricity prices for households and businesses between 2016 and 2024. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

modelAnswer.text:
The pie chart breaks down electricity generation in one country by source in 2024, while the line graph tracks the average price of electricity paid by households and businesses from 2016 to 2024.

Natural gas and wind power dominated the generation mix, whereas coal had become almost negligible. Prices for both types of consumer were broadly stable until 2020 before spiking sharply, and although they eased by 2024, they remained far higher than at the start of the period.

Natural gas supplied the largest share of electricity, at 38%, with wind not far behind at 27%. Nuclear power contributed a further 14%, while biomass and solar accounted for 9% and 7% respectively. Coal generated a mere 2%, even less than the 3% from other sources.

Households consistently paid more per unit than businesses. Between 2016 and 2020, household prices crept up from 15 to 17 cents per kWh and business prices from 11 to 12 cents. Over the following two years, however, the household price doubled to 34 cents, and the business price more than doubled to 29 cents. By 2024 they had fallen back to 27 and 21 cents respectively, still 12 and 10 cents higher than in 2016.

items.title: Weekly household energy spending by income group
items.prompt: The bar chart below shows average weekly spending on energy by households in five income groups, and the table shows the average energy used by each group. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

parts.title: Weekly household energy spending by income group
Household energy use and share of income

modelAnswer.text:
The bar chart compares average weekly energy expenditure across five household income groups, and the table details each group's annual energy consumption together with the share of income that this spending represents.

Wealthier households both spend more on energy and use more of it, yet energy costs place a far heavier burden on lower-income households, for whom they absorb a much larger proportion of earnings.

Weekly spending climbs steadily through the income bands, from $28 for the lowest fifth to $42 for the fourth, before jumping to $55 for the top fifth, almost double the figure for the poorest group. Energy consumption follows the same upward gradient: the lowest-income households use 9,800 kWh annually, while the highest-income households use 19,200 kWh, again nearly twice as much.

The relationship reverses, however, when spending is viewed as a percentage of income. The poorest fifth of households devote 11.2% of their income to energy, around four times the proportion spent by the richest fifth (2.9%). Between these extremes, the figure declines progressively, from 7.5% for the second group to 5.4% for the middle group and 4.1% for the fourth.

items.title: Cinema tickets sold, 2000–2024
items.prompt: The line graph shows the number of cinema tickets sold in one country from 2000 to 2024, and the pie chart shows how adults usually watched films in 2024. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

modelAnswer.text:
The line graph traces annual cinema ticket sales in one country from 2000 to 2024, while the pie chart identifies the main way in which adults watched films in the final year.

Ticket sales held up well for most of the period but slumped dramatically in 2020 and had not fully recovered by 2024. By that year, streaming had become the dominant means of watching films, with the cinema a relatively marginal choice.

After rising from 142 million in 2000 to 171 million in 2004, sales plateaued, remaining within a narrow range of 164 to 172 million until 2016. This stability ended abruptly in 2020, when sales plummeted to 44 million, roughly a quarter of the 2016 figure. items.title: Household waste produced
items.prompt: The table shows the amount of household waste produced in a city between 2000 and 2024, and the bar chart shows how that waste was disposed of. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

modelAnswer.text:
The table presents the total and per capita amounts of household waste generated in a city in four years between 2000 and 2024, and the bar chart shows how this waste was dealt with.

The volume of waste peaked in 2008 and declined thereafter, while methods of disposal were transformed: landfill, initially the overwhelmingly dominant method, became the least used, overtaken by both recycling and incineration.

The city produced 420 thousand tonnes of household waste in 2000, rising to 455 thousand tonnes in 2008. Output then fell in each subsequent year shown, reaching 395 thousand tonnes in 2024. Waste per person mirrored this trend but fell more steeply, from a high of 535 kg in 2008 to 425 kg in 2024, roughly a fifth lower.

In 2000, almost four fifths of household waste (79%) was sent to landfill, with recycling and composting handling 14% and incineration just 7%. Over the following 24 years, landfill's share shrank to a mere 12%, whereas recycling and composting nearly quadrupled to 52%, making it the leading method by 2016. Incineration for energy, which had grown only marginally by 2008, expanded rapidly thereafter, accounting for over a third of waste (36%) by 2024.

items.title: Average age at first marriage, 1970–2020
items.prompt: The line graph below shows the average age at which men and women in one country first married between 1970 and 2020, and the bar chart shows the number of marriages in the same period. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

modelAnswer.text:
The line graph charts the average age at which men and women in one country entered their first marriage between 1970 and 2020, and the bar chart records the number of marriages across the same period.

Two clear trends emerge: first marriages took place progressively later in life for both sexes, and the number of marriages fell continuously, more than halving over the fifty years.

In 1970, men first married at an average age of 24.4 and women at 22.4. The rise was modest in the 1970s, but it accelerated markedly from 1980, and by 2020 the respective averages had reached 33.8 and 31.9, an increase of more than nine years for each sex. Notably, the gap between men and women remained remarkably consistent, at roughly two years, throughout the period.

Meanwhile, the number of marriages dropped from 415 thousand in 1970 to 331 thousand in 1990. The steepest fall came in the following decade, when the total declined by 63 thousand to 268 thousand. The downward trend continued into the twenty-first century, and by 2020 just 196 thousand marriages were recorded, fewer than half the number fifty years earlier.

items.title: Working arrangements, 2019
items.prompt: The pie charts below show the ways in which a company's employees worked in 2019 and 2024, and the bar chart shows the company's office costs over the same period. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

modelAnswer.text:
The pie charts show how a company's workforce was divided between office-based, hybrid and fully remote working in 2019 and 2024, and the bar chart details the company's annual office costs from 2019 to 2024.

Over the five years, hybrid working replaced full-time office attendance as the predominant arrangement, and the company's office costs fell substantially, with rent accounting for most of the saving.

In 2019, 82% of employees worked full-time in the office, compared with 12% on hybrid arrangements and just 6% working fully remotely. By 2024 this pattern had been largely reversed: hybrid working accounted for 58% of staff, full-time office workers for only 24%, and the remote share had tripled to 18%.

Total office costs stood at $6.4 million in 2019. Rent was fixed at $4.8 million for the first three years, so the initial dip to $5.7 million in 2020 stemmed entirely from lower spending on energy and services, which fell from $1.6 million to $0.9 million. Rent was then cut to $3.1 million in 2022 and to $2.6 million in 2024, and energy and service costs, after a modest rebound to $1.3 million, eased back to $1.0 million. Consequently, total costs in 2024 were $3.6 million, some 44% below the 2019 figure.

items.title: Employment by sector
items.prompt: The bar chart shows the number of people employed in three sectors in a region in 1980 and 2020, and the line graph shows the region's unemployment rate during the same period. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

modelAnswer.text:
The bar chart compares employment in manufacturing, mining and services in a region in 1980 and 2020, while the line graph tracks the regional unemployment rate over the intervening four decades.

The region's economy underwent a profound structural change, with services replacing manufacturing and mining as the main source of jobs. Unemployment was volatile, surging in the early 1980s and rising again around 2010, yet by 2020 it had fallen back almost to its 1980 level.

Manufacturing was the leading employer in 1980, with 310 thousand workers, but by 2020 its workforce had shrunk by more than half to 120 thousand. The contraction in mining was even more severe, from 95 thousand jobs to just 8 thousand. Services moved in the opposite direction, more than doubling from 240 thousand to 520 thousand workers, so that total employment across the three sectors was almost unchanged.

The unemployment rate rose from 5.1% in 1980 to a peak of 13.8% in 1985, before declining steadily to 6.1% by 2005. A second, smaller increase took it to 8.9% in 2010, after which it eased again, standing at 5.3% in 2020, only marginally above the rate forty years earlier.

items.title: Electric vehicles in use, 2016–2024
items.prompt: The line graph shows the number of electric vehicles on the roads of one country from 2016 to 2024, and the bar chart shows the number of public charging points in four regions in 2016 and 2024. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

modelAnswer.text:
The line graph shows how many electric vehicles were in use in one country from 2016 to 2024, while the bar chart compares the provision of public charging points across four regions in 2016 and 2024.

Electric vehicle numbers grew at an accelerating rate throughout the period, and charging infrastructure expanded dramatically in all four regions, although the capital retained a commanding lead.

From a modest base of 45 thousand in 2016, the number of electric vehicles more than doubled in each two-year interval up to 2022, when it reached 620 thousand. It then climbed by a further 530 thousand to 1,150 thousand in 2024, roughly 25 times the initial figure.

The number of charging points increased at least tenfold in every region. The capital, which already had 1.8 thousand points in 2016, had 19.5 thousand by 2024, more than the other three regions combined (18.1 thousand). Proportionally, however, the fastest expansion took place in the Central region, where provision rose thirteenfold from 0.6 to 7.8 thousand. The South also grew rapidly, from 0.5 to 6.2 thousand, while the North, starting from the lowest base of 0.4 thousand, still had the fewest points in 2024, at 4.1 thousand.

items.title: Children's daily activities (ages 8–12)
items.prompt: The bar chart shows the average amount of time children in one country spent on different activities each day in 2004 and 2024, and the pie chart shows the devices they used to go online in 2024. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

charts.label: Main device used to go online, 2024

modelAnswer.text:
The bar chart compares how children aged 8 to 12 in one country divided their time between five daily activities in 2004 and 2024, and the pie chart identifies the main devices they used to go online in 2024.

The most striking change was the explosive growth in time spent online or gaming, which became by far the largest daily activity, while television viewing and outdoor play fell sharply. Handheld devices, particularly smartphones, were the main means of internet access.

In 2004, television and outdoor play were children's principal pastimes, occupying 125 and 115 minutes a day respectively, whereas online activities and games accounted for a mere 20 minutes. By 2024, the latter had soared to 175 minutes, almost three hours, which exceeded the combined time spent on all four other activities (162 minutes). Television and outdoor play had both more than halved, to 48 and 52 minutes, and reading had fallen from 35 to 22 minutes. Homework was the most stable activity, decreasing only marginally from 45 to 40 minutes.

Smartphones were the leading device for going online, used by 46% of children, with tablets second at 31%. Games consoles (12%) and laptops or PCs (9%) were far less common, and smart TVs were negligible at just 2%.

items.title: Water consumption in Aldburgh
items.prompt: The table below shows water consumption in a city in 2004 and 2024, and the bar chart shows the reservoir level at the end of each season in 2024. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

parts.title: Reservoir level at end of season, 2024

modelAnswer.text:
The table details daily water consumption in Aldburgh by type of use in 2004 and 2024, and the bar chart shows the city's reservoir level at the end of each season in 2024.

The city's total water use fell markedly over the twenty years, mainly because of reductions in industrial demand and leakage. In 2024, the reservoir followed a clear seasonal cycle, being fullest after winter and most depleted after summer.

Total consumption dropped from 337 to 260 million litres per day, a reduction of 77 million litres. Industry and leakage together accounted for most of this decrease: industrial use fell from 96 to 54 million litres, and losses through leakage were cut from 61 to 33 million. Homes continued to be the largest consumer, although their use eased from 142 to 128 million litres. Commerce and offices bucked the overall trend, with consumption rising from 38 to 45 million litres.

The reservoir stood at 94% of capacity at the end of winter, slipping to 82% by the end of spring. It then dropped steeply over the summer, to just 51%, before partially recovering to 67% by the end of autumn.

items.title: Average new home price, 2000–2024
items.prompt: The line graph shows the average price of a new home in one country between 2000 and 2024, and the bar chart compares average house prices with average annual earnings in the same years. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

modelAnswer.text:
The line graph tracks the average price of a new home in one country from 2000 to 2024, and the bar chart expresses average house prices as a multiple of average annual earnings over the same years.

Both measures rose markedly across the period, interrupted only by a modest dip in 2012, indicating that housing became considerably less affordable.

The average new home cost US$96 thousand in 2000, but prices increased sharply over the next eight years to US$186 thousand. After easing to US$172 thousand in 2012, they resumed their upward path, climbing to US$251 thousand by 2020 and US$298 thousand by 2024, more than three times their 2000 level.

The price-to-earnings ratio mirrored this pattern closely. In 2000, a home cost 4.1 times the average annual wage, a figure that had climbed to 6.3 by 2008 before slipping to 5.7 in 2012. Thereafter, the ratio rose without interruption, to 6.6 in 2016, 7.2 in 2020 and 8.1 in 2024. In other words, relative to earnings, housing was almost twice as expensive at the end of the period as it had been at the start, although this near doubling was far smaller than the more than threefold rise in prices themselves.

items.title: Causes of global forest loss, 2001–2020
items.prompt: The pie chart below shows the causes of global forest loss between 2001 and 2020, and the bar chart shows the area of forest lost in four regions in the same period. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

modelAnswer.text:
The pie chart breaks down the causes of global forest loss between 2001 and 2020, while the bar chart compares the area of forest lost in four regions over the same period.

Forest loss resulted from four main drivers of broadly similar significance, with urban expansion a negligible factor. Regionally, South America suffered the greatest losses, although all four regions lost substantial areas of forest.

Commodity agriculture was the single largest cause, accounting for 27% of forest loss, marginally ahead of forestry and logging at 26%. items.title: Annual museum visitors, 2016–2024
items.prompt: The line graph shows the number of visitors to a museum each year between 2016 and 2024, and the table shows the museum's sources of income in 2016 and 2024. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

modelAnswer.text:
The line graph charts annual visitor numbers at a museum from 2016 to 2024, while the table sets out the museum's income by source in the first and last of those years.

Apart from a severe slump in 2020, attendance rose throughout the period, ending at its highest level. Over the same timeframe, the museum's income grew and its funding shifted markedly away from government support towards earned revenue, particularly ticket sales.

Visitor numbers increased steadily from 610 thousand in 2016 to 720 thousand in 2019, before plunging to just 150 thousand in 2020, only around a fifth of the previous year's total. The recovery was rapid: attendance almost doubled to 280 thousand in 2021, reached 680 thousand in 2023, and hit a high of 760 thousand in 2024.

In 2016, the government grant of US$6.2 million made up well over half of the museum's US$10.7 million income. By 2024, however, the grant had been cut to US$4.1 million and was overtaken by ticket sales, which nearly doubled from US$2.4 million to US$4.6 million. Revenue from the shop and café rose by a similar proportion, from US$1.3 million to US$2.5 million, and donations edged up from US$0.8 million to US$1.1 million. As a result, total income reached US$12.3 million.

items.title: Homework in primary schools
items.prompt:
Some people believe that homework should be abolished in primary schools because young children need time to play and rest after the school day. To what extent do you agree or disagree?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

modelAnswer.text:
The question of whether primary school children should be set homework has become increasingly contentious, with critics arguing that young pupils need their evenings for play and rest. I agree with this view to a considerable extent: formal homework offers limited academic benefit at this age, and the time it consumes is better spent on activities that support children's broader development. Nevertheless, I would stop short of banning all learning outside school.

The strongest case for abolition rests on how young children actually learn. At primary level, understanding is built largely through exploration, conversation and play rather than through repetitive written exercises. A seven-year-old who spends an evening building something with friends or helping to cook a meal is practising language, problem-solving and cooperation in a way that a worksheet rarely replicates. Rest matters just as much: tired children struggle to concentrate, and a school day followed by an hour of compulsory tasks can leave little room for the sleep and relaxation they need.

Homework also tends to widen existing inequalities. Pupils whose parents have the time and confidence to help them tend to complete assignments to a high standard, whereas those from busier or less advantaged households may fall behind or become discouraged. In such cases, what is intended as extra practice ends up rewarding family circumstances rather than effort, and can turn evenings into a source of tension.

That said, there is a difference between set homework and encouraging a love of learning at home. Reading together for pleasure, for example, is widely regarded as valuable and places little strain on children. Schools could therefore replace compulsory assignments with optional, informal suggestions of this kind.

Overall, I largely support abolishing formal homework in primary schools, since young children gain more from play, rest and family life. Informal reading at home, however, should still be warmly encouraged.

items.title: AI and take-home assignments
items.prompt:
As artificial intelligence becomes more capable, universities should stop assessing students through written assignments that are completed at home. To what extent do you agree or disagree?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

modelAnswer.text:
Generative AI has made it possible for almost anyone to produce a fluent essay in seconds, and this has led some commentators to argue that universities should abandon take-home written assignments altogether. I agree with this position only to a limited extent. While unsupervised essays can no longer be trusted as the sole measure of a student's ability, eliminating them entirely would sacrifice some of the most important aims of higher education.

It is undeniable that the traditional take-home essay has become vulnerable. Detection software is unreliable, and a student who submits machine-generated text with a few careful edits may be almost impossible to identify. When grades can be obtained without genuine learning, qualifications lose credibility, and conscientious students are effectively penalised for their honesty. For modules where assessment is heavily weighted towards a single essay, the case for introducing supervised elements is therefore compelling.

However, extended written work serves purposes that invigilated exams cannot. Producing a substantial piece of writing requires students to locate and evaluate sources, sustain an argument and revise their thinking over time. These are precisely the capabilities employers and researchers value, and they cannot be demonstrated in a two-hour sitting where memory and speed are rewarded above reflection. Replacing coursework wholesale with exams would, in effect, narrow what universities teach to what can be tested under pressure.

The more productive response is to rethink how assignments are designed and verified. Requiring annotated drafts, research logs or a brief viva in which students defend their arguments makes outsourcing far less attractive. Tasks grounded in personal fieldwork, recent seminar discussions or original data are also much harder to delegate to a general-purpose model.

In short, AI has exposed genuine weaknesses in take-home assessment, but the appropriate remedy is reform rather than abolition. Universities that adapt their assignments thoughtfully can protect academic integrity without abandoning the independent thinking that written work develops.

items.title: Companies versus consumers
items.prompt:
The responsibility for protecting the environment lies mainly with large companies rather than with individual consumers. To what extent do you agree or disagree?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

modelAnswer.text:
Whether environmental protection is chiefly the duty of large corporations or of individual consumers is a question that shapes how societies respond to climate change and pollution. In my view, the primary responsibility does lie with major companies, but framing the issue as a choice between the two risks overlooking how closely their behaviour is connected.

The case for holding corporations principally accountable is persuasive. Industrial production, energy generation and global supply chains account for a large share of emissions, and decisions taken in a handful of boardrooms determine how goods are made, transported and packaged for millions of people. When a major retailer eliminates single-use plastics or an airline invests in cleaner fuels, the environmental gain dwarfs anything a conscientious shopper could achieve alone. Companies also have the capital to fund research into cleaner technologies, and they are the ones that profit from environmentally harmful practices, which strengthens the moral argument for making them pay for the damage.

Moreover, emphasising personal responsibility can be misleading. Consumers can only choose from the options available to them, and sustainable alternatives are often more expensive or simply unavailable. A family living in a suburb without reliable public transport, for instance, has little choice but to drive. Urging such people to change their habits while leaving corporate practices largely untouched shifts the burden onto those with the least power to solve the problem.

This is not to say that individuals are irrelevant. Collective consumer behaviour sends signals that companies cannot ignore, and public pressure is often what persuades governments to regulate industry more strictly. The growth of demand for plant-based food and electric vehicles illustrates how shifting preferences can reshape entire markets.

Overall, I agree that large companies bear the greater responsibility, given their scale, resources and profits. Consumers, however, remain an important catalyst, since their choices and political pressure help to ensure that corporations actually meet that responsibility.

items.title: Free public transport
items.prompt:
Public transport in cities should be completely free of charge in order to reduce traffic congestion. To what extent do you agree or disagree?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

modelAnswer.text:
Abolishing fares on buses, trams and trains is sometimes presented as a simple remedy for urban traffic congestion. While I accept that free public transport has genuine social merits, I disagree that it is, by itself, an effective way of reducing congestion, and I believe the money it would require could be spent more productively.

The appeal of fare-free travel is easy to understand. It removes a cost that weighs most heavily on low-income households, simplifies journeys for occasional users and sends a strong public signal that the city values collective transport over private cars. For young people and those on modest wages, eliminating fares might well be the deciding factor that makes the bus a realistic alternative.

The difficulty is that motorists are generally less sensitive to price than to time and convenience. A commuter who drives does so because the car offers a direct, predictable journey; if the equivalent trip by public transport involves two changes and a long wait, making it free will rarely alter that calculation. Experience in several cities suggests that fare-free schemes tend to attract people who would otherwise have walked or cycled, which increases demand on the network without taking many cars off the road.

There is also the question of funding. Ticket revenue typically covers a substantial part of operating costs, and replacing it would place a permanent burden on public budgets. When finances tighten, it is service frequency and maintenance that usually suffer first, precisely the qualities that persuade drivers to switch.

Congestion is therefore better addressed through a combination of measures: sustained investment in faster, more frequent services, dedicated bus lanes, and policies such as road pricing that reflect the true cost of driving. Targeted discounts can protect those on the lowest incomes without sacrificing essential revenue.

In conclusion, free public transport may be socially desirable, but as a strategy for reducing congestion it promises more than it is likely to deliver.

items.title: Protecting historic city centres
items.prompt:
Governments should prevent the construction of new buildings in historic city centres, even if this limits economic growth and the supply of housing. To what extent do you agree or disagree?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

modelAnswer.text:
Historic city centres are among the most visible expressions of a society's past, and the pressure to redevelop them is often intense. The proposal that governments should forbid all new construction in these districts, regardless of the economic and housing consequences, reflects a legitimate concern for heritage. However, I largely disagree with it, since a blanket prohibition would ultimately harm the very places it aims to preserve.

It is certainly true that insensitive development can do irreversible damage. A single oversized office block can dominate a skyline that has remained largely unchanged for centuries, and the demolition of a period building cannot be undone. Historic quarters also have considerable economic value in their own right, drawing visitors whose spending supports thousands of local businesses. For these reasons, protecting landmarks and the overall character of old districts should be a clear priority for planners.

Yet a complete ban confuses preservation with freezing a city in time. Historic centres have always evolved, with each generation adding buildings of its own era, and many admired streets are the result of such layering. More practically, prohibiting construction where land is most in demand drives up property prices, forces lower-income residents out and leaves the centre dominated by short-term lets and souvenir shops. The outcome is often a district that looks authentic but has lost the everyday life that once defined it.

A more sophisticated approach combines firm protection with carefully managed change. Listed buildings can be safeguarded absolutely, while strict design codes govern the height, materials and scale of anything new. Derelict sites and disused commercial buildings can be converted into homes, bringing residents back without compromising the streetscape. This allows cities to accommodate growth while keeping their historic identity intact.

In conclusion, historic centres deserve robust protection, but an outright ban on new building would sacrifice housing, vitality and affordability for the sake of a static appearance. Intelligent regulation, rather than prohibition, is the better course.

A more sophisticated approach combines firm protection with carefully managed change. Listed buildings can be safeguarded absolutely, while strict design codes govern the height, materials and scale of anything new. Derelict sites and disused commercial buildings can be converted into homes, bringing residents back without compromising the streetscape. This allows cities to accommodate growth while keeping their historic identity intact.

In conclusion, historic centres deserve robust protection, but an outright ban on new building would sacrifice housing, vitality and affordability for the sake of a static appearance. Intelligent regulation, rather than prohibition, is the better course.

items.title: Learning ability over qualifications
items.prompt:
In the future, a person's ability to learn new skills quickly will be more important than the qualifications they hold. To what extent do you agree or disagree?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

modelAnswer.text:
As automation and digital technology reshape the labour market, many commentators predict that the ability to learn quickly will soon outweigh the value of formal qualifications. I agree with this prediction to a large extent, although I believe qualifications will remain important as a baseline, particularly in regulated professions.

The central argument concerns the shrinking shelf life of knowledge. A graduate entering the workforce today may find that much of what they studied is obsolete within a decade, as new tools, regulations and business models emerge. In such an environment, what distinguishes successful employees is not what they learnt at twenty-two but how effectively they can master unfamiliar tasks at forty. A marketing specialist who can quickly grasp a new analytics platform, for instance, is often more valuable to an employer than a colleague with a more prestigious degree who struggles to adapt.

Hiring practices already reflect this shift. A growing number of companies assess candidates through practical tasks and probation periods rather than relying solely on certificates, and some technology firms have dropped degree requirements for certain roles altogether. At the same time, the availability of online courses and workplace training means that skills can be acquired and demonstrated outside traditional education, weakening the monopoly that formal credentials once held.

Nevertheless, qualifications are unlikely to disappear. In professions where mistakes can endanger lives, such as surgery or civil engineering, society rightly insists on rigorous, standardised training that cannot be replaced by a talent for fast learning. Degrees also signal persistence and a foundation of knowledge on which further learning can be built.

On balance, I expect qualifications to become a starting point rather than a guarantee of career success. Adaptability and the capacity for continuous learning will increasingly determine who thrives, while formal credentials will remain indispensable only where public safety and professional standards demand them.

items.title: Advertising to young children
items.prompt:
All advertising aimed at children under the age of twelve should be banned. To what extent do you agree or disagree?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

modelAnswer.text:
Advertisers spend vast sums targeting children, whose influence over family spending is considerable. The suggestion that all advertising aimed at under-twelves should be prohibited is therefore a significant one, and I agree with it to a large extent, while recognising that a ban would need to be carefully defined to be workable.

The most compelling argument concerns children's cognitive development. Younger children often struggle to recognise the persuasive intent behind an advertisement and are inclined to accept its claims uncritically. Marketing techniques that would barely register with an adult, such as a favourite cartoon character endorsing a snack or a toy shown in an exaggeratedly exciting setting, can be highly effective on a seven-year-old. Directing such messages at an audience that cannot defend itself against them is difficult to justify ethically.

The consequences extend beyond the individual child. Advertising to children is dominated by foods high in sugar and fat, and repeated exposure shapes preferences that may persist into adulthood, with obvious implications for public health. It also fuels what is often called "pester power", placing parents under pressure to buy products they cannot afford or would not otherwise choose, and encouraging children to measure their worth by what they own.

Critics of a ban raise two points: that it would unfairly restrict legitimate businesses, and that parents, not governments, should protect their children. Yet firms would remain free to advertise to adults, who make the actual purchasing decisions, and the sheer volume of online marketing, much of it embedded in games and videos, makes parental supervision alone unrealistic.

The main practical challenge lies in enforcement, particularly on digital platforms where age and intent are harder to define. Clear rules on content designed to appeal to children would be essential.

In conclusion, I strongly support banning advertising aimed at children under twelve. Their vulnerability to persuasion outweighs the commercial arguments against such a restriction.

items.title: Taxing unhealthy food
items.prompt:
Governments should tax unhealthy foods, such as sugary drinks and fast food, in the same way that they tax tobacco. To what extent do you agree or disagree?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

modelAnswer.text:
With obesity and related conditions placing growing strain on health systems, some argue that governments should tax sugary drinks and fast food as they tax tobacco. I agree that fiscal measures have a role to play, particularly for sugar-sweetened beverages, but I believe equating unhealthy food with tobacco is both conceptually flawed and potentially counterproductive.

The case for taxation rests on sound principles. Consumers respond to price, and the dramatic decline in smoking in many countries owes much to sustained increases in tobacco duty. Sugary drinks are an especially suitable target: they provide calories with virtually no nutritional value, they are easy to define, and there is evidence that levies on them encourage manufacturers to reduce sugar content. Revenue raised in this way can be reinvested in school meals, sports facilities or subsidies for fresh produce, amplifying the health benefit.

Nevertheless, food differs from tobacco in crucial respects. Cigarettes are harmful in any quantity, whereas burgers, chips or chocolate are problematic only as part of an unbalanced diet. A tax modelled on tobacco would therefore treat moderate consumption as though it were inherently dangerous, which many people would reasonably regard as excessive state intervention. Moreover, "fast food" is a notoriously vague category, and drawing a line between a takeaway meal and a restaurant dish would invite both confusion and avoidance.

There is also the issue of fairness. Food taxes are regressive, weighing most heavily on households with the least disposable income, and in areas where fresh food is expensive or hard to obtain, higher prices may simply reduce families' budgets rather than change what they eat. Any such tax must therefore be paired with measures that make healthy alternatives genuinely affordable.

In conclusion, targeted taxes on clearly defined products like sugary drinks are justified, but applying a tobacco-style regime to unhealthy food in general would be neither fair nor effective.

items.title: Who teaches good behaviour?
items.prompt:
Parents, rather than teachers, should be mainly responsible for teaching children good behaviour and respect for others. To what extent do you agree or disagree?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

modelAnswer.text:
The question of who should teach children good behaviour and respect for others is often framed as a choice between home and school. I agree that parents should bear the primary responsibility, since the values children absorb in their earliest years are formed largely within the family. However, I would argue that teachers play an indispensable supporting role rather than a marginal one.

The strongest argument for parental responsibility lies in the timing and nature of early learning. Children's attitudes towards others begin to take shape long before they enter a classroom, and they are shaped less by explicit instruction than by imitation. A toddler who sees a parent listen patiently, apologise when wrong and treat service workers courteously internalises these patterns almost unconsciously. Parents also have a depth of knowledge about their own child and the continuity of contact over many years that no teacher, responsible for thirty pupils for a single year, can match.

There is also a question of accountability. If parents come to assume that manners and respect will be taught at school, they may neglect this aspect of upbringing, leaving teachers to address behavioural problems that divert time from learning. Recognising that the family is the first line of moral education places responsibility where it can be exercised most effectively.

That said, schools offer something that homes cannot: a structured community of peers. Learning to share resources, wait one's turn, work with classmates one did not choose and respect people from different cultures are lessons best learnt in a group setting. Teachers who model fairness and enforce consistent rules can reinforce good habits and, crucially, compensate for children who receive little guidance at home.

In conclusion, parents should be principally responsible for teaching good behaviour and respect, but this responsibility is most effectively fulfilled when schools reinforce and extend the values children first learn within the family.

items.title: Circumstances in sentencing
items.prompt:
When deciding on a punishment, courts should consider only the crime that was committed, not the personal background or circumstances of the offender. To what extent do you agree or disagree?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

modelAnswer.text:
Whether sentencing should be based purely on the offence, or should also take account of the offender's background, touches on a fundamental tension in criminal justice between consistency and individual fairness. I disagree with the view that courts should consider only the crime, although I accept that the weight given to personal circumstances must be carefully limited.

The argument for focusing exclusively on the offence has genuine merit. Equality before the law implies that similar acts should attract similar penalties, and sentencing that varies according to personal history risks appearing arbitrary. There is also a legitimate worry that well-resourced defendants, able to present their lives sympathetically through expensive legal representation, may secure more lenient treatment than those without such advantages.

However, a system that looks only at the act itself would disregard the degree of culpability, which is central to any meaningful notion of justice. An offence committed by someone acting under coercion, suffering from a serious mental illness or driven by desperate need is not morally equivalent to the same act committed out of greed or cruelty. Most legal systems already recognise this through concepts such as mitigating and aggravating factors, and removing them would make sentences blunter rather than fairer.

Circumstances are also relevant to the forward-looking purposes of punishment. A sentence is not merely retribution; it is intended to protect the public and reduce the likelihood of reoffending. Understanding that a young offender's behaviour is rooted in addiction or an unstable home allows a court to choose interventions, such as supervised treatment, that address the underlying cause rather than simply imposing a custodial term.

The key, therefore, is proportion. The seriousness of the offence should set the broad range of any sentence, while personal circumstances inform where within that range it falls. On this basis, I believe courts are right to consider both, rather than the crime alone.
