items.title: Opinion in news reporting
items.prompt:
News organisations should report only facts and should never include the personal opinions of their journalists. To what extent do you agree or disagree?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

modelAnswer.text:
Concerns about media bias and misinformation have prompted calls for news organisations to report nothing but verifiable facts, excluding the personal views of their journalists altogether. I agree that the core of news reporting should be factual and impartial, but I disagree that opinion should never appear, since informed commentary, when clearly identified, serves a valuable public function.

The argument for strict factual reporting is rooted in the democratic role of the press. Citizens depend on the news to understand events and hold those in power to account, and they are entitled to form their own conclusions. When commentary is woven into ostensibly neutral reports, readers may absorb a journalist's perspective without recognising it as such. This subtle blurring is arguably more damaging than openly partisan coverage, because it erodes the audience's ability to distinguish evidence from interpretation, and with it their trust in the media as a whole.

Yet it is naive to suppose that facts can be presented without any judgement. Deciding which stories to cover, which sources to quote and what context to include already involves editorial choices. Moreover, many issues, from climate policy to interest rates, are so complex that raw data offers little insight to non-specialists. A correspondent with years of experience can explain why an event matters and what its likely implications are, which enriches public understanding rather than distorting it.

The more sensible standard, therefore, is transparency rather than prohibition. News reports should strive for accuracy and balance, while analysis and opinion should be explicitly labelled and presented separately, as is the practice in most respected publications. The challenge in the digital age is to preserve this distinction when articles are shared on social media, often stripped of the labels that signal their purpose.

In conclusion, factual reporting should remain the foundation of journalism, but clearly marked opinion has a legitimate place. The priority should be to keep the two distinct, not to eliminate commentary entirely.

items.title: Identity checks on social media
items.prompt:
Social media companies should be required to verify the real identity of every person who uses their platforms. To what extent do you agree or disagree?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

modelAnswer.text:
As concerns grow about online harassment, fraud and coordinated disinformation, the idea of obliging social media companies to verify the real identity of every user has gained considerable support. I agree that anonymity is sometimes abused, but I disagree with universal verification, which I believe would create serious new harms while doing relatively little to address the existing ones.

The appeal of the proposal is understandable. Anonymous accounts can be created in seconds, allowing individuals to harass others, operate networks of fake profiles or impersonate legitimate businesses with little fear of consequence. Linking every account to a verified person would, in theory, restore a degree of accountability and make it easier for victims and law enforcement to pursue those responsible.

In practice, however, the relationship between anonymity and misconduct is weaker than often assumed. A great deal of abusive content is posted openly under users' real names, indicating that social norms and platform design shape behaviour at least as much as identifiability does. Meanwhile, compelling billions of users to submit passports or identity cards would concentrate highly sensitive data in the hands of private companies, whose record in safeguarding personal information is far from reassuring. The consequences of a breach on that scale could be severe.

Equally significant is the value of anonymity to those with legitimate reasons to conceal their identity. Journalists' sources, employees exposing wrongdoing and political dissidents in repressive states often depend on pseudonyms to speak at all. For such users, mandatory verification would not merely be inconvenient; it could expose them to retaliation, with a chilling effect on precisely the kind of speech that open societies should protect.

More proportionate measures are available: verification for accounts that advertise, sell goods or reach very large audiences, stronger moderation, and swift cooperation with courts when unlawful conduct is reported.

In conclusion, universal identity checks would be a blunt instrument whose costs to privacy and freedom of expression outweigh its limited benefits.

items.title: Funding traditional crafts
items.prompt:
Governments should provide financial support for traditional arts and crafts, even when there is little public demand for them. To what extent do you agree or disagree?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

modelAnswer.text:
As global markets fill with inexpensive, mass-produced goods, many traditional arts and crafts are struggling to survive. Whether governments should fund them despite limited public demand is a question of how societies value their cultural inheritance. I agree that such support is justified, provided it is aimed at preservation and renewal rather than indefinite subsidy.

The strongest case for public funding is that traditional crafts embody knowledge that the market cannot adequately value. Techniques such as natural dyeing, instrument-making or regional embroidery have often been refined over centuries and are transmitted through years of apprenticeship rather than written manuals. Once the last generation of practitioners disappears, that knowledge is effectively irretrievable. Low demand at a given moment therefore says little about a craft's long-term worth, in the same way that a museum's value is not measured by its ticket sales.

Traditional arts also contribute to a community's identity and cohesion in ways that are difficult to quantify. Festivals, local markets and workshops centred on these crafts give places a distinctive character, foster pride among residents and can form the basis of cultural tourism. Targeted funding can help artisans reach new audiences, whether through collaborations with contemporary designers or through online platforms that connect them with buyers worldwide.

Admittedly, public budgets face competing demands, and it would be difficult to justify spending heavily on crafts while essential services are underfunded. There is also a risk that permanent subsidies preserve traditions in a lifeless, artificial form. These objections argue not against support altogether, but for designing it wisely: documenting endangered techniques, funding apprenticeships and helping practitioners develop sustainable businesses.

In conclusion, I believe governments should provide financial support for traditional arts and crafts even when demand is weak, since their cultural value far exceeds their current market value. The aim, however, should be to give these traditions a viable future rather than to keep them artificially alive.

Techniques such as natural dyeing, instrument-making or regional embroidery have often been refined over centuries and are transmitted through years of apprenticeship rather than written manuals. Once the last generation of practitioners disappears, that knowledge is effectively irretrievable. Low demand at a given moment therefore says little about a craft's long-term worth, in the same way that a museum's value is not measured by its ticket sales.

Traditional arts also contribute to a community's identity and cohesion in ways that are difficult to quantify. Festivals, local markets and workshops centred on these crafts give places a distinctive character, foster pride among residents and can form the basis of cultural tourism. Targeted funding can help artisans reach new audiences, whether through collaborations with contemporary designers or through online platforms that connect them with buyers worldwide.

Admittedly, public budgets face competing demands, and it would be difficult to justify spending heavily on crafts while essential services are underfunded. There is also a risk that permanent subsidies preserve traditions in a lifeless, artificial form. These objections argue not against support altogether, but for designing it wisely: documenting endangered techniques, funding apprenticeships and helping practitioners develop sustainable businesses.

In conclusion, I believe governments should provide financial support for traditional arts and crafts even when demand is weak, since their cultural value far exceeds their current market value. The aim, however, should be to give these traditions a viable future rather than to keep them artificially alive.

items.title: Limiting tourist numbers
items.prompt:
Popular tourist destinations should limit the number of visitors allowed each year in order to protect local communities. To what extent do you agree or disagree?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

modelAnswer.text:
Few issues illustrate the tension between economic opportunity and quality of life as sharply as mass tourism. Some argue that the most popular destinations should cap the number of visitors each year to protect local communities. I agree with this principle, but I believe that rigid annual limits are often less effective than more targeted forms of visitor management.

There is little doubt that unchecked tourism can seriously undermine residents' wellbeing. In some historic cities, the conversion of apartments into holiday lets has driven up rents to the point where long-standing residents are priced out, while local shops give way to souvenir outlets. Overcrowded streets, congested public transport and constant noise can make everyday life exhausting. When a community begins to feel like a stage set for visitors, the very authenticity that attracted tourists is lost.

The environmental case is equally compelling. Coastal ecosystems, mountain paths and archaeological sites can absorb only so much footfall before suffering lasting damage. For such places, limiting access is not merely desirable but essential if they are to survive in any recognisable form.

However, a single annual quota is a rather crude tool. Tourist pressure is usually concentrated in particular seasons, days and districts, so a yearly cap may do little to relieve overcrowding at peak times while needlessly turning visitors away in quieter periods. It could also harm the many residents whose livelihoods depend on tourism. More refined measures, such as timed entry to key sites, daily limits on cruise-ship arrivals, restrictions on short-term rentals and higher fees in peak season, can address the specific sources of pressure while preserving the income that tourism brings.

In conclusion, popular destinations are right to control visitor numbers in order to protect their residents and environment. Yet this is best achieved through flexible, carefully targeted management rather than a blunt annual ceiling.

items.title: Practical or pure research?
items.prompt:
Scientific research should be funded according to its likely practical benefits rather than simply to increase human knowledge. To what extent do you agree or disagree?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

modelAnswer.text:
Decisions about which scientific research to fund have become increasingly contested, with some arguing that public money should be directed primarily towards projects likely to yield practical benefits. I disagree with this position. Although applied research clearly merits substantial investment, making practical utility the principal test for funding would, paradoxically, reduce the practical returns of science over time.

The case for prioritising applied research is not without force. Governments are accountable to taxpayers, and when resources are scarce it seems reasonable to favour work that promises better treatments, more efficient energy or safer infrastructure. In the face of pressing problems such as antibiotic resistance, research with clear objectives offers a tangible sense of progress.

The central difficulty, however, is that the usefulness of knowledge can rarely be foreseen. Many of the technologies that define modern life emerged from inquiries pursued for their own sake: studies of quantum behaviour made possible the semiconductors in every smartphone, while research into obscure bacteria provided the tools behind modern gene editing. No funding committee assessing these projects at the outset could have predicted such outcomes. A system that rewards only anticipated benefits would systematically overlook the unexpected discoveries that often prove most valuable.

Fundamental research also sustains the wider scientific ecosystem. It trains highly skilled researchers, generates the theoretical frameworks on which applied work depends and keeps a country at the frontier of knowledge. Moreover, there is intrinsic worth in understanding the origins of the universe or the workings of the mind, questions that reflect a basic human aspiration and inspire future generations of scientists.

The most sensible approach is therefore a portfolio: dedicated funding for mission-driven research on urgent problems, alongside secure support for curiosity-driven work judged on its scientific merit.

In conclusion, while practical benefits matter, they should not be the dominant criterion for funding science, since the pursuit of knowledge itself remains the most reliable source of future innovation.

items.title: A legal four-day week
items.prompt:
Employers should be legally required to allow staff to work a four-day week without any reduction in pay. To what extent do you agree or disagree?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

modelAnswer.text:
Trials of the four-day week in various countries have produced encouraging results, prompting calls for employers to be legally required to offer it with no reduction in pay. While I am broadly sympathetic to the aims of this proposal, I disagree that it should be made compulsory, since a universal mandate would fail to account for the diversity of modern workplaces.

The potential benefits are considerable. Long working hours are associated with stress, burnout and poorer physical health, and an additional day of rest could allow employees to recover, care for relatives and engage more fully in family and community life. Many organisations that have adopted a shorter week report that staff concentrate more effectively, waste less time in unnecessary meetings and are less likely to leave, suggesting that output need not fall when hours do. For knowledge-based work in particular, time spent at a desk is a poor measure of productivity.

However, these results come largely from firms that chose to participate and were able to reorganise their work accordingly. The picture is very different in sectors where output is tied directly to hours, such as healthcare, retail, hospitality and manufacturing. A hospital cannot simply provide twenty per cent less care; to maintain services on full pay, it would need to recruit additional staff, often in areas already facing shortages. For small businesses with tight margins, the added cost could lead to redundancies or closure, ultimately harming the workers the policy is meant to help.

A more effective approach would be to promote the four-day week through incentives and evidence rather than compulsion. Governments could fund pilot programmes, publish their findings and give employees a statutory right to request flexible arrangements, which employers could refuse only on reasonable grounds.

In conclusion, a four-day week may well represent the future of work in many industries, but legislating it for every employer would be premature and potentially damaging.

items.title: Renting versus home ownership
items.prompt:
Governments should focus on improving the quality and security of rented housing rather than helping young people to buy their own homes. To what extent do you agree or disagree?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

modelAnswer.text:
In many countries, soaring property prices have put home ownership beyond the reach of a generation of young adults. One response is to argue that governments should prioritise making rented housing better and more secure, rather than trying to help young people onto the property ladder. I agree with this view to a considerable extent, although I believe the two goals are more connected than the statement suggests.

The weakness of many home-ownership schemes lies in their effect on prices. When governments offer deposit grants or subsidised mortgages without increasing the supply of homes, they largely add to demand, and much of the benefit is absorbed by higher prices. These policies also tend to favour those already on the verge of buying, offering little to young people on modest or insecure incomes, and they can be costly for the public purse.

Improving the rental sector, in contrast, would directly benefit the millions of young people who rent, many of them for far longer than previous generations did. Too often they face damp or poorly insulated homes, unpredictable rent increases and the constant possibility of being asked to leave. Enforceable quality standards, longer and more secure tenancies and protection against arbitrary eviction would allow tenants to put down roots, enrol children in local schools and plan their lives with confidence. Where renting is well regulated, as in parts of continental Europe, it is regarded as a respectable long-term choice rather than a precarious stopgap.

Ownership nonetheless matters, not least because retired people who rent must meet housing costs from a reduced income. The most effective way to support it, however, is not through demand-side subsidies but by building more homes, which would also ease pressure on rents.

In conclusion, governments should make secure, decent rented housing their immediate priority, while pursuing wider access to ownership through increasing housing supply rather than through subsidies for individual buyers.

items.title: National food self-sufficiency
items.prompt:
In a globalised world, it is no longer necessary for every country to produce enough food to feed its own population. To what extent do you agree or disagree?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

modelAnswer.text:
The expansion of global trade has transformed how food reaches our tables, and some now argue that national food self-sufficiency has become an outdated goal. I agree that complete self-sufficiency is neither necessary nor, for many countries, achievable. However, I disagree with the broader implication that nations can safely neglect their capacity to feed themselves.

There is a strong economic logic to relying on trade. Agricultural conditions vary enormously, and forcing every country to grow all its own food would be highly inefficient. Arid or densely populated states would need to divert scarce water and land to crops that can be produced far more cheaply elsewhere, raising prices for their own citizens. Open markets allow resources to be used where they are most productive and can cushion the impact of a failed harvest in any one region by drawing on supplies from others.

Yet the assumption that global markets will always function smoothly is a dangerous one. Food supply chains are long and interdependent, and they have repeatedly proved fragile in the face of conflict, extreme weather and pandemics. When supplies tighten, exporting countries often prioritise their own populations by restricting sales abroad, precisely when importers need them most. Nations with weak domestic production and limited purchasing power are the first to suffer, and food shortages can quickly lead to social unrest.

Climate change is likely to heighten these risks, as droughts and floods disrupt harvests in major producing regions more frequently. In this context, maintaining a viable farming sector, diversifying import sources and holding strategic reserves are prudent forms of insurance rather than economic nationalism.

In conclusion, globalisation has made total self-sufficiency unnecessary, but it has not removed the need for food security. Each country should aim for sufficient domestic capacity and resilience to withstand disruption, even if it continues to rely on trade for much of what it consumes.

items.title: Do we still need libraries?
items.prompt:
Public libraries are no longer necessary because most information is now available online. To what extent do you agree or disagree?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

modelAnswer.text:
The claim that public libraries have been rendered obsolete by the internet rests on the assumption that their sole purpose is to supply information. I disagree with this view. While the internet has undoubtedly changed how people find information, libraries continue to fulfil social, educational and democratic functions that online resources cannot replicate.

Perhaps the most important of these is ensuring equal access. It is easy to assume that everyone is online, yet many households still lack a reliable connection, an adequate device or the skills needed to use them effectively. As more essential services, from job applications to benefit claims, move online, a library's free computers and trained staff become a lifeline for those at risk of being left behind. Closing libraries would therefore deepen existing inequalities at the very moment when digital participation has become essential.

Libraries also address a problem the internet has intensified rather than solved: the difficulty of distinguishing reliable information from falsehood. Librarians guide users towards credible sources and help them develop the critical skills to evaluate what they read. Moreover, much high-quality content, including many academic journals and recent books, remains behind paywalls, and libraries make it freely available to anyone.

Beyond information, libraries function as some of the few remaining public spaces that are open to everyone and require no payment. Students without a quiet place to study at home, parents attending reading sessions with toddlers and older people seeking company all rely on them. In an increasingly fragmented society, such shared spaces help sustain a sense of community.

This is not to suggest that libraries should remain unchanged. They must continue to evolve, expanding digital lending and offering training in technology. But adaptation is an argument for investment, not closure.

In conclusion, public libraries remain necessary because their value extends far beyond information retrieval, encompassing equality of access, digital literacy and community life.

items.title: Discouraging overconsumption
items.prompt:
Governments should take action to discourage people from buying more goods than they actually need. To what extent do you agree or disagree?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

modelAnswer.text:
Consumer culture in many prosperous countries encourages people to buy far more than they need, from fast fashion to frequently upgraded phones. The suggestion that governments should actively discourage this behaviour raises questions about both sustainability and personal freedom. On balance, I agree that intervention is justified, provided it targets the systems that drive overconsumption rather than policing individual purchases.

The environmental argument is compelling. The production, shipping and disposal of consumer goods account for a considerable share of resource use and emissions, and the problem is aggravated by products designed to be replaced rather than repaired. A garment worn a handful of times before being discarded, or a device abandoned because a single component has failed, represents a significant waste of materials and energy. Because these environmental costs are largely borne by society rather than by the buyer, the market alone has little incentive to correct them.

Governments possess tools that individuals do not. Legislation requiring durability, access to spare parts and a right to repair would extend the life of countless products. Tax policy could make repair and second-hand goods cheaper relative to new ones, while tighter rules on advertising, particularly the targeted online promotions that exploit impulse buying, would reduce the constant pressure to acquire more. Measures of this kind reshape the choices available without dictating what anyone must buy.

The main objections are that such policies infringe personal liberty and threaten economic growth. The first is less persuasive when intervention focuses on product standards and marketing rather than consumer decisions. The second deserves more attention, since many jobs depend on retail spending, but a shift towards repair, refurbishment and services can generate employment of its own.

In conclusion, governments are right to discourage excessive consumption, though the most effective and legitimate way to do so is by changing how goods are made and marketed, rather than by restricting what people are allowed to buy.

items.title: Foreign languages in primary school
items.prompt:
Some people believe that children should begin learning a foreign language at primary school. Others think it is better for them to start at secondary school. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

modelAnswer.text:
Few educational questions generate as much debate as when a child should first encounter a foreign language. Some maintain that it should be introduced in primary school, whereas others contend that it is more sensible to wait until secondary level. Having weighed both positions, I would argue that an early start is preferable, although its success depends on how it is implemented.

The case for delaying language study rests largely on the capabilities of older learners. By the age of eleven or twelve, pupils have developed the analytical skills needed to understand how a language is structured, and they can apply techniques such as comparing its grammar with that of their first language. This allows them to make rapid, systematic progress. Moreover, deferring a second language gives younger children time to consolidate reading and writing in their mother tongue, a foundation on which all later learning depends. From this perspective, early lessons may consume valuable classroom time without producing meaningful results.

Nevertheless, there are compelling reasons to begin sooner. Young children acquire language largely through imitation and play, and they are generally uninhibited about experimenting with unfamiliar sounds. Consequently, those who start early often develop more natural pronunciation and a more intuitive feel for the language than learners who begin in adolescence, when embarrassment can hold them back. An early start also provides more years of exposure, and sustained contact over a long period is what ultimately produces confident, fluent speakers.

On balance, I find the second argument more persuasive. The concerns raised about primary-level teaching are genuine, but they relate to poor delivery rather than to the principle itself. If lessons are brief, oral and enjoyable, and are led by properly trained teachers, they complement rather than compete with literacy in the first language.

In conclusion, while older pupils learn grammar more efficiently, the advantages of early exposure are difficult to replicate later in life. Children should therefore begin a foreign language in primary school, with formal study left to secondary level.

modelAnswer.text:

Some maintain that it should be introduced in primary school, whereas others contend that it is more sensible to wait until secondary level. Having weighed both positions, I would argue that an early start is preferable, although its success depends on how it is implemented.

The case for delaying language study rests largely on the capabilities of older learners. By the age of eleven or twelve, pupils have developed the analytical skills needed to understand how a language is structured, and they can apply techniques such as comparing its grammar with that of their first language. This allows them to make rapid, systematic progress. Moreover, deferring a second language gives younger children time to consolidate reading and writing in their mother tongue, a foundation on which all later learning depends. From this perspective, early lessons may consume valuable classroom time without producing meaningful results.

Nevertheless, there are compelling reasons to begin sooner. Young children acquire language largely through imitation and play, and they are generally uninhibited about experimenting with unfamiliar sounds. Consequently, those who start early often develop more natural pronunciation and a more intuitive feel for the language than learners who begin in adolescence, when embarrassment can hold them back. An early start also provides more years of exposure, and sustained contact over a long period is what ultimately produces confident, fluent speakers.

On balance, I find the second argument more persuasive. The concerns raised about primary-level teaching are genuine, but they relate to poor delivery rather than to the principle itself. If lessons are brief, oral and enjoyable, and are led by properly trained teachers, they complement rather than compete with literacy in the first language.

In conclusion, while older pupils learn grammar more efficiently, the advantages of early exposure are difficult to replicate later in life. Children should therefore begin a foreign language in primary school, with formal study left to secondary level.

items.title: The purpose of universities
items.prompt:
Some people think that the main purpose of a university is to prepare students for employment. Others believe that universities should give people the opportunity to pursue knowledge for its own sake. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

modelAnswer.text:
The role of higher education has become increasingly contested as tuition costs rise and labour markets change. One camp holds that a university exists chiefly to equip students for employment; another maintains that it should be a place where knowledge is pursued for its own sake. In my view, a university that sacrifices the latter in favour of the former undermines what makes it distinctive.

It is easy to see why the employment argument resonates. For most undergraduates, a degree represents a substantial financial commitment, and it is reasonable for them to expect that it will improve their career prospects. Governments that subsidise higher education likewise want a return on that investment in the form of skilled professionals, whether doctors, engineers or data analysts. Seen in this light, courses detached from the needs of the economy can appear to be an expensive luxury.

However, this view rests on a narrow conception of usefulness. Many of the capabilities employers prize most, such as the capacity to evaluate evidence, construct an argument and adapt to unfamiliar problems, are cultivated precisely through open-ended academic study rather than job-specific training. Furthermore, skills tailored to today's labour market may be obsolete within a decade, whereas a deep understanding of a discipline endures. At the level of society, fundamental research undertaken without any commercial aim has repeatedly laid the groundwork for later technological breakthroughs.

For these reasons, I believe the pursuit of knowledge should remain at the heart of a university's mission, with employability treated as a valuable by-product rather than the overriding objective. This does not mean ignoring students' career needs; work placements and professional guidance can sit comfortably alongside rigorous academic study. What should be resisted is the notion that a subject is worthwhile only if it leads directly to a particular job.

In conclusion, although universities clearly have a role in preparing people for work, their deeper and more enduring purpose is to advance and share knowledge, which ultimately serves both individuals and the economy better.

items.title: Smartphones for young children
items.prompt:
Some people think that children should be given their own smartphone as soon as they start school. Others believe that children should not have one until they are teenagers. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

modelAnswer.text:
The age at which children should be given a smartphone is a question that divides parents and educators. One view is that a child should have their own device from the first day of school; the opposing view is that ownership should be postponed until adolescence. While both positions reflect genuine concern for children's welfare, I believe that delaying full smartphone access is the more responsible course.

Advocates of early ownership frame the issue in terms of security and preparation. A smartphone enables parents to stay in touch with their children throughout the day and to track their location, which offers considerable peace of mind. There is also an argument that digital literacy is now as fundamental as reading, and that children who become familiar with technology early will navigate it more competently later. Finally, some parents fear that a child without a phone will be socially isolated if most classmates already own one.

Those who favour waiting, however, raise concerns that are harder to dismiss. Young children lack the self-discipline to limit their own screen time, and devices engineered to maximise engagement can easily displace sleep, outdoor play and face-to-face interaction, all of which are vital for healthy development. Equally worrying is children's vulnerability online: a seven-year-old is unlikely to recognise manipulative content or the risks of communicating with strangers, and even well-configured parental controls can be circumvented.

Weighing these arguments, I am persuaded that the risks of early ownership outweigh its advantages. The legitimate need for contact can be met by a basic handset without internet access, and digital skills can be taught under supervision at school or at home. Once children reach their early teens, a smartphone can be introduced gradually, with agreed limits that are relaxed as they demonstrate responsibility.

In conclusion, although giving young children smartphones offers reassurance and convenience, these benefits can be achieved in safer ways. Postponing ownership until the teenage years allows children to develop the maturity they need to use such devices wisely.

items.title: AI in recruitment decisions
items.prompt:
Some people argue that decisions about which job applicants to employ should be made by artificial intelligence because it is more objective than humans. Others believe that such decisions should always be made by people. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

modelAnswer.text:
The use of artificial intelligence in recruitment has prompted a lively debate. Proponents argue that algorithms can assess candidates more objectively than human interviewers, whereas opponents maintain that decisions of such consequence should always rest with people. Although AI has a legitimate role in the hiring process, I would argue that handing it the final say would be a mistake.

The appeal of automated selection lies in its apparent neutrality. Human judgement is notoriously susceptible to prejudice: recruiters may warm to candidates who resemble themselves, or be swayed by first impressions that bear no relation to competence. A well-designed system, by contrast, applies the same criteria to every application without fatigue or favouritism. For organisations that receive thousands of applications, this consistency, combined with the speed of automated screening, is highly attractive.

Yet the promise of objectivity is, in practice, difficult to fulfil. Algorithms learn from historical data, and if past recruitment favoured particular genders, ethnic groups or educational backgrounds, the software is likely to absorb and even amplify those preferences while giving them a veneer of scientific authority. Furthermore, the qualities that often distinguish an outstanding employee, such as judgement, resilience and the capacity to collaborate, are precisely those that resist quantification. Finally, automated rejection raises a serious problem of accountability, since applicants are rarely able to learn why they were turned down or to challenge the outcome.

For these reasons, I believe AI should inform rather than determine hiring decisions. It can usefully handle routine tasks such as sorting applications or flagging relevant qualifications, but the assessment of a person's suitability requires human insight, and those making the decision must be answerable for it.

In conclusion, while artificial intelligence can reduce certain inconsistencies in recruitment, it is neither as impartial nor as perceptive as its advocates suggest. The responsibility for choosing who to employ should therefore remain firmly with people.

items.title: Technology or lifestyle change
items.prompt:
Some people believe that new technology will solve the world's environmental problems. Others think that the only real solution is for people to change the way they live. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

modelAnswer.text:
Faced with mounting evidence of environmental decline, societies are divided over where the solution lies. Some believe that technological progress will eventually resolve the crisis, while others insist that meaningful change can only come from altering the way people live. Although both perspectives contain important truths, I would argue that neither is adequate without the other.

The optimism surrounding technology is not without foundation. In recent decades, renewable energy has become cheaper and more widely available, battery technology has improved considerably, and innovations in areas such as building insulation and precision farming have reduced waste. Crucially, technological solutions do not depend on persuading billions of individuals to sacrifice their comfort, which makes them politically and socially more achievable than widespread behavioural change. From this perspective, human ingenuity offers the most practical route to a sustainable future.

However, relying solely on innovation carries significant risks. Many of the most ambitious technologies remain unproven at scale, and waiting for them to mature may squander time that the planet does not have. There is also a well-documented tendency for efficiency gains to be offset by increased consumption: as products become cheaper and cleaner to run, people often simply use more of them. Without a shift in attitudes towards consumption, waste and travel, technology risks treating the symptoms of environmental damage rather than its underlying causes.

In my view, the two approaches are mutually reinforcing. Technology is most effective when it makes sustainable behaviour convenient, as affordable public transport or efficient home heating does, and lifestyle changes are easier to sustain when practical alternatives exist. Policy should therefore pursue both, funding research while also using regulation and incentives to discourage wasteful habits.

In conclusion, while technological advances are indispensable in tackling environmental problems, they cannot succeed in isolation. A genuine solution requires people to reconsider how they live, supported by innovations that make greener choices easier.

items.title: Paying for climate action
items.prompt:
Some people believe that wealthy countries should pay most of the cost of tackling climate change. Others argue that the cost should be shared equally by all countries. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

modelAnswer.text:
As the costs of addressing climate change mount, so does the question of who should bear them. One view holds that wealthy nations should shoulder most of the financial burden; another insists that the costs should be divided equally among all countries. I believe that a fair arrangement must reflect differences in both responsibility and capacity, which means that richer countries should pay considerably more.

The argument for placing the main burden on wealthy countries is rooted in historical responsibility. The nations that industrialised first have emitted the bulk of the carbon dioxide that has accumulated in the atmosphere, and their current prosperity was built, in large part, on that fossil-fuel-driven growth. It therefore seems just that they should now fund a substantial share of the transition. They are also far better placed to do so, possessing the capital, infrastructure and research capacity that many developing countries lack.

Advocates of equal contributions nevertheless make a case that deserves serious consideration. Emissions are no longer concentrated in the traditional industrial powers; several rapidly developing economies now produce a significant proportion of global emissions. Exempting them from financial responsibility could weaken their commitment to decarbonisation and breed resentment among taxpayers in wealthier states. Moreover, since climate change threatens every country, some would argue that a shared problem demands an equally shared solution.

In my view, however, treating unequal nations equally would itself be inequitable. Requiring a country where much of the population lacks reliable electricity to contribute as much as one of the world's richest economies would hinder its development while doing little for the climate. A more defensible approach would scale contributions according to historical emissions, current emissions and national income, ensuring that every country participates while the heaviest costs fall on those most able to bear them.

In conclusion, although all nations have a stake in combating climate change, fairness requires that wealthy countries fund the greater part of the effort, with others contributing in proportion to their means.

items.title: Roads or public transport
items.prompt:
Some people think that governments should build more roads to reduce traffic problems. Others believe that the money would be better spent on railways and other forms of public transport. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

modelAnswer.text:
Congested roads impose significant costs on economies and on the quality of urban life, and governments face a choice about how to respond. One view is that expanding the road network is the most direct solution; another is that the same funds would achieve more if spent on railways and other forms of public transport. While road investment has its place, I believe that public transport represents the better use of money in most circumstances.

The argument for building roads is intuitive. If traffic is heavy, providing more lanes should, in principle, allow vehicles to move more freely and reduce journey times. Roads are also indispensable for the movement of goods, emergency services and residents of rural areas, where population densities are too low to support frequent bus or rail services. For these communities, well-maintained roads are not a luxury but a lifeline.

Nevertheless, the benefits of road expansion in cities tend to be short-lived. Additional capacity makes driving more convenient, which encourages more people to drive and gradually recreates the original congestion, a phenomenon often described as induced demand. Public transport, by contrast, is inherently more space-efficient: a single rail line can carry far more passengers than a lane of private cars. Well-designed networks also bring wider advantages, including cleaner air, lower carbon emissions and greater mobility for those who cannot afford to drive or are unable to.

In my view, therefore, governments should concentrate urban transport spending on rail, trams and buses, while reserving road construction for areas where no viable alternative exists and for essential maintenance. The key is to make public transport sufficiently frequent, reliable and affordable that it becomes the natural choice rather than a last resort.

In conclusion, although building roads can offer temporary relief and remains vital in rural areas, investment in public transport provides a more lasting and equitable solution to traffic problems.

items.title: Green space versus development
items.prompt:
Some people believe that land in cities should be used mainly for parks and other green spaces. Others think that this land is better used for housing and businesses. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

modelAnswer.text:
Land in cities is a scarce and valuable resource, and how it is allocated shapes the lives of millions of residents. Some argue that it should be used predominantly for parks and other green spaces, whereas others believe that housing and commercial premises should take precedence. In my view, although the demand for homes is pressing, green space must be treated as essential infrastructure rather than as a dispensable amenity.

The case for prioritising housing and business is compelling in many cities. Chronic shortages of affordable accommodation force workers to endure long commutes or to leave urban areas altogether, which harms both their quality of life and the local economy. Commercial development, meanwhile, generates employment, attracts investment and provides the tax revenue that funds public services. Seen from this angle, reserving large areas for parks might appear to be an indulgence that a growing city can ill afford.

However, this reasoning underestimates the tangible value of green space. Parks offer residents, particularly those living in flats without gardens, a place to exercise, socialise and escape the pressures of urban life, with well-documented benefits for physical and mental health. They also perform important environmental functions: vegetation absorbs rainwater, mitigating the risk of flooding, and helps to counteract the heat that builds up in densely built areas. Crucially, once green space is developed, it is rarely, if ever, recovered.

Rather than framing the issue as a stark choice, I believe cities should pursue housing growth in ways that preserve and even enhance green areas. Building at higher densities, redeveloping former industrial land and converting underused offices into homes can all increase supply without encroaching on parks. New developments, in turn, can be required to incorporate gardens, tree-lined streets and shared open spaces.

In conclusion, while the need for homes and businesses is undeniable, green space is too important to be treated as expendable. Careful planning allows cities to meet both needs, but existing parks should be protected rather than sacrificed.

They also perform important environmental functions: vegetation absorbs rainwater, mitigating the risk of flooding, and helps to counteract the heat that builds up in densely built areas. Crucially, once green space is developed, it is rarely, if ever, recovered.

Rather than framing the issue as a stark choice, I believe cities should pursue housing growth in ways that preserve and even enhance green areas. Building at higher densities, redeveloping former industrial land and converting underused offices into homes can all increase supply without encroaching on parks. New developments, in turn, can be required to incorporate gardens, tree-lined streets and shared open spaces.

In conclusion, while the need for homes and businesses is undeniable, green space is too important to be treated as expendable. Careful planning allows cities to meet both needs, but existing parks should be protected rather than sacrificed.

items.title: Job loyalty or job changes
items.prompt:
Some people think that it is better to stay with the same employer for many years. Others believe that changing jobs frequently brings greater benefits. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

modelAnswer.text:
Whereas a single lifelong employer was once the norm, many workers today move between organisations several times during their careers. This has sparked debate over whether long-term loyalty or frequent change is more advantageous. Having considered both sides, I would argue that the answer depends partly on career stage, but that a willingness to move is generally more beneficial.

There is much to be said for staying with one employer. Over time, an employee accumulates detailed knowledge of the organisation's systems, clients and culture, which can make them indispensable and position them well for internal promotion. Long tenure also tends to bring stability, both financial and emotional, together with close working relationships that can make the workplace more fulfilling. Employers, for their part, often reward such commitment with additional benefits and greater trust.

Nevertheless, frequent job changes carry advantages that are difficult to ignore. Moving to a new organisation is often the most effective way to secure a substantial increase in salary, since external candidates can negotiate from a stronger position than existing staff. Each move also exposes the employee to unfamiliar challenges, methods and colleagues, accelerating the acquisition of skills and broadening their professional network. In a labour market where entire industries can be transformed within a decade, such adaptability is arguably a greater form of security than loyalty to a single firm.

On balance, I believe that moving between employers is more beneficial, particularly in the early and middle stages of a career, when breadth of experience matters most. That said, changing jobs too often can undermine credibility and prevent people from seeing projects through to completion. The most rewarding pattern is perhaps to stay long enough in each role to achieve something meaningful before moving on.

In conclusion, while long service offers stability and recognition, periodic job changes generally provide faster growth, higher earnings and greater resilience in an uncertain economy.

items.title: Profit and social responsibility
items.prompt:
Some people believe that the main purpose of a business is to make a profit for its owners. Others argue that businesses also have a responsibility to benefit society as a whole. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

modelAnswer.text:
The question of what businesses are ultimately for has become more pressing as corporations grow in size and influence. One school of thought maintains that the sole purpose of a business is to maximise returns for its owners; another holds that companies bear a broader responsibility to society. While I accept that profitability is indispensable, I would argue that a narrow focus on shareholder returns is neither ethically defensible nor, in the long run, commercially wise.

Advocates of the profit-centred view make a coherent case. Owners and shareholders provide the capital that allows a company to exist, and they do so on the understanding that it will be managed in their financial interest. A profitable enterprise also contributes to society as a matter of course, by employing people, paying taxes and supplying goods and services that meet genuine demand. On this view, asking companies to pursue social goals risks diluting their efficiency and allowing unelected executives to make decisions that properly belong to governments.

However, this argument overlooks the extent to which business activity affects people who have no say in it. Pollution, unsafe working conditions and misleading marketing all impose costs on communities, workers and consumers, often while the company itself profits. Given the power that large firms wield, it is reasonable to expect them to take responsibility for these consequences. Moreover, responsible conduct increasingly aligns with self-interest: firms with strong ethical reputations tend to attract loyal customers and talented staff, and are better protected against regulatory and reputational risks.

In my view, then, profit and social responsibility should be seen as complementary rather than competing aims. A business must be financially sound to survive, but its legitimacy ultimately depends on the trust of the society in which it operates, and that trust must be earned.

In conclusion, although generating profit is a fundamental objective, businesses have a duty to consider their wider impact, and those that embrace this duty are likely to prove more successful and sustainable over time.

items.title: Who is responsible for health?
items.prompt:
Some people believe that individuals should be responsible for their own health. Others think that governments should play a major role in encouraging people to lead healthy lives. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

modelAnswer.text:
Few would dispute that good health depends heavily on everyday behaviour, yet there is considerable disagreement about who should take responsibility for it. Some maintain that health is essentially a personal matter, whereas others believe governments should actively encourage citizens to lead healthier lives. In my view, individual responsibility and state involvement are not mutually exclusive, and the latter is often necessary for the former to be meaningful.

The argument for personal responsibility rests on the principle of autonomy. Adults are entitled to make decisions about their own diet, activity levels and habits, even when those decisions carry risks, and government intervention in such matters can easily become paternalistic. There is also a practical point: lasting change in behaviour tends to come from personal motivation rather than external pressure, so public campaigns may achieve little if people are not genuinely committed to improving their health.

Nevertheless, this view underestimates how strongly circumstances shape behaviour. People on low incomes may find nutritious food less affordable and less accessible than processed alternatives, while those living in areas without parks or safe streets have fewer opportunities to exercise. Commercial pressures, such as the aggressive marketing of high-sugar products to children, further tilt the balance towards unhealthy choices. Governments are uniquely placed to counteract these influences through regulation, taxation, urban planning and education. Furthermore, because the cost of treating preventable illness is largely borne by taxpayers, the state has a clear interest in reducing it.

For these reasons, I believe governments should play a major role, not by dictating how people live, but by creating conditions in which healthy choices are realistic for everyone. Individuals would still be responsible for their decisions, but they would make them in an environment that supports rather than undermines their wellbeing.

In conclusion, while personal responsibility remains important, it cannot be exercised equally when circumstances differ so widely. Active government involvement is therefore essential to enabling people to lead healthier lives.

items.title: Referendums or representatives
items.prompt:
Some people think that important national decisions should be made directly by the public through referendums. Others believe that such decisions are better left to elected politicians and experts. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

modelAnswer.text:
The question of how far ordinary citizens should be directly involved in national decision-making goes to the heart of what democracy means. Some believe that major issues should be settled by referendum, giving the public the final word, whereas others argue that such matters are better entrusted to elected representatives and specialists. While referendums have a place in a healthy democracy, I believe they are poorly suited to most important decisions.

The appeal of direct democracy is easy to understand. A referendum allows every voter to express a view on a specific question, producing a result that carries considerable moral authority. It can also re-engage citizens who feel alienated from mainstream politics, and it provides a means of resolving contentious issues that parliaments have been unable or unwilling to settle. From this perspective, entrusting decisions to politicians risks allowing a narrow political class to disregard public opinion.

However, the practical limitations of referendums are considerable. Many national questions involve intricate trade-offs, uncertain long-term consequences and technical detail that few voters have the time or background to evaluate thoroughly. In such circumstances, campaigns tend to reward emotive messaging over careful analysis, and misleading claims can prove decisive. Moreover, the binary format of a referendum forces a nuanced issue into a simple choice, leaving no scope for amendment or compromise, and the result can be extremely difficult to reverse. Representative institutions, by contrast, allow policies to be scrutinised, refined and revisited, while voters retain the power to remove politicians who fail them.

On balance, I believe that elected representatives, informed by expert advice, should make most important national decisions. Referendums can be justified for questions of fundamental constitutional significance, provided that voters have access to impartial information, but they should remain the exception rather than the rule.

In conclusion, although referendums offer a direct expression of the popular will, representative democracy is generally better equipped to handle complex decisions responsibly and accountably.

items.title: Parents and career choices
items.prompt:
Some people think that parents should guide their children towards a particular career. Others believe that young people should be free to choose their own career. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

modelAnswer.text:
The extent to which parents should influence their children's choice of career is a question on which cultures and families differ considerably. Some believe that parents, with their greater experience, should direct their children towards a particular profession, while others hold that young people must be free to make this decision for themselves. My own view is that parental guidance is valuable, but only when it informs rather than overrides a young person's choice.

The argument for parental direction is not without merit. Parents generally have a clearer picture than teenagers of the practical realities of working life, including the stability, income and progression that different fields offer. Young people, meanwhile, may be drawn to glamorous but precarious occupations, or may simply lack the information to make a well-founded decision. Parents who have made sacrifices to fund their children's education can therefore feel both entitled and obliged to ensure that it leads somewhere secure.

Nevertheless, the costs of directing a child into an unwanted career can be considerable. Motivation is a powerful determinant of success, and a person who has chosen their field is far more likely to persevere through the demanding early years of a career than one who is fulfilling someone else's ambitions. Moreover, parents' knowledge of the job market is often rooted in the past; occupations that once seemed secure may be vulnerable to automation, while entirely new fields are opening up. A choice imposed on the basis of outdated assumptions may prove neither fulfilling nor safe.

Weighing these considerations, I believe parents should act as well-informed advisers. By encouraging their children to explore different options, seek work experience and think realistically about their strengths, they can help them make a sound decision without taking it out of their hands.

In conclusion, while parental experience can be a valuable resource, young people should ultimately be free to choose their own careers, since a career that is genuinely chosen is more likely to be both successful and satisfying.

items.title: Punishment or rehabilitation
items.prompt:
Some people believe that the main purpose of prison is to punish offenders. Others think that prisons should focus on helping offenders to return to society as law-abiding citizens. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

modelAnswer.text:
How a society treats those it imprisons reveals a great deal about its values. One view holds that the principal purpose of prison is to punish offenders for their crimes; another maintains that prisons should prioritise preparing inmates to return to society as law-abiding citizens. Although punishment is an unavoidable element of imprisonment, I would argue that rehabilitation should be its central aim.

The case for punishment rests on principles of justice and deterrence. Many people feel that those who inflict harm on others deserve consequences proportionate to their actions, and that a sentence perceived as lenient fails to respect victims. It is also argued that the prospect of a harsh prison regime discourages potential offenders, and that prioritising prisoners' welfare sends the wrong message about the seriousness of crime.

However, this approach has significant limitations. Since the great majority of prisoners are eventually released, the question is not whether they will rejoin society but in what condition. An offender who leaves prison without skills or support, and with stronger links to criminal networks, is highly likely to reoffend, creating new victims and returning to custody at great public expense. Rehabilitation programmes, by contrast, address the underlying causes of offending, whether a lack of education, unemployment or addiction, and thereby offer more lasting protection for the public. Moreover, the deterrent value of harsh conditions is questionable, as many crimes are committed impulsively or by people who do not expect to be caught.

For these reasons, I believe that the deprivation of liberty should be regarded as the punishment itself, and that time spent in prison should be used to reduce the likelihood of future offending. This does not mean ignoring the need to protect the public from genuinely dangerous individuals, but even in such cases the goal of reform should not be abandoned.

In conclusion, while punishment has a legitimate role, prisons best serve society when they focus on rehabilitation, as this ultimately leads to fewer crimes and fewer victims.

items.title: Celebrities as role models
items.prompt:
Some people think that famous people have a responsibility to act as role models for young people. Others believe that celebrities should be free to live their lives as they wish. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

modelAnswer.text:
The influence of celebrities on young people has grown enormously with the rise of social media, prompting debate about what, if anything, famous people owe their audiences. Some argue that celebrity brings with it a duty to act as a role model, whereas others contend that public figures are entitled to live as they please. In my view, celebrities have a genuine but limited responsibility, one that applies to their public conduct rather than to every aspect of their lives.

Those who believe celebrities should be role models emphasise the scale of their influence. Young people often identify closely with the stars they follow, adopting their styles, opinions and habits, and when a well-known figure normalises behaviour such as heavy drinking or casual cruelty online, the effects can ripple through a large and impressionable audience. Furthermore, celebrities derive their wealth and status from public admiration, so it seems fair to expect them to recognise the obligations that accompany such privilege.

On the other hand, there are strong grounds for resisting this expectation. Fame is frequently a by-product of talent in a particular field, and a gifted athlete or musician has not necessarily chosen, or trained, to serve as a moral example. Demanding flawless conduct from them is not only unrealistic but can also justify intrusive media coverage of their private lives. Moreover, placing the burden of guiding young people on celebrities risks diverting attention from those who should bear it primarily, namely parents, educators and communities.

Balancing these arguments, I believe celebrities should be expected to exercise care in how they use their public platforms, avoiding the promotion of harmful behaviour, while their private lives should largely remain their own. At the same time, young people should be taught to admire achievement without uncritically imitating the individuals behind it.

In conclusion, although celebrities cannot reasonably be required to be perfect, their considerable influence carries a responsibility to act with care in public, even as they retain the right to a private life.

items.title: Immigrants and cultural identity
items.prompt:
Some people believe that people who move to live in another country should adopt the customs and way of life of their new home. Others think that they should maintain their own cultural traditions. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

modelAnswer.text:
As migration reshapes societies around the world, the question of how newcomers should relate to the culture of their adopted country has become increasingly prominent. Some maintain that immigrants ought to adopt the customs and way of life of their new home, while others believe they should retain their own cultural traditions. In my view, this is a false choice: successful integration involves adapting in some respects while preserving one's heritage in others.

The argument for adopting local customs centres on social cohesion and personal opportunity. Newcomers who master the language and understand prevailing norms are far better placed to secure employment, access public services and form friendships beyond their own community. Where migrant groups remain largely separate, mutual suspicion can develop on both sides, fuelling prejudice and limiting social mobility. Adapting to the host culture can therefore be seen as both a practical necessity and a gesture of goodwill.

Those who favour preserving cultural traditions, however, raise equally important points. A person's language, faith, cuisine and customs are deeply bound up with their sense of self, and pressure to abandon them can be alienating, particularly for older migrants. Moreover, cultural diversity is a source of vitality for host societies, enriching their food, arts and ideas; many of the world's most vibrant cities are defined precisely by the traditions that successive waves of migrants have brought with them.

Immigrants should respect the law, embrace fundamental values such as equality, and make a genuine effort to learn the local language, since these form the basis of a common public life. Beyond this, they should be free to maintain the traditions that give their lives meaning, and host societies should welcome rather than merely tolerate them.

In conclusion, rather than choosing between assimilation and separation, immigrants and their new communities benefit most from a balance in which shared civic values coexist with a diversity of cultural traditions.

items.title: Home or office working
items.prompt:
Some people believe that working from home is better for employees. Others think that working in an office alongside colleagues is more effective. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

modelAnswer.text:
The widespread adoption of remote working has prompted a reassessment of where work is best done. Some believe that working from home is clearly preferable for employees, while others maintain that an office shared with colleagues is more effective. In my view, each setting suits different kinds of work, and the most productive arrangement is one that combines them deliberately.

The case for home working rests largely on autonomy and wellbeing. Eliminating the commute gives employees back hours each week and reduces both travel costs and stress. Many find that a quiet home environment enables sustained concentration that is difficult to achieve amid the distractions of a busy office. Remote work also widens access to employment, allowing people with caring responsibilities, health conditions or homes far from urban centres to participate more fully in the workforce.

Nevertheless, the office offers benefits that are not easily replicated online. Collaboration is often more fluid in person, where questions can be resolved in moments and chance conversations can spark ideas that would never surface in a scheduled video call. For those early in their careers, proximity to experienced colleagues is an invaluable, if informal, form of training. There is also a social dimension: prolonged remote working can leave people isolated, and the blurring of boundaries between home and work can make it hard to switch off.

Framing the issue as a choice between the two is therefore unhelpful. Tasks requiring deep concentration are often best carried out at home, whereas teamwork, mentoring and relationship-building benefit from shared physical space. Organisations should adopt hybrid arrangements designed around the nature of the work rather than habit, giving employees flexibility while preserving the collaborative culture that offices foster.

In conclusion, while working from home offers clear advantages for employees' comfort and focus, the office remains essential for collaboration and learning. A thoughtfully designed combination of the two is likely to serve both employees and organisations best.

items.title: Funding an ageing population
items.prompt:
Some people think that the best way to support an ageing population is to raise the retirement age. Others believe that younger working people should pay higher taxes instead. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

modelAnswer.text:
Demographic change is placing growing pressure on pension and healthcare systems, as the proportion of older people rises relative to those of working age. Some believe the most effective response is to raise the retirement age, whereas others argue that younger workers should instead pay higher taxes. In my view, a gradual rise in the retirement age is the more equitable solution, although it must be implemented with sensitivity to differences between occupations.

The argument for increasing taxes on the working population rests on fairness to those approaching retirement. Many older people have contributed to the system throughout their working lives in the reasonable expectation of retiring at a particular age, and changing the rules late in their careers can seem like a breach of trust. Moreover, the capacity to keep working is unevenly distributed: an office worker may comfortably remain employed until seventy, but someone who has spent decades in manual labour may simply be physically unable to do so.

Nevertheless, relying on higher taxes carries significant drawbacks. Younger generations in many countries already face high housing costs and considerable educational debt, and increasing their tax burden further could reduce their disposable income, discourage them from starting families and deepen intergenerational resentment. Furthermore, retirement ages were often fixed when life expectancy was considerably lower; linking them to current longevity simply restores the original balance between working life and retirement. Keeping healthy, experienced people in employment for longer also benefits the economy by retaining valuable skills.

On balance, I believe that raising the retirement age gradually, with plenty of notice, distributes the cost more fairly. Crucially, such a policy should include provisions for earlier retirement in physically demanding jobs and encourage flexible arrangements such as phased or part-time retirement.

In conclusion, although asking younger workers to pay more would spare older people from working longer, a carefully managed increase in the retirement age offers a fairer and more sustainable means of supporting an ageing population.

items.title: Responsibility for online content
items.prompt:
Some people think that social media companies should be held responsible for the content that appears on their platforms. Others believe that the individual users who post the content should be responsible. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

modelAnswer.text:
As social media has become a primary source of news and communication for many people, concern about harmful content, including misinformation, harassment and extremist material, has intensified. Some argue that the companies operating these platforms should be held responsible for what appears on them, while others insist that accountability lies with the individuals who post it. In my view, responsibility must be shared, but the role of the platforms has been significantly underestimated.

The case for holding users responsible rests on a basic principle of personal accountability. Each post is written by an individual who chooses its content, and it would seem perverse to excuse someone who spreads defamatory or threatening material simply because they did so online. There are also practical objections to placing the burden on companies. The volume of content uploaded every day is so vast that comprehensive monitoring is impossible, and platforms facing legal liability might respond by removing anything remotely contentious, with damaging consequences for free expression.

However, this view overlooks the active role that platforms play. They are not passive noticeboards: their recommendation systems determine what users see, and because provocative content tends to generate engagement, it is often amplified far beyond its original audience. Since these companies profit directly from this engagement, it is difficult to argue that they bear no responsibility for its effects. They also possess resources and technical expertise that no individual user could match, and anonymity frequently makes it impossible to identify the original author at all.

For these reasons, I believe a system of shared accountability is most appropriate. Individuals should face legal consequences for unlawful content, just as they would offline, while platforms should be obliged to respond promptly to reported material, limit the promotion of harmful posts and be transparent about how their algorithms operate.

In conclusion, although users are responsible for the content they create, social media companies shape and profit from its distribution, and they should therefore be held accountable for the part they play.
