items.title: Experiences or possessions
items.prompt:
Some people believe that it is better to spend money on experiences, such as travel and entertainment. Others think it is wiser to spend money on possessions that last. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

modelAnswer.text:
Decisions about how to spend money reveal much about what people value. Some argue that the wisest use of income is to pay for experiences, such as travel and entertainment, whereas others maintain that it is more prudent to buy possessions that will last. While both have a place in a balanced life, I believe that experiences generally offer the greater and more enduring reward, once essential needs have been met.

The case for durable possessions is grounded in practicality. A well-made coat, a dependable vehicle or a comfortable home provides tangible benefits every day, often for many years, and the cost per use of a quality item can be remarkably low. Certain assets, notably property, may also appreciate in value, offering a degree of financial security that no holiday can match. From this perspective, spending heavily on fleeting experiences might seem short-sighted, particularly for those on modest incomes.

Nevertheless, the value of experiences is frequently underestimated. Although a journey or a concert is over quickly, the memories it creates can be revisited for a lifetime and often grow more cherished with time. Experiences also tend to be shared, strengthening bonds with family and friends, and they can broaden perspectives in ways that possessions rarely do, whether through exposure to another culture or the acquisition of a new skill. By contrast, the pleasure derived from a new purchase often fades as people grow accustomed to it, prompting a cycle of further buying that brings diminishing satisfaction.

In my view, therefore, the most sensible approach is to invest in a limited number of durable, genuinely useful items and to devote discretionary spending largely to experiences. This avoids accumulating possessions that bring little lasting joy, while still providing the stability that essential goods offer.

In conclusion, although possessions that last can deliver comfort and security, experiences tend to provide richer and longer-lasting fulfilment, and they therefore represent the wiser use of money beyond life's necessities.

items.title: Taking a gap year
items.prompt:
Many students now take a year off between finishing school and starting university. Do the advantages of this outweigh the disadvantages?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

modelAnswer.text:
The practice of postponing university for a year, once associated mainly with affluent students travelling overseas, has become a mainstream option for school leavers. In my view, when the year is structured rather than aimless, the benefits it offers clearly outweigh the drawbacks.

Perhaps the strongest argument in favour of a gap year is that it leads to better-informed decisions about higher education. Students who move straight from school to university often commit to a three- or four-year course on the basis of limited self-knowledge, and a poor match between student and subject is a common reason for dropping out. A year spent in employment or volunteering exposes young people to the realities of working life, allowing them to test their interests before investing heavily in a degree. Equally valuable is the personal growth that comes from handling responsibilities outside the protective environment of school: someone who has held down a job, paid rent or organised their own travel is likely to arrive at university more self-reliant and more focused.

That said, the disadvantages should not be dismissed. A break of twelve months can erode study habits, and a minority of students never return to education at all, particularly if a job offers an immediate income that seems more attractive than further study. The year also postpones graduation and entry into a career, which carries a real cost in lost earnings. Furthermore, the more glamorous forms of gap year, such as extended travel abroad, remain out of reach for many families, which means the experience can reinforce existing inequalities.

On balance, however, most of these risks stem from poor planning rather than from the gap year itself. Where students set clear goals, combining paid work with volunteering or skills development, they tend to return to education with greater purpose.

Overall, therefore, I believe the advantages of a well-planned gap year outweigh its disadvantages, since the maturity and clarity it provides can shape the rest of a student's academic and professional life.

items.title: Online university courses
items.prompt:
In many universities, online courses are increasingly replacing traditional classroom teaching. What are the advantages and disadvantages of this trend?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

modelAnswer.text:
The steady replacement of lecture halls with virtual classrooms is one of the most visible changes in higher education in recent years. Although this trend has made university study more accessible and adaptable, it also risks diluting some of the most valuable aspects of a traditional education.

The principal benefit of online provision is its capacity to widen participation. Because lectures can be accessed from anywhere, students in remote regions, those with disabilities that make travel difficult and adults balancing study with employment are no longer disadvantaged by geography or rigid timetables. Digital materials are also more flexible as learning tools: a recorded lecture can be revisited before an examination, subtitled or slowed down, giving learners greater control over how they absorb information. For universities, meanwhile, online delivery allows a single course to reach thousands of students without a corresponding increase in staff or facilities.

Yet these gains come at a cost. Learning at university is not merely the transfer of information; it is also shaped by debate, questioning and collaboration, which tend to flourish in shared physical spaces. In a live seminar, a tutor can challenge a weak argument or draw a quiet student into the discussion, whereas in an online forum such interaction is often delayed, superficial or absent altogether. Isolation is a related concern, as students who rarely meet their peers may feel less connected to their institution and more likely to abandon their studies. There are practical limitations too: laboratory work, clinical training and studio-based design cannot be meaningfully replicated at a distance.

Equally important is the issue of unequal access to technology. A course delivered entirely online assumes a reliable device and a stable internet connection, which not every student can take for granted.

In summary, online courses offer flexibility, reach and efficiency, but at the expense of interaction, community and practical training. The most effective universities are likely to be those that combine digital tools with meaningful face-to-face teaching rather than abandoning the classroom altogether.

items.title: AI in medical diagnosis
items.prompt:
In many countries, artificial intelligence is now being used to help doctors identify illnesses. Do the advantages of this outweigh the disadvantages?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

modelAnswer.text:
The use of artificial intelligence to assist in diagnosing illness has moved rapidly from experimental research to everyday clinical practice in many countries. While the technology is not without its hazards, I am convinced that, used responsibly, it offers benefits that far outweigh its drawbacks.

The most compelling case for diagnostic AI lies in its accuracy and consistency. Algorithms trained on vast collections of medical images can identify minute abnormalities in scans that might escape a tired or inexperienced clinician, and unlike humans, they do not become less attentive at the end of a long shift. Earlier detection of conditions such as tumours can transform a patient's prognosis, turning a potentially fatal illness into a treatable one. AI also addresses a practical problem faced by health systems almost everywhere: a shortage of specialists. By screening routine cases, it frees doctors to concentrate on complex diagnoses and on the human side of medicine, and it can extend a degree of specialist expertise to rural clinics that have no radiologist on site.

The concerns, nevertheless, are real. Diagnostic systems are only as good as the data used to build them, so a tool developed mainly with records from one population may perform poorly for others, potentially widening existing inequalities in care. There is also the question of accountability: when an algorithm contributes to a misdiagnosis, it is unclear whether responsibility lies with the doctor, the hospital or the software developer. Moreover, the large-scale collection of health records required to train these systems inevitably raises questions of confidentiality.

Crucially, though, none of these problems is inherent to the technology. They can be mitigated through rigorous testing on diverse patient groups, clear legal frameworks and the principle that AI supports, rather than replaces, clinical judgement.

In conclusion, the risks associated with AI in diagnosis demand careful regulation, but they are outweighed by its potential to detect disease earlier, ease pressure on doctors and bring expert assessment to those who currently lack it.

While the technology is not without its hazards, I am convinced that, used responsibly, it offers benefits that far outweigh its drawbacks.

The most compelling case for diagnostic AI lies in its accuracy and consistency. Algorithms trained on vast collections of medical images can identify minute abnormalities in scans that might escape a tired or inexperienced clinician, and unlike humans, they do not become less attentive at the end of a long shift. Earlier detection of conditions such as tumours can transform a patient's prognosis, turning a potentially fatal illness into a treatable one. AI also addresses a practical problem faced by health systems almost everywhere: a shortage of specialists. By screening routine cases, it frees doctors to concentrate on complex diagnoses and on the human side of medicine, and it can extend a degree of specialist expertise to rural clinics that have no radiologist on site.

The concerns, nevertheless, are real. Diagnostic systems are only as good as the data used to build them, so a tool developed mainly with records from one population may perform poorly for others, potentially widening existing inequalities in care. There is also the question of accountability: when an algorithm contributes to a misdiagnosis, it is unclear whether responsibility lies with the doctor, the hospital or the software developer. Moreover, the large-scale collection of health records required to train these systems inevitably raises questions of confidentiality.

Crucially, though, none of these problems is inherent to the technology. They can be mitigated through rigorous testing on diverse patient groups, clear legal frameworks and the principle that AI supports, rather than replaces, clinical judgement.

In conclusion, the risks associated with AI in diagnosis demand careful regulation, but they are outweighed by its potential to detect disease earlier, ease pressure on doctors and bring expert assessment to those who currently lack it.

items.title: Living in high-rise apartments
items.prompt:
More and more people in cities now live in high-rise apartment buildings. Do the advantages of this outweigh the disadvantages?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

modelAnswer.text:
Across the world's major cities, the skyline is increasingly dominated by residential towers, and a growing share of urban households now live many floors above the street. Although vertical living has undeniable shortcomings, I would argue that, in densely populated cities, its advantages prevail.

The strongest case for high-rise housing is a practical one. Land in city centres is scarce and expensive, and building upwards allows far more homes to be created on the same footprint than low-rise development ever could. This density has wider benefits: it limits urban sprawl into farmland and green belts, and it makes public transport, shops and services economically viable because enough people live within walking distance of them. For residents, the result is often a shorter commute and easier access to employment, education and leisure, which can significantly improve quality of life.

The drawbacks, however, are genuine. Tall buildings can be socially isolating, since the anonymity of long corridors and shared lifts rarely encourages the casual encounters that build neighbourly relationships. Families may struggle without private gardens, and older or disabled residents are particularly vulnerable when lifts fail. Safety is a further concern: evacuating hundreds of people from upper floors during a fire is inherently more complex than escaping from a house, and poorly maintained towers can become hazardous.

Yet these issues largely reflect how such buildings are designed and managed rather than the concept itself. Well-planned developments incorporate communal green spaces, community rooms and robust fire-safety systems, demonstrating that high-density living can be both safe and socially vibrant.

In conclusion, high-rise apartments may compromise privacy, outdoor space and, at times, community spirit, but these costs can be mitigated through thoughtful design. Given their efficient use of land and the accessibility they offer, I believe their advantages clearly outweigh their disadvantages.

items.title: Multinationals in developing countries
items.prompt:
Large international companies are increasingly opening factories and offices in developing countries. Do the advantages of this outweigh the disadvantages for the people of these countries?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

modelAnswer.text:
The relocation of factories and offices by multinational corporations to lower-income countries is one of the defining features of the global economy. Its impact on local populations is mixed, but I would contend that, where host governments regulate effectively, the advantages for ordinary citizens outweigh the disadvantages.

The most immediate gain is employment. In economies with high levels of informal or subsistence work, a job with a foreign firm often provides the first regular wage a household has received, together with a degree of stability that enables families to plan, save and invest in their children's education. Beyond income, these positions frequently involve formal training, exposing workers to modern production methods, management practices and quality standards. Such knowledge rarely stays within one company; it spreads as employees move on or establish suppliers of their own, gradually raising the productivity of the wider economy. Foreign investment can also stimulate improvements in transport and energy that benefit the whole population.

The costs, however, can be severe. Some corporations deliberately seek out countries with lax labour and environmental laws, and the consequences can include excessive working hours, dangerous workplaces and serious contamination of land and water. There is also the risk of dependency: an economy built around foreign-owned plants is vulnerable if a company decides to relocate again in search of even cheaper costs, leaving entire towns without work. Moreover, much of the value generated flows back to shareholders overseas rather than being reinvested locally.

Importantly, these harms are largely a function of governance rather than of foreign investment itself. Countries that enforce labour rights, require environmental safeguards and encourage links with domestic suppliers tend to capture far more of the benefits.

In conclusion, multinational investment carries real risks of exploitation and instability, yet the jobs, skills and infrastructure it brings can transform living standards. On balance, and with sound regulation, its advantages for local people outweigh its disadvantages.

items.title: Short-term employment contracts
items.prompt:
Many companies now employ workers on short-term contracts rather than offering them permanent jobs. What are the advantages and disadvantages of this for workers?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

modelAnswer.text:
The shift away from permanent employment towards fixed-term and project-based contracts has reshaped working life in many economies. For employees, this change offers a certain degree of freedom, but it also transfers much of the risk that employers once carried onto individual workers.

On the positive side, short-term contracts can suit people whose priorities do not fit a conventional career path. A recent graduate, for example, may use a series of placements to sample different industries before committing to one, while a parent may value the ability to work intensively for several months and then take time off. For those with scarce, in-demand skills, contract work can be financially rewarding, as employers are often willing to pay a premium for expertise they need only temporarily. Moving between organisations also broadens professional networks and exposes workers to a variety of practices, which can make them more adaptable.

The drawbacks, however, fall most heavily on those with the least bargaining power. Without the assurance of continued employment, workers find it hard to plan ahead: securing a mortgage, supporting dependants or even booking a holiday becomes a gamble when income may stop within months. Temporary staff frequently miss out on entitlements such as sick pay, pension contributions and parental leave, and employers have little incentive to invest in training someone who may soon leave. Over time, this can trap people in a cycle of insecure jobs with limited prospects for promotion. The psychological toll should not be overlooked either, as persistent uncertainty is a well-known source of stress.

To sum up, short-term contracts can offer flexibility, variety and, for skilled professionals, higher earnings. For the majority of workers, however, these advantages come at the price of financial insecurity, reduced benefits and weaker career development, which is why such arrangements work best when they are genuinely chosen rather than imposed.

items.title: Supermarkets replacing local shops
items.prompt:
In many towns, small local shops are being replaced by large supermarkets and shopping centres. Do the advantages of this outweigh the disadvantages?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

modelAnswer.text:
The decline of the independent high-street shop in the face of competition from supermarkets and shopping centres is a familiar story in many towns. While the change has undoubtedly benefited shoppers in certain respects, I would argue that, taken as a whole, its advantages are outweighed by its costs.

The case for large retailers rests largely on price and convenience. Economies of scale allow supermarkets to negotiate lower prices from suppliers and pass at least some of these savings on to customers, which matters considerably to families whose budgets are stretched. Their extended opening hours, extensive product ranges and ample parking also suit modern lifestyles, in which many people have little time to visit several separate shops. For consumers, then, the immediate benefits are tangible.

The disadvantages, however, are broader and longer-lasting. Independent shops are typically owned by local residents, so the money spent in them tends to circulate within the community, supporting other local businesses and jobs. When they are replaced by national chains, a greater share of that spending is channelled elsewhere. The physical fabric of towns suffers too: once enough shops close, footfall declines, remaining businesses struggle and high streets can enter a spiral of decline marked by vacant units. There is also a social dimension that is easily overlooked. Small shops often serve as informal meeting points where neighbours exchange news, and for older or less mobile residents, a daily visit to a nearby store may be an important source of human contact. Out-of-town shopping centres, by contrast, are designed around the car and can leave such people isolated.

In conclusion, supermarkets and shopping centres offer genuine savings and convenience, but these gains are largely private and short-term, whereas the erosion of local economies and community life affects entire towns. For this reason, I believe the disadvantages outweigh the advantages.

items.title: Paid social media promotion
items.prompt:
Companies are increasingly paying popular social media users to promote their products. Do the advantages of this outweigh the disadvantages?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

modelAnswer.text:
Influencer marketing, in which brands pay popular social media users to feature their products, has become one of the fastest-growing forms of advertising. While it offers undeniable advantages to businesses and, to a lesser extent, to consumers, I would argue that its disadvantages ultimately carry more weight.

The appeal for companies is easy to understand. Influencers command highly engaged audiences, often defined by specific interests such as fitness, gaming or cookery, so a brand can place its message directly in front of the people most likely to buy. This precision makes campaigns more cost-effective than broad television advertising, and it gives small and new businesses a realistic route to visibility. Consumers may benefit too, since a detailed video demonstration can reveal more about how a product performs than a polished thirty-second commercial.

Nevertheless, the model rests on a fundamental tension. Its effectiveness depends on audiences perceiving the influencer as an authentic, independent voice, yet the content is, by definition, paid for. When sponsorship is concealed or disclosed only in small print, followers are effectively misled into treating advertising as personal recommendation. The problem is compounded by the age profile of many audiences: children and teenagers are less equipped to recognise persuasive intent and more susceptible to the carefully curated lifestyles on display, which can fuel both overconsumption and insecurity about body image. Furthermore, because influencers are rewarded for promotion rather than expertise, products such as dubious supplements or risky financial schemes can reach large audiences with little scrutiny.

Admittedly, clearer labelling requirements could reduce some of these harms, but enforcing them across millions of posts remains extremely difficult.

In conclusion, paid promotion on social media is an efficient and accessible marketing channel, yet its reliance on blurring commerce and personal opinion, combined with its reach among young people, means that in my view the disadvantages outweigh the advantages.

items.title: City centre congestion charges
items.prompt:
Some cities charge drivers a fee to enter the city centre at busy times of day. Do the advantages of this outweigh the disadvantages?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

modelAnswer.text:
Charging motorists to enter city centres at peak times has been adopted by a number of cities seeking to tackle congestion and pollution. Although the policy raises legitimate questions of fairness, I believe that, when well designed, its advantages clearly outweigh its disadvantages.

The rationale for such charges is that road space in a city centre is a scarce resource which, when provided free, is inevitably overused. By attaching a price to driving at the busiest times, a congestion charge encourages motorists to reconsider journeys that are not essential, to travel at quieter times or to switch to public transport. The result is faster, more reliable journeys for buses, deliveries and emergency services, whose efficiency is vital to the functioning of a city. The environmental gains are equally significant: reduced traffic means lower emissions and less noise in precisely the places where people are most concentrated. Moreover, the revenue generated can be ring-fenced for improving public transport, so that the alternatives to driving become steadily more attractive.

The main objection is that a flat fee is regressive. For a well-paid professional, the charge may be a trivial inconvenience, whereas for a low-paid worker who depends on a car, it can represent a substantial share of their daily earnings. Retailers in central districts also fear a loss of trade if shoppers choose to drive to suburban malls instead.

These concerns deserve serious attention, but they are arguments for refining the scheme rather than rejecting it. Exemptions for residents and disabled drivers, discounts for essential workers and investment in affordable public transport can all reduce the unequal impact, while a less congested, more pleasant centre may in fact attract more visitors on foot.

In conclusion, although congestion charges can bear more heavily on those with lower incomes, their capacity to reduce traffic, cut pollution and fund better transport makes them, on balance, a worthwhile policy whose benefits outweigh its costs.

items.title: Holidays in your own country
items.prompt:
Many people now choose to take their holidays in their own country rather than travelling abroad. What are the advantages and disadvantages of this?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

modelAnswer.text:
Choosing to explore one's own country instead of heading overseas has become an increasingly popular way to take a holiday. This preference brings clear financial, practical and environmental benefits, although it can also limit the broader horizons that international travel provides.

Chief among the advantages is affordability. Domestic trips avoid the expense of long-haul flights and foreign currency, and they can often be arranged at short notice, making regular breaks accessible to households that could not stretch to an annual trip abroad. They are also considerably less demanding: there are no language barriers, visa applications or unfamiliar healthcare systems to navigate, which is particularly reassuring for older travellers and families with young children. From a national perspective, domestic tourism keeps spending within the country, sustaining small hotels, guesthouses and restaurants in regions that may have few other sources of income. Finally, shorter journeys, especially by rail, generally have a far smaller carbon footprint than international flights.

Yet something is undeniably lost. Travelling abroad confronts people with different languages, values and ways of life, and this exposure can challenge assumptions and foster a more open-minded outlook in a way that familiar surroundings rarely do. Domestic holidays may also lack novelty for those who have grown up visiting the same resorts, and residents of smaller countries in particular may find the range of landscapes and climates limited. A further, more practical drawback is congestion: when large numbers of people holiday at home during the same school breaks, popular beauty spots can become overcrowded and local infrastructure stretched.

In conclusion, holidaying in one's own country is economical, convenient and comparatively sustainable, and it provides welcome support for local economies. Its main limitation is that it offers fewer opportunities for cultural discovery, which is why many people may still value an occasional journey further afield.

items.title: Renewable energy on farmland
items.prompt:
In some areas, large areas of farmland and countryside are being used for solar and wind energy projects. Do the advantages of this outweigh the disadvantages?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

modelAnswer.text:
As countries race to decarbonise their energy systems, farmland and open countryside are increasingly being given over to solar arrays and wind turbines. This has provoked fierce local opposition in some areas, yet I believe that, if sited thoughtfully, such projects deliver benefits that outweigh their costs.

The central argument for these developments is environmental necessity. Replacing coal and gas with renewable electricity is essential if the worst effects of climate change are to be avoided, and generating that electricity at scale requires space that dense urban areas simply cannot provide. Rural sites offer open exposure to sun and wind, relatively low land costs and room for installations large enough to supply thousands of homes. Such projects can also strengthen the rural economy: rental payments from energy companies give farmers a reliable income that cushions them against poor harvests and volatile food prices, while local communities may receive funds for shared facilities.

The objections, however, are not trivial. Agricultural land is a finite resource, and converting large areas of fertile fields to energy generation could undermine a country's capacity to feed itself. Landscapes that have been valued for generations may be transformed by industrial-scale structures, affecting both residents' attachment to their surroundings and the tourism on which some rural areas depend. Poorly planned schemes can also fragment habitats and endanger bird populations.

Crucially, though, most of these drawbacks depend on where and how projects are built rather than on renewable energy itself. Prioritising lower-grade farmland, combining solar panels with grazing, and avoiding sensitive habitats and migration routes can substantially reduce the conflict between energy, food and nature.

In conclusion, the loss of some farmland and scenic value is a genuine cost, but it must be weighed against the far greater threat posed by climate change. With careful planning, the advantages of rural renewable energy projects clearly outweigh the disadvantages.

data.title: Renewable energy on farmland

modelAnswer.text:
As countries race to decarbonise their energy systems, farmland and open countryside are increasingly being given over to solar arrays and wind turbines. This has provoked fierce local opposition in some areas, yet I believe that, if sited thoughtfully, such projects deliver benefits that outweigh their costs.

The central argument for these developments is environmental necessity. Replacing coal and gas with renewable electricity is essential if the worst effects of climate change are to be avoided, and generating that electricity at scale requires space that dense urban areas simply cannot provide. Rural sites offer open exposure to sun and wind, relatively low land costs and room for installations large enough to supply thousands of homes. Such projects can also strengthen the rural economy: rental payments from energy companies give farmers a reliable income that cushions them against poor harvests and volatile food prices, while local communities may receive funds for shared facilities.

The objections, however, are not trivial. Agricultural land is a finite resource, and converting large areas of fertile fields to energy generation could undermine a country's capacity to feed itself. Landscapes that have been valued for generations may be transformed by industrial-scale structures, affecting both residents' attachment to their surroundings and the tourism on which some rural areas depend. Poorly planned schemes can also fragment habitats and endanger bird populations.

Crucially, though, most of these drawbacks depend on where and how projects are built rather than on renewable energy itself. Prioritising lower-grade farmland, combining solar panels with grazing, and avoiding sensitive habitats and migration routes can substantially reduce the conflict between energy, food and nature.

In conclusion, the loss of some farmland and scenic value is a genuine cost, but it must be weighed against the far greater threat posed by climate change. With careful planning, the advantages of rural renewable energy projects clearly outweigh the disadvantages.

items.title: Adult children living at home
items.prompt:
Increasingly, young adults are continuing to live with their parents after they have finished their education. What are the advantages and disadvantages of this for both the young adults and their parents?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

modelAnswer.text:
In many societies, the age at which young people leave the family home is steadily rising, with growing numbers remaining with their parents well after they have completed their education. This trend carries a mixture of advantages and disadvantages for both generations, and its overall impact depends heavily on how the arrangement is managed.

For young adults, the benefits are largely economic. At a time when housing costs absorb an ever-larger proportion of starting salaries, living at home enables graduates to build savings, repay debts and accept lower-paid but career-enhancing positions that they could not otherwise afford. The family home can also serve as a safety net during an uncertain transition into working life. Parents may gain as well: the presence of an adult child can provide companionship, particularly for those who live alone, and practical assistance with everything from home repairs to navigating online services. In some cultures, multigenerational living is valued in its own right as a way of preserving close family ties.

The disadvantages, however, are equally real. Remaining under the parental roof can postpone the development of self-reliance, since many of the responsibilities that force young people to mature, such as paying rent and running a household, are absorbed by others. Limited privacy may also constrain their social lives. For parents, the arrangement can mean extra expense and a delayed opportunity to enjoy the freedom they may have anticipated once their children had grown up. Perhaps most significantly, adults with different routines and expectations sharing a home can generate friction, and unresolved tensions may strain relationships that would otherwise be harmonious.

In conclusion, continued co-residence offers young adults financial breathing space and parents companionship and support, but it risks delaying independence and generating conflict. The arrangement tends to work best when it is treated as a temporary stage, with clear expectations on both sides.

items.title: Health tracking technology
items.prompt:
Many people now use smartwatches and mobile phone apps to monitor their health and fitness. Do the advantages of this outweigh the disadvantages?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

modelAnswer.text:
The use of smartwatches and mobile applications to record everything from daily steps to sleep quality and heart rhythm has become commonplace. While this constant self-monitoring has its downsides, I would argue that, for most users, the advantages outweigh them.

The chief benefit is behavioural. Many people know in principle that they should move more, sleep better and eat more sensibly, but struggle to translate that knowledge into action. By turning vague intentions into concrete, measurable goals and providing immediate feedback, fitness trackers make healthy behaviour visible and rewarding, and features such as streaks or friendly competitions can sustain motivation over months. Beyond motivation, some devices can flag potentially significant irregularities, such as an unusually high resting heart rate, prompting users to consult a doctor sooner than they otherwise would. For people managing chronic conditions, digital records can also give doctors a far richer picture than occasional clinic visits allow.

There are, however, legitimate reservations. Consumer devices are not medical instruments, and inaccurate readings can either create needless anxiety or offer false reassurance. For some individuals, the constant stream of data fosters an unhealthy preoccupation with numbers, turning exercise and even sleep into sources of pressure. Most troubling, perhaps, is the question of privacy: health data is extraordinarily sensitive, and users often have little understanding of how it may be stored, analysed or shared with third parties such as advertisers or insurers.

These concerns warrant stronger regulation and greater user awareness, but they do not negate the value of the technology. Treated as a guide rather than a diagnosis, and protected by robust data laws, health trackers can play a genuinely positive role.

In conclusion, despite issues of accuracy, obsession and data security, the capacity of smartwatches and apps to encourage healthier habits and support earlier medical attention means that their advantages outweigh their disadvantages.

items.title: Security cameras in public places
items.prompt:
Many cities have installed large numbers of security cameras in public places in order to reduce crime. Do the advantages of this outweigh the disadvantages?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

modelAnswer.text:
Surveillance cameras have become a familiar feature of streets, stations and squares in many cities, justified primarily as a means of reducing crime. Although their spread raises serious questions about privacy and civil liberties, I believe that, under proper regulation, their advantages outweigh their disadvantages.

The strongest argument for public CCTV lies in its investigative value. Footage can establish a clear sequence of events, identify suspects and corroborate or challenge witness statements, often transforming cases that would otherwise remain unsolved. This is particularly important for crimes such as street robbery, where victims may have only a fleeting glimpse of the offender. Cameras may also exert a deterrent effect, especially in car parks and transport hubs, where opportunistic offences are common. Beyond crime, surveillance systems allow authorities to manage crowds at large events, locate missing people and coordinate rapid responses to accidents.

The disadvantages, nonetheless, deserve careful consideration. Blanket surveillance changes the nature of public space: people who know they are constantly observed may feel less free to gather, protest or simply behave spontaneously. The potential for misuse is considerable, whether through unauthorised access, the leaking of footage or, more worryingly, the combination of cameras with facial recognition to track individuals without their knowledge. Critics also point out that cameras are less effective against impulsive crime than their supporters claim, and that some offending is merely displaced to unmonitored streets, which raises doubts about whether the substantial public expenditure is justified.

These risks, however, point to the need for firm safeguards rather than the removal of cameras altogether. Strict limits on data retention, independent oversight and transparent rules on facial recognition can preserve most of the benefits while protecting civil liberties.

In conclusion, security cameras are not a complete solution to crime, and their misuse could threaten personal freedom. Nevertheless, their value in solving and deterring offences means that, carefully regulated, their advantages outweigh their disadvantages.

items.title: Recruiting skilled foreign workers
items.prompt:
Some countries encourage skilled workers from abroad to settle there in order to fill shortages in the labour market. Do the advantages of this outweigh the disadvantages for the receiving country?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

modelAnswer.text:
Many economies now rely on targeted immigration schemes to attract qualified professionals from abroad, particularly in sectors such as healthcare, engineering and technology. Although this strategy is not without complications, I would argue that, for the receiving country, its advantages clearly outweigh its disadvantages.

The most compelling benefit is the speed with which skills gaps can be closed. Domestic training pipelines take years to respond to changes in demand, and in the meantime shortages of nurses or software engineers can lengthen waiting lists, delay infrastructure projects and deter investment. Recruiting professionals who are already qualified allows these needs to be met almost immediately, and without the host country bearing the cost of their education. Skilled migrants also tend to be of working age and in well-paid employment, so they make a substantial contribution to public finances, which is increasingly valuable in societies where a shrinking workforce must support a growing number of retirees. Moreover, diverse teams often bring new perspectives, languages and international networks that strengthen innovation and trade.

The disadvantages are nonetheless significant. Rapid population growth in particular regions can outpace the supply of housing and school places, and if this pressure coincides with stagnant wages in some sectors, it can fuel resentment and social division. Employers may also come to regard overseas recruitment as a cheaper alternative to developing local talent, leaving domestic workers without opportunities to acquire in-demand skills. Finally, successful integration requires sustained investment in language support and the recognition of foreign qualifications, without which highly trained migrants may end up underemployed.

Crucially, these problems stem mainly from poor planning rather than from skilled migration itself, and they can be addressed through coordinated housing policy, parallel investment in domestic training and effective integration programmes.

In conclusion, attracting skilled workers from abroad carries social and practical challenges, but its contribution to essential services, public finances and economic dynamism means that its advantages outweigh its disadvantages for the receiving country.

items.title: Government spending on space research
items.prompt:
Some governments are investing large sums of money in space research programmes. What are the advantages and disadvantages of this?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

modelAnswer.text:
Space research has long been one of the most expensive and ambitious undertakings a government can pursue, and several countries are now expanding their programmes considerably. The merits of such investment are substantial, but so too are the objections, particularly regarding cost and priorities.

The case in favour rests first on the practical returns. Much of modern life depends on infrastructure that emerged from space programmes: satellites underpin weather forecasting, telecommunications, navigation and disaster monitoring, while technologies developed for spaceflight have been adapted for use in medicine and materials science. Space-based observation is also indispensable for understanding our own planet, providing long-term data on ice cover, sea levels and deforestation that would be impossible to gather from the ground. Beyond these tangible benefits, space exploration pushes the boundaries of human knowledge and, perhaps just as importantly, captures the public imagination, encouraging young people to pursue careers in science and engineering.

Against this, critics raise a powerful moral argument. When public resources are finite, allocating vast sums to exploring distant planets can appear difficult to justify while citizens lack adequate healthcare, housing or education. The benefits of space research are often long-term and uncertain, whereas the needs of the poor are immediate and pressing. There are environmental and practical concerns as well: each launch consumes enormous quantities of fuel, and the accumulation of debris in orbit increasingly threatens the satellites on which everyday services depend. Moreover, national prestige can sometimes drive spending more than genuine scientific value.

In conclusion, government investment in space research yields important technologies, scientific insight and inspiration, yet it competes with urgent social needs and carries environmental risks. The challenge for policymakers is therefore not whether to fund space programmes at all, but how to ensure that such spending remains proportionate and delivers clear public benefit.

items.title: Organised activities versus free play
items.prompt:
Many children now spend much of their free time in organised activities, such as sports clubs and music lessons, rather than playing freely. Do the advantages of this outweigh the disadvantages?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

modelAnswer.text:
In many families, children's leisure time is now carefully organised around sports clubs, music lessons and tutoring sessions, with unstructured play increasingly squeezed out. While organised activities undoubtedly have value, I would argue that when they come to dominate childhood, their disadvantages outweigh their advantages.

The benefits of structured activities are clear. Expert coaching allows children to acquire skills, from swimming to playing an instrument, that they would be unlikely to master alone, and the discipline of regular practice teaches persistence and the satisfaction of gradual improvement. Team sports and ensembles also foster cooperation and a sense of belonging, while giving children the experience of both success and disappointment in a supportive setting. For parents with demanding jobs, supervised activities offer the additional reassurance that their children are safe and productively occupied.

Free play, however, contributes to development in ways that adult-led activities cannot replicate. When children are left to their own devices, they must invent games, agree on rules and resolve conflicts among themselves, exercising creativity, negotiation and problem-solving in a genuinely independent way. Unstructured time also allows them to explore their own interests rather than those chosen for them, and simply to rest. A childhood filled with back-to-back commitments risks producing young people who are accomplished but anxious, accustomed to constant evaluation and uncomfortable with boredom, which is itself an important stimulus for imagination. The cost of multiple activities can also place considerable strain on family budgets and widen the gap between children from wealthier and poorer households.

In conclusion, organised activities provide valuable skills, discipline and safety, but they cannot substitute for the independence and creativity that free play nurtures. When structured activities largely replace unsupervised play, I believe the disadvantages outweigh the advantages, and families should deliberately protect time for children simply to play.

items.title: Private companies running public services
items.prompt:
In some countries, public services such as water supply, electricity and railways are run by private companies rather than by the government. Do the advantages of this outweigh the disadvantages?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

modelAnswer.text:
The transfer of utilities and railways from state ownership to private operators has been one of the most contested economic policies of recent decades. While private management can bring genuine improvements in efficiency, I would argue that, for services on which every citizen depends, the disadvantages ultimately prevail.

The principal argument for privatisation is that the discipline of the market drives better performance. State-run organisations are sometimes criticised for overstaffing, slow decision-making and political interference, whereas private firms, answerable to shareholders, have a clear incentive to control costs and innovate. Private capital can also fund investment in new trains, power stations or treatment plants without adding to public debt, and in sectors where competition is feasible, such as electricity retail, consumers may benefit from lower prices and more responsive service.

The weakness of this argument is that many essential services do not lend themselves to meaningful competition. A household cannot choose between rival water networks, and a commuter cannot select an alternative railway line; in such cases privatisation simply replaces a public monopoly with a private one. Once the pressure of competition is absent, the profit motive may encourage operators to raise charges, pay generous dividends and defer costly maintenance, leaving the public to deal with the consequences, from leaking pipes to unreliable trains. Accountability is also weakened: citizens can vote out a government that mismanages public services, but they have far less influence over a private company. Furthermore, because these services are necessities rather than optional purchases, price rises fall disproportionately on the poorest households.

Strict regulation can moderate some of these problems, but regulators often struggle to match the expertise and resources of the companies they oversee.

In conclusion, although private operators may deliver efficiency gains and fresh investment, the monopoly nature of many essential services, weaker accountability and the risk to vulnerable households mean that, in my view, the disadvantages of privatisation outweigh its advantages.

items.title: Online news sources
items.prompt:
Many people now get their news mainly from online sources rather than from newspapers or television. What are the advantages and disadvantages of this?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

modelAnswer.text:
The way people consume news has been transformed in a single generation, with websites, apps and social media now replacing the morning paper and the evening bulletin for a large share of the population. This transition has democratised access to information, yet it has also weakened some of the safeguards that traditional media provided.

The advantages are considerable. Online platforms deliver news almost instantaneously, allowing readers to follow developing stories in real time rather than waiting for the next edition or broadcast. Much of this content is free and available on a device most people carry at all times, which has made current affairs accessible to groups who might never have bought a newspaper. The sheer breadth of sources is also valuable: a reader can compare how a single event is covered by outlets in different countries, consult specialist analysis on niche subjects and even see footage captured by eyewitnesses on the ground. In this sense, the internet has diversified the range of voices that shape public debate.

However, the same openness brings serious drawbacks. Because anyone can publish, the traditional filters of editorial oversight and fact-checking are frequently absent, and misleading or entirely fabricated stories can circulate widely before they are challenged. The economic model of much online journalism compounds the problem: revenue depends on clicks, which rewards sensationalism over careful reporting. items.title: The shift to cashless payments
items.prompt:
In many countries, people are increasingly using cards and mobile phone apps to pay for things instead of cash. Do the advantages of this outweigh the disadvantages?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

modelAnswer.text:
The steady decline of cash in favour of cards, contactless technology and mobile wallets has been one of the quieter revolutions in everyday life. Although this shift poses genuine risks for certain groups, I am convinced that its advantages outweigh its disadvantages, provided that access to cash is not abolished altogether.

For consumers, the appeal of digital payments lies chiefly in their convenience. Transactions are completed in seconds, purchases can be made online or across borders without exchanging currency, and money can be sent to friends or family at the touch of a button. Electronic payments also offer greater security for individuals: a stolen wallet full of notes is usually lost for good, whereas a card can be frozen instantly and fraudulent transactions are often refunded. At a wider level, a largely cashless economy is more transparent. Because every payment leaves a record, it becomes considerably harder to conceal income from tax authorities or to launder the proceeds of crime, which ultimately benefits honest taxpayers. Businesses, meanwhile, save on the costs of handling, securing and banking physical money.

The drawbacks, however, should not be underestimated. Those who are elderly, on low incomes or living in areas with poor connectivity may find themselves excluded from essential services if cash ceases to be accepted. Digital payments can also make spending feel less tangible, which may encourage some people to overspend or fall into debt. Furthermore, a society dependent on electronic systems is exposed to cyber-attacks and outages, and the detailed data generated by every transaction raises legitimate questions about surveillance and privacy.

These concerns, though serious, argue for safeguards rather than a rejection of digital payments. Guaranteeing that cash remains legal tender and widely accepted, while enforcing robust data-protection standards, would address the most significant risks.

In conclusion, the move away from cash brings efficiency, security and transparency that benefit individuals and society as a whole. As long as vulnerable groups are protected, the advantages of this trend clearly outweigh its disadvantages.

items.title: Phones in the classroom
items.prompt:
In many schools, students are becoming increasingly distracted by mobile phones during lessons. What problems does this cause, and what can be done to solve them?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

modelAnswer.text:
In classrooms across the world, the smartphone has become a persistent rival for students' attention. While the device itself is not inherently harmful, its presence during lessons undermines both individual learning and the functioning of the class, and addressing this requires action from schools, teachers and families alike.

The most serious consequence is the erosion of sustained concentration. Learning complex material, whether an algebraic proof or the causes of a historical conflict, depends on following a line of reasoning without interruption. A single glance at a message may seem trivial, yet it fractures that reasoning, and a student who is interrupted repeatedly is left with a fragmented grasp of the topic that later surfaces as poor performance in assessments. Beyond the individual, phones damage the shared environment of the classroom. Teachers forced to police screen use lose time that should be spent teaching, and the constant tension between enforcement and instruction can sour relationships between staff and pupils. Moreover, distraction is contagious: one student scrolling through videos can draw the attention of an entire row.

The most direct remedy is an unambiguous, school-wide policy. Requiring phones to be stored in lockers or sealed pouches during the school day removes the temptation altogether, and applying the rule uniformly prevents the inconsistency that students are quick to exploit. However, restriction alone treats the symptom rather than the cause. Schools should also build digital literacy into the curriculum, helping young people understand how apps are designed to capture attention and how to regain control over their own habits. Parents have a complementary role in reinforcing these messages at home, while teachers can reduce the appeal of the phone by making lessons more participatory and less reliant on passive listening.

In short, mobile phones weaken concentration, waste teaching time and strain classroom relationships. A consistent ban, combined with education that equips students to manage technology themselves, offers the most durable solution.

items.title: Overcrowding in large cities
items.prompt:
Many large cities are becoming overcrowded as people move from rural areas to find work. What problems does this cause, and what measures could be taken to deal with them?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

modelAnswer.text:
Across much of the world, cities continue to swell as rural residents arrive in pursuit of work. Although this migration fuels economic growth, it frequently outpaces the capacity of urban areas to absorb newcomers, producing social and environmental strains that demand a coordinated policy response.

The most visible consequence is a crisis of housing. When population growth exceeds the rate of construction, prices rise beyond the reach of low-paid workers, who are pushed into overcrowded rented rooms or informal settlements on the urban fringe. These districts typically lack reliable water, sanitation and electricity, creating conditions in which disease spreads easily. A second set of problems stems from overstretched infrastructure. Transport networks designed for far smaller populations become gridlocked, lengthening commutes and worsening air quality, while schools and clinics struggle to meet demand. The result is a decline in living standards not only for migrants but for established residents too, which can in turn breed resentment between the two groups.

Tackling these difficulties requires measures both inside and outside the city. Within urban areas, governments should prioritise the construction of affordable housing and pair it with mass transit, so that new residential zones are connected to centres of employment rather than isolated from them. Upgrading informal settlements with basic services, rather than simply clearing them, is often a more humane and cost-effective approach. Equally important, however, is reducing the imbalance that drives migration in the first place. Investment in rural infrastructure, agricultural modernisation and regional industry can create viable livelihoods outside the major cities, while incentives for businesses to establish themselves in secondary towns would distribute economic opportunity more evenly.

In conclusion, rapid urban migration strains housing, transport and public services, lowering the quality of life for many residents. The most lasting solution lies in combining well-planned urban investment with a serious commitment to developing rural regions.

items.title: Housing for essential workers
items.prompt:
In many cities, housing has become so expensive that essential workers, such as nurses and teachers, can no longer afford to live near their workplaces. What problems does this cause, and what solutions can you suggest?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

modelAnswer.text:
The soaring cost of urban housing has created a paradox in many cities: the people whose work keeps them functioning, including nurses, teachers and care staff, increasingly cannot afford to live in them. This essay argues that the problem damages both the wellbeing of these workers and the quality of public services, and that it calls for targeted housing policy alongside broader reform.

At a personal level, being priced out imposes a heavy daily toll. Essential workers displaced to distant towns face lengthy commutes that, combined with irregular shifts, leave little time for rest or family life. Chronic fatigue is not merely unpleasant; in professions where alertness matters, such as nursing, it can compromise the safety of those in their care. Unsurprisingly, many eventually conclude that the sacrifice is not worth it and either leave the profession or move to cheaper regions. For the city, the cumulative effect is a persistent shortage of skilled staff. Schools rely on a rotating cast of supply teachers, hospitals spend heavily on agency nurses, and residents experience longer waits and less continuity of care. Emergency services, too, become less resilient when those who staff them live an hour or more away.

The most direct response is to provide housing designated for key workers, with rents set as a proportion of income rather than market value. Public bodies are often well placed to do this, since hospitals, universities and councils frequently own land that could be developed for staff accommodation. Location-based salary supplements can offer further relief, although they risk being absorbed by rising rents if supply remains constrained. Ultimately, therefore, such measures must be accompanied by a sustained expansion of affordable housing, achieved through planning reform and public construction.

In conclusion, unaffordable housing exhausts essential workers and weakens the services cities depend on. Dedicated key-worker housing offers immediate relief, but lasting improvement depends on building enough homes for ordinary earners.

items.title: Reducing food waste
items.prompt:
Large amounts of food are wasted every day by households, restaurants and supermarkets. What are the causes of this problem, and what can be done to reduce it?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

modelAnswer.text:
Despite widespread concern about food insecurity, vast quantities of edible food are discarded daily in homes, restaurants and supermarkets. The causes differ across these settings, but in each case waste stems from habits and systems that prioritise convenience over efficiency, and it can be reduced considerably through a mix of education, regulation and incentives.

In households, waste is largely a product of how people shop and store food. Relatively low prices in wealthier countries mean that discarding a half-used loaf carries little financial sting, while bulk promotions encourage people to buy more than they can realistically consume before it spoils. Misleading date labels compound the problem: many consumers fail to distinguish between a use-by date, which concerns safety, and a best-before date, which relates only to quality, and so throw away food that is still perfectly edible. The commercial sector has its own drivers. Supermarkets impose strict cosmetic standards that exclude misshapen produce before it even reaches the shelves, and they routinely overstock to avoid empty displays. Restaurants, for their part, often serve generous portions as a marker of value, much of which is left uneaten.

Tackling these causes calls for measures tailored to each. Simplifying date labelling, and removing best-before dates from items such as fresh fruit altogether, would prevent a great deal of unnecessary disposal at home, particularly if accompanied by public campaigns on meal planning and storage. For retailers, legislation obliging large stores to redistribute surplus edible food to charities has proved workable in several countries and could be adopted more widely. Supermarkets could also be encouraged to sell imperfect produce at a discount, and restaurants to offer flexible portion sizes.

In conclusion, food waste arises from overbuying, confusing labels and commercial practices that value appearance and abundance. Clearer information, redistribution laws and changes to retail and catering practice together offer a realistic path to reducing it.

items.title: Preparing for extreme weather
items.prompt:
Extreme weather events, such as floods and heatwaves, are becoming more common in many parts of the world. What problems does this create for local communities, and how can communities be better prepared?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

modelAnswer.text:
Floods, storms and prolonged heatwaves, once regarded as rare events, are now a recurring feature of life in many parts of the world. Their consequences for local communities are wide-ranging, affecting property, health and livelihoods, but much of the harm can be mitigated if communities invest in preparation rather than simply reacting after disaster strikes.

The most tangible impact is the destruction of homes and infrastructure. A single severe flood can render entire streets uninhabitable, sever transport links and knock out power and water supplies, isolating residents from essential services. The costs of recovery fall disproportionately on low-income households, which are less likely to be insured and more likely to live in vulnerable locations. Heatwaves, though less visibly destructive, can be even more deadly. Prolonged high temperatures place severe strain on older people and those with chronic illnesses, particularly in densely built urban areas where heat is retained overnight. There are also slower economic consequences: repeated crop failures erode farmers' livelihoods, and small businesses forced to close again and again may never reopen.

Preparation must therefore operate on several levels. Physical adaptation is the foundation, from flood defences and permeable drainage to building codes that require better insulation and shading. Land-use planning matters just as much, since continuing to build on floodplains simply multiplies future losses. Infrastructure alone is insufficient, however, without effective communication. Reliable early warning systems, delivered through mobile networks and local media, give residents time to act, while clearly marked evacuation routes ensure that warnings translate into safety. Finally, strong community networks can make a decisive difference. Neighbourhood schemes that identify isolated or elderly residents, together with designated cooling centres, help ensure that the most vulnerable are not overlooked.

In conclusion, extreme weather damages property, endangers health and undermines local economies. Communities that combine resilient infrastructure, prudent planning and well-organised warning and support systems will be far better equipped to withstand these growing threats.

items.title: Tackling traffic congestion
items.prompt:
Traffic congestion is a growing problem in many towns and cities. What problems does it cause, and what can be done to solve them?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

modelAnswer.text:
As car ownership has risen, the road networks of many towns and cities have become chronically congested, with rush-hour gridlock now an accepted part of urban life. This situation carries substantial economic, environmental and social costs, yet it is far from inevitable, and a number of well-tested measures can relieve it.

The economic burden of congestion is considerable. Time spent stationary in traffic is time lost to productive work or leisure, and unpredictable journey times make it harder for businesses to schedule deliveries and for employees to arrive punctually. These inefficiencies ripple through the economy, raising costs for firms and ultimately for consumers. The environmental and health consequences are equally serious. Stop-start driving is particularly inefficient, so congested streets generate disproportionate levels of exhaust emissions, degrading air quality and contributing to respiratory and heart disease. Residents of busy corridors also endure persistent noise, while heavy traffic discourages walking and cycling, reinforcing sedentary lifestyles.

Expanding road capacity might appear to be the obvious answer, but new roads tend to attract additional traffic and soon fill up again. A more effective strategy is to reduce demand for car travel. Frequent, affordable and reliable public transport is central to this, since people will only abandon their cars if a genuine alternative exists. Congestion charging, under which drivers pay to enter central zones at peak times, can then discourage non-essential journeys while generating revenue to fund transport improvements. Cities can further reshape travel habits by building safe, segregated cycle routes and by encouraging employers to adopt flexible hours and remote working, which spreads demand more evenly across the day.

In conclusion, congestion wastes time, burdens the economy and damages public health. Rather than building ever more roads, authorities should reduce reliance on cars through high-quality public transport, pricing mechanisms and support for active travel.

Congestion charging, under which drivers pay to enter central zones at peak times, can then discourage non-essential journeys while generating revenue to fund transport improvements. Cities can further reshape travel habits by building safe, segregated cycle routes and by encouraging employers to adopt flexible hours and remote working, which spreads demand more evenly across the day.

In conclusion, congestion wastes time, burdens the economy and damages public health. Rather than building ever more roads, authorities should reduce reliance on cars through high-quality public transport, pricing mechanisms and support for active travel.

items.title: Young people and jobs
items.prompt:
Many young people find it difficult to get a job after they finish their education. What are the reasons for this, and what can be done to help them?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

modelAnswer.text:
For many young people, the move from education into the workforce has become a prolonged and discouraging process, with months or even years passing before they secure stable employment. This difficulty has several interlocking causes, but it can be eased through closer cooperation between educators, employers and governments.

A fundamental cause is the mismatch between what education provides and what the labour market demands. Academic curricula often prioritise theoretical knowledge, leaving graduates ill-prepared for the practical and interpersonal demands of the workplace, while rapid technological change means that some skills are outdated almost as soon as they are taught. Compounding this is the so-called experience trap: employers, reluctant to invest in training, advertise even junior roles as requiring prior experience, which school leavers and graduates by definition do not possess. Structural factors play a part as well. In economies with sluggish growth, firms freeze recruitment, and because young people lack the seniority and networks of older workers, they bear a disproportionate share of the impact. The expansion of higher education has also intensified competition, as a degree no longer distinguishes an applicant in the way it once did.

Solutions should therefore target the transition itself. Embedding work placements and industry-led projects within courses would give students both relevant skills and demonstrable experience before they graduate. High-quality apprenticeships, which combine paid employment with structured training, offer an equally valuable route and deserve the same prestige as university study. Governments can reduce the risk employers perceive in hiring newcomers by subsidising wages or training costs for a limited period. Finally, careers guidance that draws on up-to-date labour market information would enable young people to make informed decisions about what to study.

In conclusion, youth unemployment stems from skills mismatches, the experience trap and wider economic weakness. By bridging the gap between education and work, societies can help young people establish themselves far more quickly.

items.title: Sedentary modern lifestyles
items.prompt:
In many countries, people are spending more time sitting down and less time being physically active. What problems does this cause, and how can people be encouraged to become more active?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

modelAnswer.text:
Over recent decades, daily life in many countries has become strikingly sedentary. Desk-based jobs, car-dependent commuting and screen-based leisure mean that many adults now spend the majority of their waking hours seated. This shift carries significant costs, but carefully designed interventions can make physical activity a more natural part of everyday routines.

The most serious consequences are for health. Prolonged inactivity is a major risk factor for obesity, cardiovascular disease and type 2 diabetes, and it contributes to musculoskeletal problems such as chronic back pain. The effects are not solely physical: regular movement is associated with better sleep, lower stress and improved mood, so its absence can leave people more vulnerable to anxiety and depression. These individual problems accumulate into a wider social burden. Health services must treat a growing number of preventable, long-term conditions, while employers face reduced productivity and higher rates of absence.

Simply urging people to exercise more has limited effect, because inactivity is largely a product of how environments and routines are structured. The most promising approach is therefore to design activity back into daily life. Towns that provide continuous cycle networks, pleasant walking routes and accessible green spaces make active travel the convenient choice rather than a sacrifice. Workplaces can contribute by offering flexible breaks, sit-stand desks and facilities such as showers and bicycle storage that make active commuting practical. Schools arguably have the greatest long-term influence, since a positive early experience of sport and play shapes habits for life; ensuring that physical education is varied and inclusive, rather than purely competitive, is key. Subsidised leisure centre membership can further lower barriers for low-income groups.

In conclusion, sedentary lifestyles damage physical and mental health and impose broader economic costs. Rather than relying on exhortation, societies should reshape their built environments, workplaces and schools so that being active becomes the easiest option.

items.title: Loneliness in old age
items.prompt:
Loneliness is becoming increasingly common among older people in many societies. What problems does this cause, and what can be done to address it?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

modelAnswer.text:
In many societies, a combination of longer life expectancy, smaller families and greater geographical mobility has left a growing number of older people living alone with limited social contact. The resulting loneliness is far more than a private sorrow; it has serious consequences for health and public services, and it demands a response from families, communities and the state.

The most profound impact is on wellbeing. Prolonged isolation is strongly associated with depression and a loss of purpose, and it is increasingly recognised as a risk to physical health in its own right. Older people without regular social interaction may also experience faster cognitive decline, as conversation and shared activity help to keep the mind engaged. Isolation creates practical vulnerabilities as well: someone who lives alone and has few visitors may lie undiscovered for hours after a fall, and may be more susceptible to fraud or neglect. These individual harms translate into collective costs, since lonely older people tend to make greater use of doctors, hospitals and residential care.

Addressing the problem means rebuilding the social connections that modern life has eroded. Families remain central, and even regular calls can provide reassurance and a sense of being valued. Yet many older people have no close relatives nearby, so community provision is essential. Local authorities and charities can sustain lunch clubs, exercise groups and learning opportunities that give people both a reason and a means to leave home, provided that accessible transport is available. Volunteer befriending services offer companionship to those who are housebound, while intergenerational schemes, such as pairing students with older residents, foster mutual understanding and benefit both parties. Doctors, too, can refer isolated patients to such activities rather than relying solely on medication.

In conclusion, loneliness in later life undermines health and places growing pressure on services. Sustained investment in community networks, supported by families and volunteers, offers the most effective remedy.
