items.title: Protecting people from fraud
items.prompt:
Online fraud and identity theft are increasing as more people use the internet for shopping and banking. What problems does this cause, and what measures could be taken to protect people?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

modelAnswer.text:
The convenience of online shopping and banking has come at a price: as more of our financial lives move onto digital platforms, fraudsters and identity thieves have found ever more opportunities to exploit them. The resulting harm extends well beyond individual losses, and countering it requires coordinated effort from institutions, governments and users themselves.

The immediate damage is financial. Victims may see their savings drained or discover purchases made with cloned card details, and while banks often reimburse unauthorised transactions, those who were manipulated into making a payment themselves may receive nothing. Identity theft can be more insidious still. Using stolen personal information, criminals can open accounts, apply for credit or commit further offences in another person's name, leaving the victim to spend months restoring their financial reputation. The psychological toll is also significant; many victims describe feelings of violation and shame, and some withdraw from online services entirely. At a societal level, widespread fraud erodes trust in digital commerce and imposes substantial costs on businesses, which are ultimately passed on to consumers.

Because modern fraud targets both systems and people, protection must address both. Financial institutions should adopt robust authentication, such as one-time codes and biometric checks, alongside monitoring systems that flag anomalous transactions in real time. Regulators can reinforce this by requiring companies to meet minimum security standards and to compensate customers fairly when those standards fail. Yet technology alone cannot stop a victim from being persuaded to hand over details voluntarily. Sustained public education, particularly aimed at older and less experienced users, is therefore vital in teaching people to recognise phishing messages and pressure tactics. Finally, since many fraud networks operate across borders, police forces need specialist expertise and effective international cooperation to pursue offenders.

In conclusion, online fraud inflicts financial, psychological and economic damage. Combining secure technology, sensible regulation, public awareness and international enforcement offers the most credible defence.

items.title: False information online
items.prompt:
False information can now spread very quickly through social media. What problems does this cause, and what can be done to reduce the spread of false information?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

modelAnswer.text:
Social media has made it possible for a rumour posted in one country to reach millions of screens worldwide before any journalist has had the chance to verify it. The speed and scale at which falsehoods now travel create problems that go well beyond individual misunderstanding, and tackling them requires action on several fronts.

The most immediate danger concerns decisions that affect health and safety. False claims about miracle cures or the risks of established treatments can lead people to reject sound medical advice, with consequences not only for themselves but for those around them. Misinformation also has a corrosive effect on social cohesion. Fabricated stories that scapegoat minority groups can inflame hostility, and online rumours have at times been followed by real-world violence. In the political sphere, deliberately misleading content can distort public debate and undermine confidence in elections. Underlying all of these is a gradual erosion of trust: when accurate and inaccurate information circulate side by side, many people become cynical about every source, making it harder for legitimate institutions to communicate during genuine emergencies.

Since the problem stems partly from how platforms are designed, the companies behind them must bear much of the responsibility. Algorithms that reward engagement tend to amplify sensational content, so platforms should adjust them to reduce the reach of material flagged as false and invest in faster moderation. Transparent labelling, linking disputed claims to reliable sources, can also help users judge what they read. Regulation may be needed to ensure these commitments are honoured, though it must be carefully framed to avoid restricting legitimate expression. In the longer term, the most durable defence is a public able to evaluate information critically. Media literacy should be embedded in school curricula, teaching students to check sources, recognise manipulated images and notice when content is designed to provoke outrage.

In conclusion, misinformation threatens health, social cohesion and trust in institutions. Better platform design, careful regulation and widespread media literacy together offer the most effective response.

items.title: Protecting minority languages
items.prompt:
Many minority languages are disappearing because fewer young people are learning to speak them. What problems does this cause, and what can be done to protect these languages?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

modelAnswer.text:
Many of the world's minority languages may fall silent within a generation or two, largely because children are no longer acquiring them. The disappearance of such a language is not merely a technical loss; it has cultural, social and personal consequences, and while reversing the decline is difficult, it is by no means impossible.

At the broadest level, each language represents a unique store of human knowledge. Oral histories, poetry, traditional understanding of the local environment and distinctive ways of categorising experience are embedded in vocabulary and grammar, and much of this resists translation. When a language dies, this heritage is largely lost not only to its community but to humanity as a whole. The consequences are also felt within families. Where grandparents are most at ease in the heritage language and grandchildren speak only the dominant one, conversations may be reduced to practical exchanges, weakening the transmission of values and memories between generations. For young people themselves, losing an ancestral language can mean losing a vital link to their identity, sometimes leaving them feeling that they belong fully to neither their own community nor the wider society.

Efforts to protect endangered languages are most effective when they combine institutional support with community ownership. Official recognition and funding for bilingual or immersion schooling can give children fluency at the age when language is most easily acquired. However, schooling alone rarely succeeds unless the language is also spoken at home, so programmes that support parents are equally important. A language also needs a modern presence if young people are to value it: broadcasting, digital content and music in the language signal that it belongs to the present rather than the past. Finally, documentation through recordings, dictionaries and grammars provides a foundation for revival should the number of speakers fall further.

In conclusion, the decline of minority languages erodes cultural knowledge, family bonds and personal identity. Sustained investment in education, family use and contemporary media can give these languages a genuine future.

items.title: Switching off from work
items.prompt:
Many employees work long hours and find it difficult to stop thinking about work in their free time. What problems does this cause for individuals and their families, and what solutions can you suggest?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

modelAnswer.text:
For a growing number of employees, work no longer ends when they leave the office. Long hours, combined with smartphones that keep them permanently reachable, mean that professional concerns now spill into evenings, weekends and holidays. This essay examines the toll this takes on individuals and their families, and suggests how a healthier balance might be restored.

For the individual, the absence of genuine recovery time is profoundly harmful. The mind needs periods of detachment to recover from sustained effort, and when these are lost, stress accumulates into chronic exhaustion and, eventually, burnout. Disrupted sleep is a common early sign, as people lie awake rehearsing tomorrow's deadlines. Paradoxically, the pattern is also counterproductive for employers, since fatigued staff tend to be less creative, more error-prone and more likely to take sick leave or resign. The impact on families can be just as damaging. Children whose parents are physically present but mentally preoccupied may feel that they come second to a screen, and the everyday rituals that sustain family life, from shared meals to bedtime conversations, are gradually squeezed out. Between partners, an unequal burden of household responsibilities can breed resentment.

Addressing the problem requires change at both organisational and personal levels. Employers can set explicit policies discouraging out-of-hours communication, and several countries have legislated a right to disconnect, giving employees legal protection when they choose not to respond. Realistic workloads matter just as much, because a ban on evening emails achieves little if the volume of work cannot be completed within normal hours. Leadership culture is decisive here: when senior staff visibly protect their own time, others feel permitted to do the same. Individuals, in turn, can create clear boundaries, such as disabling work notifications and reserving certain times for family and leisure.

In conclusion, overwork undermines health, productivity and family relationships. Sensible workplace policy, backed by leaders who model balance and individuals who guard their personal time, offers the most realistic solution.

items.title: Ageing rural communities
items.prompt:
In many rural areas, young people are leaving to live in cities, leaving behind an increasingly elderly population. What problems does this cause for rural communities, and what can be done to solve them?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

modelAnswer.text:
Across many countries, the countryside is emptying of its young. Drawn by universities, better-paid work and the amenities of urban life, school leavers and young adults depart in large numbers, and relatively few return. The communities they leave behind grow steadily older, facing a combination of economic, social and practical difficulties that call for deliberate intervention.

The economic consequences are often the first to appear. Farms struggle to find successors and seasonal labour, while shops and small firms lose both staff and customers. Each closure makes the area less appealing to potential residents, so decline tends to become self-reinforcing. Demographic ageing then compounds the problem. Older residents typically require more health and social care, yet rural areas are already poorly served by doctors and hospitals, and the adult children who might once have provided informal support now live hours away. As numbers fall further, schools, bank branches and bus routes are withdrawn on grounds of cost, leaving those who remain, particularly people who no longer drive, isolated and dependent.

Reversing this trend requires giving young people genuine reasons to stay or return. The most powerful lever is probably digital infrastructure: reliable high-speed broadband makes remote work viable, allowing professionals to hold city-based jobs while living rurally. Targeted incentives, such as grants for rural start-ups, affordable housing reserved for local families and support for young farmers, can reinforce this. Services, meanwhile, must be redesigned rather than simply withdrawn. Remote consultations, visiting clinics and shared community hubs that combine a post office, café and health point can maintain access at a sustainable cost. items.title: The brain drain
items.prompt:
Many developing countries are losing skilled professionals, such as doctors and engineers, who move to work in wealthier countries. What problems does this cause for developing countries, and what can be done about it?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

modelAnswer.text:
The migration of skilled professionals from developing to wealthier countries is driven by understandable personal ambitions: higher salaries, better equipment and clearer career paths. Yet the cumulative effect of these individual decisions can be severe for the countries they leave, and mitigating it requires action from both sending and receiving nations.

The most acute consequence is a shortage of expertise precisely where it is most needed. Health systems in lower-income countries, already under strain, lose doctors and nurses they can ill afford to lose, with rural populations typically suffering most as the remaining staff concentrate in cities. The departure of engineers, scientists and academics likewise weakens a country's capacity to build infrastructure, innovate and train the next generation. There is also a significant fiscal dimension. Developing countries often subsidise higher education heavily, so each departing graduate represents a public investment whose returns are enjoyed elsewhere; in effect, poorer nations end up subsidising the workforce of richer ones. Over time, this can entrench global inequality.

Since the causes are largely economic and professional, the most effective responses address working conditions rather than simply restricting movement. Improving salaries, investing in facilities and creating transparent paths to promotion can persuade many professionals that a rewarding career is possible at home. Bonding schemes, under which graduates of state-funded programmes serve domestically for a set period, can secure a return on public investment, provided they are fair rather than punitive. Governments can also cultivate their diaspora, offering incentives for return and channels through which emigrants contribute knowledge remotely. Receiving countries bear responsibility too: adhering to ethical recruitment codes and co-funding training in source countries would help ensure that migration benefits both sides.

In conclusion, the loss of skilled professionals weakens essential services, wastes public investment and deepens global inequality. A combination of better domestic conditions, well-designed retention schemes and responsible recruitment abroad offers the most balanced solution.

items.title: AI and job security
items.prompt:
As artificial intelligence is used more widely in the workplace, many people are worried that their jobs will disappear. What problems might this cause, and how can governments and individuals prepare for these changes?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

modelAnswer.text:
As artificial intelligence moves from research laboratories into everyday workplaces, anxiety about the future of employment has grown. Although new technologies have historically created new kinds of work as well as destroying old ones, the speed and breadth of AI adoption could make this transition unusually disruptive, and preparing for it is a shared responsibility of governments and individuals.

The most immediate concern is displacement. AI systems can already draft documents, analyse data and handle customer queries, which places many clerical, administrative and even some professional roles at risk. Workers whose skills become redundant in mid-career may struggle to find comparable employment, facing not only a loss of income but a loss of status and purpose. There is also a distributional problem. The gains from automation are likely to flow disproportionately to those who own the technology and to highly skilled specialists, while less qualified workers bear most of the risk, potentially widening inequality and fuelling political discontent.

Governments should focus on easing the transition rather than resisting technological change. Large-scale, accessible retraining, ideally designed with employers so that it leads to real vacancies, would help displaced workers move into expanding fields. Schools and universities need to prioritise capabilities that complement AI, such as judgement, creativity and collaboration, alongside the digital literacy needed to work with intelligent systems. A modernised safety net, linking income support to training, would give people the security to retrain rather than accept the first available job.

Individuals, for their part, can reduce their vulnerability by treating learning as a career-long process. Becoming proficient with the AI tools relevant to their field, and cultivating distinctly human strengths such as persuasion and empathy, makes workers more likely to be augmented by technology than replaced by it.

In conclusion, AI threatens displacement and greater inequality, but coordinated investment in skills and social protection, combined with personal adaptability, can make the transition far more manageable.

items.title: Less family time together
items.prompt:
In many families, parents and children spend less time together than they did in the past. What are the causes of this, and what can be done to improve the situation?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

modelAnswer.text:
Many parents today would readily admit that they spend less time with their children than their own parents spent with them. This shift is not the result of indifference but of economic, social and technological pressures, and while these cannot be removed entirely, families and employers can take practical steps to counteract them.

Economic demands are perhaps the most powerful cause. In many households, two incomes are now necessary to meet housing and living costs, and both parents may face long hours and lengthy commutes. The boundary between work and home has also blurred, as smartphones allow employers to reach staff at any time, so even evenings at home can be interrupted by messages and deadlines. Children's lives, meanwhile, have become increasingly scheduled. Parents anxious to give their children every advantage enrol them in tutoring, sport and music, leaving little unstructured time in which the family can simply be together. Technology intensifies the problem within the home itself: households in which each member retreats to a personal screen may be under one roof yet largely disconnected.

Addressing this requires deliberately protecting family time rather than expecting it to occur naturally. Simple, consistent rituals, such as a shared evening meal with devices set aside, create a daily space for conversation. Parents may also benefit from questioning whether every extracurricular activity is essential, since a less crowded timetable leaves room for the spontaneous moments that children often value most. Employers, however, hold considerable influence. Flexible hours, remote working and a culture that respects time off would allow parents to be present when it matters, such as at the end of the school day. Governments can reinforce this through adequate parental leave and protection against excessive working hours.

In conclusion, long working hours, overscheduled childhoods and pervasive technology have eroded family time. Protecting it depends on conscious choices at home, supported by workplaces and policies that value family life.

items.title: Hospital waiting times
items.prompt:
In many countries, patients have to wait a long time to receive treatment in public hospitals. What are the causes of this problem, and what solutions can you suggest?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

modelAnswer.text:
In many countries with publicly funded healthcare, lengthy waiting lists have become one of the most visible signs of a system under strain. Patients may wait months for diagnostic tests or surgery, sometimes seeing their condition deteriorate in the meantime. The causes are several and interrelated, and so are the solutions.

At the heart of the problem is a mismatch between rising demand and constrained capacity. Ageing populations mean that more people are living with chronic conditions requiring ongoing treatment, while advances in medicine have expanded the range of procedures that can be offered. Capacity, by contrast, has not kept pace. Medical staff take years to train, and public hospitals often lose experienced doctors and nurses to better-paid private practice or to other countries, leaving those who remain overstretched. Inefficiencies elsewhere in the system compound these shortages. When adequate social care is unavailable, patients who are medically fit to leave hospital occupy beds for days or weeks, creating bottlenecks that ripple back through wards and emergency departments. Similarly, weak primary care means that many conditions which could be managed in the community end up in hospital.

The most sustainable response is to expand and retain the workforce, which means increasing training places while improving pay, working conditions and career development in the public sector. Staffing alone will not suffice, however, unless patient flow is improved. Investing in social care would allow timely discharge, and strengthening local clinics would intercept minor complaints before they reach hospital. Hospitals can also increase throughput by separating planned surgery from emergency services, so that routine operations are not cancelled whenever emergency admissions surge. Digital scheduling and remote follow-up appointments offer further gains in efficiency.

In conclusion, long waits stem from rising demand, workforce shortages and bottlenecks elsewhere in the system. Addressing them requires sustained investment in staff alongside reforms that allow patients to move through care more smoothly.

items.title: Debt from buying on credit
items.prompt:
Many people get into debt because they buy goods on credit that they cannot really afford. What problems does this cause, and what can be done to prevent it?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

modelAnswer.text:
Access to credit has never been easier. Credit cards, retail finance and instant buy-now-pay-later options allow consumers to acquire goods at the touch of a button, often without fully registering what they will eventually pay. For those who borrow beyond their means, the consequences can be severe, and preventing them requires action from educators, lenders and regulators alike.

The most direct harm is the way debt can escalate. High interest and penalty charges mean that modest purchases can grow into substantial obligations, and borrowers who fall behind may resort to further borrowing to service existing debts, entering a cycle from which escape is difficult. A poor credit history can then restrict access to housing and affordable loans for years. The personal toll extends well beyond finances. Persistent money worries are closely associated with anxiety, sleep problems and depression, and financial strain is a frequent source of tension between partners that affects children as well. On a societal scale, high levels of household debt leave economies more fragile, since heavily indebted consumers cut spending sharply when conditions deteriorate.

Prevention should begin with education. Teaching financial literacy in schools, covering budgeting, compound interest and the true cost of borrowing, equips young people to make informed decisions before they are targeted by lenders. Education alone, however, cannot counter marketing designed to make borrowing feel effortless. Regulators should therefore require rigorous affordability checks, clear disclosure of the total repayable amount and limits on excessive charges, and should bring newer forms of short-term credit under the same rules as conventional loans. Retailers could also be discouraged from presenting finance as the default option at checkout. Finally, free and impartial debt advice helps those already in difficulty to act before their situation worsens.

In conclusion, unaffordable credit can trap people in escalating debt, damage their wellbeing and weaken the wider economy. Financial education, combined with responsible lending rules, offers the most effective safeguard.

items.title: Why small businesses fail
items.prompt:
A large number of small businesses fail within the first few years of opening. What are the reasons for this, and what can be done to help small businesses succeed?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

modelAnswer.text:
Opening a small business is, for many people, the realisation of a long-held ambition, yet a considerable share of new ventures close within a few years. Their failure rarely has a single cause; rather, it usually reflects a combination of financial fragility, gaps in expertise and a difficult competitive environment, each of which can be addressed.

Financial weakness is the most common underlying factor. Founders frequently underestimate both their start-up costs and the time needed to reach profitability, so that fixed expenses such as rent, wages and loan repayments consume their capital before revenue has had a chance to build. Late payments from larger clients can then create a cash-flow crisis even for a business that is fundamentally viable. A second factor is the gap between technical skill and business acumen. An excellent chef or designer may have little experience of pricing, bookkeeping or marketing, and misjudgements in these areas can prove fatal. Finally, small firms operate at a structural disadvantage against large chains and online platforms, whose purchasing power allows them to undercut prices, while high commercial rents in many town centres add to the pressure.

Support is therefore most effective when it tackles these weaknesses directly. Access to patient, affordable finance, whether through government-backed loans or temporary relief from business taxes, would give new firms a longer runway to establish themselves. Legislation requiring prompt payment by large companies would protect smaller suppliers from avoidable cash-flow problems. Just as important is building capability: mentoring schemes that pair founders with experienced entrepreneurs, alongside practical training in finance and marketing, can prevent many costly errors. Small businesses themselves can strengthen their position by competing on qualities that large firms struggle to match, such as personal service, specialist knowledge and local loyalty.

In conclusion, small businesses fail mainly because of undercapitalisation, limited management experience and unequal competition. Targeted finance, fair payment practices and accessible mentoring could allow far more of them to thrive.

items.title: Adults returning to education
items.prompt:
Many adults decide to return to education later in life. Why do they do this? What difficulties might they face?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

modelAnswer.text:
Lifelong learning, once regarded as unusual, has become an increasingly familiar pattern, with many people enrolling on courses long after they have left school. Their reasons tend to be both practical and personal, but the path back into education is often complicated by commitments and anxieties that younger students rarely face.

Economic change is perhaps the strongest driving force. As automation and new technologies reshape the labour market, skills that once guaranteed secure employment can quickly become obsolete, and workers who wish to remain employable may have little choice but to retrain. Someone who has spent fifteen years in retail, for instance, might study accounting or data analysis to move into a more stable sector. Yet not every decision is driven by necessity. For many, returning to education is a matter of unfinished business: they may have abandoned their studies to support a family or to start earning, and a degree taken in middle age represents a goal finally achieved rather than a mere qualification.

The difficulties these learners face are, however, considerable. Time is the most pressing constraint, as coursework has to be fitted around full-time jobs, childcare and household responsibilities, often leaving study for late evenings or weekends. This juggling act can be exhausting, and it is one of the main reasons mature students withdraw before completing their courses. Money presents a further obstacle, because fees must usually be met from a household budget that is already stretched, and cutting working hours to study is a luxury few can afford. Less visible, but equally significant, is the psychological barrier. Adults who have not written an essay for decades may doubt their abilities and feel out of place among classmates half their age.

In short, adults return to education to keep pace with a changing economy and to fulfil long-held aspirations. Although lack of time, financial pressure and self-doubt can make the experience demanding, these obstacles are far easier to overcome when institutions offer flexible timetables and targeted support.

Less visible, but equally significant, is the psychological barrier. Adults who have not written an essay for decades may doubt their abilities and feel out of place among classmates half their age.

In short, adults return to education to keep pace with a changing economy and to fulfil long-held aspirations. Although lack of time, financial pressure and self-doubt can make the experience demanding, these obstacles are far easier to overcome when institutions offer flexible timetables and targeted support.

items.title: Technology and independent thinking
items.prompt:
People increasingly rely on technology, such as search engines and navigation apps, rather than their own memory and knowledge. Why has this happened? What effect does it have on people's ability to think for themselves?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

modelAnswer.text:
Few people today would set off for an unfamiliar destination without a navigation app, and even fewer would try to recall an obscure fact when a search engine can supply it instantly. This growing reliance on technology stems largely from its convenience and ubiquity, and although it has clear benefits, I believe it risks eroding people's capacity to think independently.

The shift can be explained by several interrelated factors. The most obvious is accessibility: smartphones have placed vast quantities of information within constant reach, making the effort of memorisation seem unnecessary. At the same time, the pace of modern life encourages people to delegate routine mental tasks. A commuter juggling work messages and family arrangements has little incentive to learn a route by heart when an app will not only guide them but also adjust for traffic. Furthermore, these tools are generally accurate, so people have come to trust them more than their own, sometimes unreliable, recollection.

The consequences for independent thought are more troubling. Memory and reasoning are closely linked; people who store knowledge internally are better able to make connections, spot inconsistencies and form original judgements. When everything is looked up on demand, this internal framework is never built. Navigation offers a telling example: drivers who follow turn-by-turn instructions often develop little sense of how a city fits together and can become disoriented as soon as the signal drops. More broadly, search engines present information that has already been filtered and ranked, which can encourage passive acceptance rather than critical evaluation. Admittedly, technology can also stimulate thinking by exposing users to a wider range of sources, but this depends on people actively questioning what they find.

In conclusion, dependence on digital tools has arisen because they are fast, reliable and constantly available. While they undoubtedly save time, habitual reliance on them can weaken memory and discourage critical reasoning, so they are best treated as aids to thinking rather than replacements for it.

items.title: AI and human creativity
items.prompt:
Artificial intelligence can now produce paintings, music and stories. How does this affect the value that people place on human creativity? Should there be limits on the use of artificial intelligence in creative industries?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

modelAnswer.text:
Now that algorithms can compose symphonies, write short stories and produce convincing portraits, the question of what makes human creativity valuable has become more pressing than ever. I would argue that AI is simultaneously cheapening some forms of creative work and deepening appreciation for others, and that carefully designed limits on its use are both justified and necessary.

The most immediate impact is economic. Commercial creativity, such as stock illustrations, advertising jingles or product descriptions, is increasingly treated as a commodity that AI can supply instantly and at negligible cost. In these areas, the perceived worth of human skill is clearly falling, and many freelance designers and writers have already seen demand for their services shrink. Yet this is only part of the picture. Art has never been valued solely for its surface qualities; audiences are also drawn to the intention, experience and vulnerability behind it. A song about loss means more when listeners know that its writer has actually grieved. Paradoxically, therefore, the flood of machine-generated content may make work that is demonstrably human rarer and more prized, much as handcrafted goods gained prestige after industrial production became widespread.

Regarding limits, a blanket ban would be neither practical nor desirable, since AI can be a genuinely useful instrument in the hands of artists. However, two forms of regulation seem essential. First, the data used to train these systems frequently consists of copyrighted work taken without permission, so creators should have the right to opt out and to receive fair payment when their work is used. Second, transparency is crucial: audiences and buyers deserve to know whether a piece was produced by a person or a program, which clear labelling requirements would guarantee.

In conclusion, AI is devaluing routine creative work while potentially elevating the status of authentic human expression. Rather than prohibiting the technology, societies should limit its use through fair rules on training data and mandatory disclosure, protecting artists while allowing innovation to continue.

items.title: Second-hand clothing trend
items.prompt:
In many places, people are becoming more interested in buying second-hand clothes. Why is this happening? What other steps can people take to reduce the environmental impact of the clothes they buy?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

modelAnswer.text:
Charity shops and online resale platforms are enjoying a surge in popularity, as buyers who would once have insisted on new clothes increasingly choose pre-owned alternatives. This shift reflects a combination of ethical, economic and cultural factors, and while it is a positive development, it is only one of several ways in which consumers can make their clothing habits more sustainable.

Perhaps the most significant driver is a heightened awareness of the environmental cost of fashion. Widespread media coverage has exposed the industry's heavy use of water, its reliance on synthetic fibres and the mountains of discarded garments that end up in landfill, prompting many shoppers to reconsider their habits. Economic pressures reinforce this trend: with household budgets under strain, a designer jacket at a fraction of its retail price is an attractive proposition. Cultural attitudes have also shifted. Among younger consumers in particular, vintage clothing is seen not as a sign of hardship but as a way of expressing individuality, and resale apps have made browsing for such items as effortless as shopping on the high street.

Beyond buying second-hand, the single most effective step is to consume less. Choosing fewer, better-made garments and wearing them for longer reduces demand for new production far more than any recycling scheme. Caring for clothes properly also matters; washing at lower temperatures, air-drying rather than tumble-drying, and carrying out simple repairs can extend a garment's life considerably. When items are no longer wanted, they should be donated, swapped or sold rather than thrown away. Finally, consumers can use their purchasing power to reward manufacturers that are transparent about their supply chains and that use recycled or responsibly sourced materials.

In conclusion, the appeal of second-hand clothing stems from environmental concern, financial prudence and changing tastes. Its benefits can be multiplied if people also buy less, look after what they own and support genuinely responsible brands.

items.title: Strangers next door
items.prompt:
In many cities today, people hardly know their neighbours. Why is this the case? How can a stronger sense of community be created in cities?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

modelAnswer.text:
Paradoxically, cities pack people together more densely than anywhere else, yet many urban residents could not name the person living on the other side of their wall. This anonymity has social, economic and architectural roots, but it is not inevitable, and there are practical ways in which a sense of community can be rebuilt.

One fundamental reason is the structure of urban working life. Long hours and extended commutes turn many homes into little more than places to sleep, so residents are seldom around at the times when neighbourly contact might occur. Transience compounds the problem. In cities where a large proportion of people rent, tenants may move every year or two, and there is little motivation to build relationships that seem likely to be short-lived. Architecture also plays a part: high-rise blocks with anonymous corridors and underground parking allow people to travel from their car to their flat without encountering anyone. Finally, online social networks now satisfy much of the need for connection that was once met locally, making it easy to feel sociable while remaining a stranger to one's neighbours.

Rebuilding community therefore requires action on several levels. Planners can design spaces that encourage chance encounters, such as courtyards, shared gardens and pedestrian-friendly streets lined with small shops and cafés, since relationships tend to grow out of repeated informal contact rather than organised gatherings. Local authorities can supplement this by funding regular events, from street parties to volunteering schemes, which give residents a shared purpose. Technology, too, can be turned to advantage; neighbourhood apps that allow people to borrow items or offer help frequently lead to offline friendships. Longer tenancy agreements would also help, giving renters the stability needed to put down roots.

In conclusion, city dwellers remain strangers because of demanding schedules, frequent relocation, isolating architecture and online distractions. Thoughtful urban design, community events and local digital networks, supported by more secure housing, can go a long way towards restoring neighbourly ties.

items.title: Choosing self-employment
items.prompt:
Some people choose to work for themselves rather than for an employer. Why do they make this choice? What qualities are needed to be successful when working for yourself?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

modelAnswer.text:
For a growing share of the workforce, the security of a regular salary is no longer enough to outweigh the appeal of being one's own boss. People are drawn to self-employment for a mixture of personal and financial reasons, but turning that choice into a sustainable livelihood requires a demanding combination of character traits.

Autonomy lies at the heart of most decisions to go it alone. Working for an employer typically means accepting fixed hours, predetermined tasks and the judgement of a line manager, whereas independent workers can shape their own schedules and choose projects that genuinely interest them. For a parent who wants to be present at the school gate, or someone who does their best work late at night, this freedom can be transformative. There is also the prospect of greater reward: rather than seeing the benefits of their efforts absorbed by a company, the self-employed keep what they earn, and a thriving business may eventually generate far more than a salary ever would. Technology has made the leap less daunting, as online platforms allow even a single freelancer to reach clients around the world.

Yet freedom brings its own pressures, and certain qualities distinguish those who thrive from those who struggle. Self-motivation is paramount; without external deadlines or supervision, procrastination can quietly undermine a promising venture. Equally vital is resilience, since irregular income, demanding clients and unsuccessful pitches are an inevitable part of independent work. Successful freelancers also tend to be versatile, combining expertise in their field with the ability to market themselves, negotiate fees and manage finances. Finally, a degree of tolerance for risk is essential, as there is no guaranteed income at the end of each month.

In conclusion, people become self-employed chiefly to gain autonomy and to benefit directly from their own work. Achieving lasting success, however, depends on self-motivation, resilience, versatility and a willingness to live with uncertainty.

items.title: Advertising and manufactured desire
items.prompt:
Advertisements often try to persuade people that they need products they did not previously want. How do advertisers achieve this? Should anything be done to control it?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

modelAnswer.text:
Much of modern advertising is not designed to meet existing demand but to manufacture it, persuading consumers that a product they had never heard of is suddenly indispensable. The techniques involved have become increasingly sophisticated, and in my view they warrant a degree of regulation, although not an outright ban.

At the core of most campaigns lies emotional association. Advertisers rarely sell objects on their practical merits; instead they sell the feelings and identities attached to them. A pair of trainers becomes a symbol of athletic success, while a luxury handbag is presented as evidence of sophistication. By repeatedly pairing a product with images of happiness, attractiveness or status, advertisers create a sense that ownership will deliver these qualities. A related tactic is the creation of dissatisfaction. Cosmetic and technology companies in particular are adept at convincing consumers that what they already own is inadequate, so that a perfectly functional phone begins to feel embarrassing the moment a new model is launched. Digital platforms have intensified these methods, allowing firms to target individuals with personalised messages and to reach them through influencers whose endorsements feel like the advice of a friend.

Some control over these practices seems reasonable. Children, who are especially susceptible to persuasion, deserve particular protection, and restrictions on advertising during children's programming or on apps aimed at them would be a sensible starting point. Clear disclosure rules for sponsored content would help adults recognise when they are being marketed to, and stricter limits on the collection of personal data would curb the most intrusive forms of targeting. However, advertising also finances free media and enables smaller companies to compete, so heavy-handed prohibition would do more harm than good.

In conclusion, advertisers generate new desires by attaching emotional meaning to products, fostering dissatisfaction and exploiting personal data. Targeted regulation, focusing on children, transparency and privacy, would limit manipulation while preserving the legitimate benefits of advertising.

items.title: Barriers to healthy eating
items.prompt:
Many people find it difficult to eat a healthy diet, even when they know which foods are good for them. Why is this? Who should be responsible for helping people to eat more healthily?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

modelAnswer.text:
It is one of the curiosities of modern life that people can recite the benefits of vegetables and the dangers of sugar, yet still reach for a takeaway at the end of the day. The reasons lie less in ignorance than in the circumstances in which food choices are made, and for this reason I believe responsibility for improving diets must be shared, with governments playing the leading role.

Time pressure is a fundamental obstacle. For people working long hours or juggling several jobs, preparing a balanced meal from scratch can feel like an unrealistic demand, whereas ready meals and fast food require no effort at all. Price reinforces this pattern: calorie for calorie, processed food is often cheaper than fresh produce, so households on tight budgets may have little real choice. Perhaps most importantly, the food environment itself works against good intentions. Products high in sugar, salt and fat are engineered to be highly palatable, promoted relentlessly and positioned prominently in shops, which means that choosing the healthy option requires constant willpower. Knowledge, in other words, is rarely a match for convenience, cost and temptation combined.

Given these pressures, it would be unrealistic to expect individuals to solve the problem alone. Governments are best placed to reshape the environment in which choices are made, whether through taxes on sugary drinks, subsidies for fresh produce, restrictions on junk-food advertising or clear front-of-pack labelling. Food manufacturers should also be held accountable, for instance through targets to reduce harmful ingredients. Schools have a role in teaching cooking and providing nutritious meals, thereby shaping habits early. Individuals, of course, retain ultimate control over what they eat, but personal responsibility is far easier to exercise when the healthy choice is also the easy one.

In conclusion, poor diets persist because of time pressure, cost and a food environment designed to tempt. While individuals must play their part, governments, supported by industry and schools, should take the lead in making healthy eating affordable and convenient.

items.title: Young people and voting
items.prompt:
In many countries, young people are less likely to vote in elections than older people. Why might this be the case? What are the consequences of this for society?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

modelAnswer.text:
In many democracies, a striking generational divide exists at the ballot box, with people in their late teens and twenties voting at markedly lower rates than their parents and grandparents. This gap can be traced to disillusionment, limited political education and practical barriers, and its consequences extend well beyond young people themselves.

Perhaps the most significant factor is a perception that politics is not designed for them. Young voters frequently see parliaments dominated by older figures and debates that seem remote from their immediate concerns, such as unaffordable rents or insecure employment. When the connection between casting a vote and improving one's own life appears weak, abstaining can seem a rational response rather than mere apathy. This detachment is reinforced by inadequate civic education; many school leavers have little understanding of how government works or how party programmes differ, and uncertainty easily turns into disengagement. Practical obstacles add a further layer. Young adults change address frequently for study or work, and cumbersome registration procedures can mean that they are unable to vote even if they wish to.

The consequences for society are considerable. Politicians seeking re-election rationally direct their attention towards the groups most likely to turn out, which can result in policies that protect pensions and property values while underinvesting in education, affordable housing and long-term environmental measures. items.title: Children and possessions
items.prompt:
Many children today own more toys and possessions than children in the past. Why is this? How does this affect their development?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

modelAnswer.text:
A glance into many modern children's bedrooms reveals shelves crowded with toys, games and electronic devices on a scale that would have astonished earlier generations. This abundance is largely a product of economic and social change, and while it is not wholly harmful, I believe it often works against the qualities that children most need to develop.

Several forces lie behind this shift. Greater affluence and the global manufacturing of inexpensive goods mean that toys which were once special treats are now everyday purchases. Demographic change has amplified the effect: with fewer children per family, and often several grandparents eager to give presents, gifts that were once shared among siblings are now lavished on one or two children. Marketing, meanwhile, has become more direct and persistent. Children encounter advertising through online videos and games as well as television, and the constant release of new models and collectable ranges fuels a sense that what they have is never quite enough. Some parents, pressed for time, may also use gifts as a substitute for attention.

The developmental consequences depend partly on what children own, but quantity matters. Well-chosen toys such as building sets, art materials and books can foster creativity, concentration and fine motor skills. Yet when possessions are plentiful, each one tends to be valued less, and children may flit between them without the sustained engagement that deep play requires. A child with a cardboard box and a few figures is often forced to invent entire worlds, whereas one surrounded by ready-made entertainment has less need for imagination. There is also a risk that a steady stream of new items teaches children to seek satisfaction through acquisition, making patience, gratitude and the ability to cope with disappointment harder to learn.

In conclusion, children own more because of rising wealth, smaller families and relentless marketing. Although some possessions can enrich development, an excess tends to weaken imagination and encourage materialistic habits, so fewer, better-chosen items are generally preferable.

items.title: Preventing teenage crime
items.prompt:
In some areas, crime committed by teenagers is a growing concern. Why do some young people become involved in crime? What role should schools play in preventing this?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

modelAnswer.text:
Teenage crime attracts considerable public attention, and in some areas it appears to be rising. Although there is no single explanation for why young people offend, the most common causes are social rather than individual, and schools, where adolescents spend much of their time, are in a strong position to help prevent it.

The family environment is frequently the starting point. Young people who grow up with little supervision, or amid conflict and instability, may lack both the guidance and the emotional security that discourage risky behaviour. In such circumstances, the pull of peers becomes especially powerful. Adolescence is a stage at which acceptance by one's group matters intensely, and where that group treats theft or violence as a badge of status, the pressure to participate can be difficult to resist. Poverty and a lack of opportunity compound these influences: in neighbourhoods where jobs are scarce and youth facilities have closed, crime may seem to offer money, excitement and respect that are unattainable by legitimate means.

Schools can respond to each of these pressures. With the most regular contact with young people of any institution, they are ideally placed to identify early warning signs, such as truancy, declining grades or abrupt changes in behaviour, and to connect vulnerable students with counselling before problems escalate. They can also offer the sense of belonging that some teenagers seek elsewhere, through sports teams, creative projects and mentoring by trusted adults. Perhaps most importantly, schools should work hard to keep struggling pupils in education rather than resorting quickly to exclusion, since those who drop out are left with time on their hands and diminished prospects. Nevertheless, schools cannot compensate entirely for problems at home, and their efforts are most effective when coordinated with families and local services.

In conclusion, youth crime is driven largely by family instability, peer pressure and lack of opportunity. Schools can make a significant contribution through early identification, positive activities and inclusive policies, but only as part of a broader, coordinated approach.

items.title: News and echo chambers
items.prompt:
Many people choose to read or watch only news that supports opinions they already hold. Why do people do this? What effects does this have on society?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

modelAnswer.text:
The modern media landscape offers an almost unlimited choice of news sources, yet many people use this freedom to confine themselves to outlets that echo what they already believe. This behaviour has deep psychological roots and is reinforced by technology, and its effects on society are, in my view, predominantly damaging.

At the most basic level, people seek out confirming information because it is reassuring. Having one's views validated produces a sense of certainty and belonging, whereas encountering strong counter-arguments can be unsettling and may even feel like a personal attack. This natural bias is amplified by the design of digital platforms. Recommendation algorithms are optimised for engagement, and since users tend to click on content that aligns with their views, they are fed a steady diet of similar material until alternative perspectives effectively disappear from their screens. Commercial incentives play a role as well: news organisations have discovered that cultivating a loyal audience with a distinct ideological identity can be more profitable than attempting to appeal to everyone.

The social consequences are significant. When citizens inhabit separate informational worlds, they lose not only a shared set of opinions but also a shared set of facts, which makes productive debate extremely difficult. Views tend to harden, since they are rarely tested against opposing evidence, and people increasingly regard those who disagree not as fellow citizens with different priorities but as ignorant or malicious. This polarisation can paralyse decision-making on complex issues that require compromise. Furthermore, echo chambers provide fertile ground for misinformation, because claims that flatter a group's assumptions are shared eagerly and seldom checked.

In conclusion, selective news consumption stems from a desire for reassurance, reinforced by algorithms and commercial strategy. Its effects, including polarisation, the erosion of common ground and the spread of falsehoods, pose a real threat to healthy public discourse.

items.title: Engaging with local history
items.prompt:
Many people enjoy learning about the history of the place where they live. Why is this? How can local history be made more interesting for young people?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

modelAnswer.text:
For many people, the history of their own town or region holds an appeal that grand narratives of empires and wars cannot match. This enthusiasm stems largely from the personal and tangible nature of local history, and although young people are often less engaged, there are effective ways of bringing the subject to life for them.

The most fundamental reason is that local history helps people understand who they are. Learning why a village grew up around a particular crossroads, or how a factory once sustained an entire neighbourhood, gives residents a sense of continuity that can be especially valuable in a rapidly changing world. Local history is also immediate in a way that national history rarely is. The evidence is visible in everyday surroundings, from the architecture of the high street to the names of lanes and pubs, so each discovery transforms a familiar route into something richer. Finally, it often intersects with family history; parish records or old photographs may reveal where one's great-grandparents worked or worshipped, creating a direct emotional link with the past.

Engaging young people requires moving away from passive learning. Rather than being presented with dates and summaries, students could act as historians themselves, interviewing elderly residents, examining old maps or investigating the history of their own school. Such projects give them ownership of their findings and reveal that history is made up of real people's lives. Digital technology offers further possibilities: augmented reality apps can overlay historical images onto present-day streets, and short video formats allow students to share what they have uncovered in a style that appeals to their peers. Local museums, too, can attract younger audiences with interactive exhibitions rather than static displays.

In conclusion, local history resonates with people because it strengthens identity, gives meaning to familiar places and connects them with their ancestors. By encouraging active investigation and embracing digital media, schools and museums can make it equally compelling for the young.

items.title: Travelling for the photograph
items.prompt:
Many tourists now visit places mainly to take photographs to share online. Why is this happening? How does it change the experience of travelling?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

modelAnswer.text:
At many famous landmarks, it is now common to see visitors queuing not to enter a building or admire a view, but to reproduce a photograph they have already seen online. This trend reflects the central role of social media in modern life, and it is subtly changing what it means to travel.

The underlying cause is the way image-sharing platforms have turned travel into a form of self-presentation. A holiday was once a private experience, recounted afterwards to a few friends; today it can be broadcast in real time to hundreds of followers, and the approval this generates offers a powerful incentive to seek out striking backdrops. Influencers amplify the effect by popularising particular viewpoints, which then become obligatory stops for their audiences. The tourism industry has been quick to capitalise on this, designing hotels, cafés and attractions with photogenic features precisely because every shared image serves as free promotion. Ubiquitous smartphone cameras, of course, have removed any practical limit on how many pictures can be taken.

The consequences for the experience of travelling are considerable. When the primary goal is to capture an image, attention shifts from the place itself to how it will appear to others, and the unplanned encounters and quiet observation that once defined travel can be crowded out. Itineraries also become more uniform, as visitors converge on the same well-known spots while neighbourhoods without an obvious visual hook are ignored. For residents of popular destinations, this concentration brings congestion, while visitors may arrive only to find a place swamped by others with the same idea. That said, photography can still enrich travel when it encourages people to look closely and preserve meaningful memories rather than simply to accumulate evidence of having been somewhere.

In conclusion, photo-driven tourism has grown out of social media culture, industry marketing and constant access to cameras. While it need not be harmful, it risks turning travel from an act of discovery into a performance staged for an online audience.

items.title: Rebuilding trust in science
items.prompt:
In some countries, public trust in scientists and experts appears to be declining. Why might this be happening? How could this trust be rebuilt?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

modelAnswer.text:
In several countries, the authority once enjoyed by scientists and other experts appears to be weakening, with some people openly dismissing expert advice on matters ranging from medicine to climate. This decline has multiple causes, some rooted in technology and others in the conduct of experts themselves, and restoring trust will require changes on both sides.

The transformation of the information environment is a central factor. Online platforms allow unverified claims to circulate as widely as peer-reviewed findings, and content that is dramatic or emotionally charged typically travels further than cautious, qualified explanations. In this crowded space, genuine expertise can appear to be merely one opinion among many. A second factor is a widespread misunderstanding of how science works. Scientific knowledge is provisional by nature, so advice is revised as evidence accumulates; however, to those who expect definitive answers, such revisions can look like confusion or deception. Finally, trust has been eroded by perceptions of bias. When experts are seen to be closely aligned with governments, or when research is funded by industries with a financial stake in the outcome, it is easy to suspect that conclusions have been shaped by interests rather than evidence.

Rebuilding confidence must therefore begin with openness. Scientists and public bodies should explain not only what they recommend but why, and be candid about uncertainty rather than projecting a false certainty that later has to be withdrawn. Full disclosure of funding sources would go some way towards addressing suspicions of hidden agendas. Experts also need to engage with communities directly, through local events and accessible media, rather than communicating solely through official statements. In the longer term, education has a vital role: teaching young people how evidence is gathered and assessed would equip them to distinguish credible research from persuasive misinformation.

In conclusion, trust in experts is being undermined by an unregulated information environment, misconceptions about scientific uncertainty and suspicions of bias. Greater transparency, honest communication and stronger scientific literacy offer the best prospect of restoring it.

items.title: Technology and free time
items.prompt:
Although modern technology saves time on many everyday tasks, many people feel they have less free time than ever. Why is this? What can be done to help people have more free time?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

modelAnswer.text:
Technology has spared people countless hours of domestic drudgery and administrative effort, yet complaints about a lack of time have never been more common. This apparent contradiction can be explained by the way the time saved is reabsorbed by work and digital distraction, and reclaiming leisure will require action from employers, governments and individuals alike.

The first explanation lies in the erosion of boundaries between work and private life. Devices that make it possible to work from anywhere also make it possible to be contacted everywhere, and in many workplaces an unspoken expectation has developed that emails will be answered promptly, whatever the hour. As a result, even time spent at home is frequently interrupted by professional demands. Secondly, efficiency tends to raise expectations rather than reduce effort: when a task can be completed in half the time, the typical response is to take on more tasks, not to rest. Finally, much of the time technology frees is quietly consumed by technology itself. Social media feeds and streaming platforms are deliberately designed to be absorbing, and hours spent on them rarely feel like genuine leisure, leaving people both occupied and unrefreshed.

Addressing the problem requires structural as well as personal change. Employers could make it clear that staff are not required to respond outside working hours, and legislation guaranteeing a right to disconnect would give such policies greater force. Shorter working weeks, where output can be maintained, would allow productivity gains to be shared with workers as additional free time rather than extra workload. Individuals, too, can reclaim hours by curbing their use of attention-grabbing apps, disabling notifications and deliberately protecting periods of the day for rest, hobbies or social contact.

In conclusion, people feel short of time because technology has extended the reach of work, raised expectations and created new distractions. Firmer boundaries set by employers and governments, combined with more deliberate personal habits, would allow the time saved by technology to become genuine free time.

Firmer boundaries set by employers and governments, combined with more deliberate personal habits, would allow the time saved by technology to become genuine free time.

items.title: The rise of living alone
items.prompt:
More and more people are choosing to live alone. Why is this happening? What effects does this trend have on society?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

modelAnswer.text:
Living alone, once associated mainly with widowhood or unusual circumstances, has become a mainstream choice in many societies. This shift reflects profound changes in values, economics and demography, and while it brings certain benefits, its wider effects on society are, on balance, a cause for concern.

Changing social norms are a key driver. Marriage now tends to occur later, if at all, and living independently is widely regarded as a desirable marker of adulthood rather than a temporary stage before settling down. Greater prosperity has enabled people to act on this preference, since many can afford a home of their own. Demographic trends reinforce the pattern: as life expectancy rises, a growing number of older people outlive their partners and choose to remain in familiar surroundings rather than move in with their children. Increased mobility plays a part as well, with people relocating for work to cities where they have no family ties.

The consequences are varied. Economically, single-person households have stimulated demand for compact apartments, convenience products and services tailored to individuals, and living alone allows people to pursue careers and interests with considerable freedom. However, because more dwellings are needed to house the same population, the trend places heavy strain on housing supply and contributes to rising rents in already crowded cities. It also has environmental implications, as people living alone typically consume more energy and space per person. Most significantly, it can foster isolation. Many who live alone lead rich social lives, but for others, particularly the elderly, solitude can turn into loneliness, with damaging effects on wellbeing. As traditional family networks thin out, the responsibility for care increasingly falls on public services.

In conclusion, the rise in solo living stems from evolving attitudes, economic independence, longer lifespans and mobility. Although it offers autonomy and new economic opportunities, its impact on housing, resources and social connection means that societies need to plan for its consequences.

items.title: Global brands and local culture
items.prompt:
International brands and fast-food chains can now be found in almost every country in the world. Why has this happened? How does it affect local businesses and culture?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

modelAnswer.text:
From burger chains to coffee houses and sportswear labels, a handful of international brands have established a presence in almost every country on earth. Their spread is the product of economic liberalisation and global media, and its effects on local enterprises and cultural identity are, in my view, more harmful than beneficial, although not uniformly so.

The expansion has been driven above all by the opening of national markets. As governments have lowered trade barriers and actively courted foreign investment, multinational corporations have found it increasingly straightforward to establish outlets abroad, often through franchising arrangements that limit their financial risk. Advances in logistics mean that products can be sourced and distributed across continents with remarkable efficiency. Equally important is cultural reach. Films, television and social media have familiarised audiences everywhere with the same logos, and for many consumers, particularly the young, these brands carry an aura of modernity and cosmopolitan status long before a branch opens nearby.

For local businesses, the arrival of a global chain can be devastating. Such companies enjoy economies of scale, sophisticated marketing and the ability to absorb initial losses, advantages that independent restaurants and shops simply cannot match. Where these smaller enterprises close, profits that once circulated within the community are instead transferred abroad. The cultural consequences are subtler but equally significant. As international menus and products become the norm, traditional cuisine and crafts may come to seem old-fashioned, and town centres across the world grow increasingly indistinguishable. Nevertheless, the picture is not entirely bleak: multinationals provide employment and training, many adapt their offerings to local tastes, and competition can prompt local firms to differentiate themselves by emphasising authenticity.

In conclusion, global brands have proliferated because of open markets, efficient supply chains and the influence of global media. Although they bring jobs and some healthy competition, they frequently undermine independent businesses and erode the cultural distinctiveness that makes places unique.

items.title: Foreign aid that works
items.prompt:
Wealthy countries often give financial aid to poorer countries. Why do they do this? What kind of help do you think is most effective in the long term?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

modelAnswer.text:
Financial aid from wealthy to poorer nations is a long-established feature of international relations, yet the reasons behind it are rarely purely altruistic, and the forms it takes vary greatly in their lasting impact. In my view, aid that strengthens a country's own capacity to generate wealth and provide services is by far the most effective over time.

The motives of donor countries are typically a blend of principle and self-interest. On a moral level, there is a widely shared sense that prosperous nations have an obligation to relieve suffering, particularly in the aftermath of disasters or during famines. At the same time, aid serves diplomatic ends. Supporting a developing country can secure its goodwill, strengthen alliances and extend a donor's influence in regions of strategic importance. Economic calculation also plays a role: a more prosperous partner becomes a larger market for exports and a more stable place to invest, and some aid is explicitly tied to contracts for the donor's own firms. Lastly, since epidemics and instability rarely respect borders, reducing poverty abroad can serve donors' own security.

When it comes to long-term effectiveness, the crucial distinction is between assistance that meets immediate needs and assistance that builds lasting capability. Emergency relief is indispensable in a crisis, but sustained cash transfers to governments risk fostering dependency and can be diverted by corruption. Investment in education, by contrast, pays dividends for generations, while support for primary healthcare raises productivity as well as wellbeing. Infrastructure such as reliable electricity, roads and irrigation enables farmers and entrepreneurs to expand, creating employment that no donation could sustain. These projects are most successful when shaped by local communities, which ensures that they reflect genuine priorities and continue once foreign involvement ends.

In conclusion, wealthy countries give aid out of a mixture of compassion, diplomacy and economic interest. The most effective long-term help is not money alone but investment in the education, health and infrastructure that allow poorer nations to prosper independently.

items.title: Young people and saving
items.prompt:
Many young people today find it difficult to save money. Why is this? What could encourage young people to save more?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

modelAnswer.text:
For many young adults, building up savings now feels like an unattainable goal. The explanation lies partly in economic conditions beyond their control and partly in a consumer environment that makes spending effortless, but there are practical ways in which saving could be made both easier and more appealing.

Structural pressures are the most obvious obstacle. Housing costs in many cities have far outpaced wages, so rent alone can absorb a substantial share of a young worker's income, and entry-level jobs are increasingly insecure or poorly paid. Loan repayments for education leave even less room for anything else. These constraints are compounded by the culture in which young people live. Social media presents a constant stream of holidays, restaurants and new products, making modest living feel like missing out, while frictionless digital payments and instalment schemes disguise the true cost of purchases. Furthermore, many young adults leave school without ever having been taught to budget, so even those with some spare income may lack the habits needed to retain it.

Encouraging saving therefore requires a combination of education, design and incentives. Personal finance should be taught in schools as a practical skill, covering budgeting, interest and the dangers of high-cost credit, so that good habits are formed before the first salary arrives. Financial technology can also be harnessed for positive ends: automatic transfers on payday and apps that round up transactions into savings make putting money aside the default rather than an act of willpower. Governments could strengthen motivation by offering bonuses or tax advantages on savings for specific goals, such as a first home, and tighter regulation of instalment schemes would make the cost of borrowing more transparent.

In conclusion, young people struggle to save because of high living costs, insecure work and a culture that encourages consumption. By teaching financial skills early, designing tools that make saving automatic and offering meaningful incentives, society could help them build greater financial security.

items.title: Studying at foreign universities
items.prompt:
More and more students are choosing to study at universities in other countries. Is this a positive or negative development?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

modelAnswer.text:
The number of students enrolling at universities outside their home countries has risen steadily in recent decades. Although this movement of young people is not without costs, I would argue that it is a predominantly positive development, both for the students themselves and for the wider world.

For individual students, the advantages are considerable. Studying abroad often provides access to specialised programmes, well-funded laboratories and academics at the forefront of their fields, resources that may be scarce at home. Equally valuable is the experience of living independently in an unfamiliar society. Navigating a new education system, managing a budget and building friendships across cultural and linguistic boundaries cultivate a degree of resilience that few domestic degrees can match.

The benefits also extend beyond the individual. International campuses bring together people who might otherwise never meet, and the professional networks formed there can later underpin cooperation between businesses, research institutions and even governments. When graduates return home, they frequently bring new expertise and fresh perspectives with them, which can stimulate innovation in sectors ranging from healthcare to engineering.

It would be naive, however, to ignore the drawbacks. The so-called brain drain is a genuine concern, as a proportion of graduates settle permanently abroad, depriving their home countries of skills that are badly needed. Furthermore, the considerable expense involved means that overseas study remains largely the preserve of affluent families. Yet these problems stem less from international study itself than from limited opportunities for graduates at home and insufficient financial support, both of which governments can address through targeted scholarships and incentives to return.

In conclusion, while the loss of talent and unequal access are legitimate concerns, the academic, personal and societal gains of studying abroad clearly outweigh them. This is, therefore, a trend to be welcomed rather than feared.
